title: Comp table marks are words, and the type chip names the real count
details: Residential reports showed gray † ‡ § next to Size and $/SF; the section mark next to a dollar figure read as a second $. Those are now calc / size / adj with a legend. The chip beside the property type is the table's own comp count, so a bare 5 can no longer sit next to Residential while the map holds 8.

title: Map pin photos show the building from the street when the camera is actually there
details: Aerial still paints on hover so the popup stays snappy. Street View overlays it only when a camera sits within 35 m of the snapped building and is aimed at it. A fence, a neighbor, or the street in front of a warehouse 404s and the roof stays. The Google round-trip is billed only for the pin you hover, not for the whole map.

title: Pasting an address no longer turns the field blue
details: Chrome paints a light-blue autofill sheet when it recognises a pasted street address, and the existing cover only ran in dark mode, so the desk address field went blue on a white card. An inset shadow in the card colour now covers it in light too, including the focus state Chrome restyles after the paste.

title: Focus and Lookback show one chevron in dark mode
details: The desk selects restored the native arrow after a background shorthand wiped the site chevron, so dark mode stacked three or four arrows on Focus and Lookback. They now keep the one SVG. The pointer row under the desk used a gap class that was never in the vendored CSS, so the middle dot overlapped For brokers.

title: The search desk's corners follow the card again
details: Straightening the title hairline put a square white header on the market chamber. The desk cannot overflow:hidden (that clips the explorer dropdown), so the square fill poked past the 6px card at the top-right. The heads now carry the radius themselves; stacked on a phone, both top corners sit on the building head and the market head stays square.

title: Map pin photos are the roof, and hover is snappy
details: Hovering a comp pin waited 120ms, faded the popup in, then fetched Street View through our proxy — often a fence, parking lot, or the building next door, half a second late. Moving off waited another 320ms plus Leaflet's fade. Popups now show the aerial close-up of the snapped building (Esri tiles, prefetched after the footprint lands). Open is 60ms, close is 80ms, no fade.

title: The line between Value a building and Or read a market is straight
details: The two chamber titles now sit on one shared hairline, same padding and line-height on both sides, so the rule runs straight across the split instead of stopping under the building form. The hidden property-type select also moved out of the address row: a sibling there kept the address cell from matching :last-child, so that row painted a second right border on top of the desk divider and the vertical line jogged for the length of the address field.

title: A comp hub no longer sells anything to the client reading it
details: A client opening their broker hub was shown Pricing in the header, and once signed in a free account also got an Upgrade to Pro button in its account menu. That is a pitch aimed at somebody else guest, inside a workspace the broker owns, and it is exactly what the hub design ruled out: the client side is free forever and carries no upgrade prompt. Hubs now show nothing about Pro. Every other page is unchanged. Nothing about what a client can DO changed: they never had the vault or any paid feature, and a client who wants to buy can still reach pricing everywhere else.

title: A hub page has a way back to the app, and its Post note button is readable
details: Two faults from a real client using a real hub. The page was built with a flag that strips both the My Desk and Sign in links from the header, copied from a page that renders its own; the hub renders neither, so a client who left the hub could not find it again and had nothing to click when told to sign in. Both links are back, and a hub a client belongs to already lists on My Desk under Comp hubs. Separately the Post note button styled its label with a colour variable that does not exist, so the declaration was invalid and the text fell back to the same colour as the button, leaving a blank rectangle. Every colour the page uses is now checked against the ones the theme really defines.

title: An account can have a profile photo
details: The account circle was an initial. Signed-in members can now add a photo from My Desk (or Change photo in the account menu): it replaces the initial in the app header, on every server-rendered page, and on the desk itself. Stored as a data URI like a branding logo, but off the users row so the session lookup never pulls the bytes; a short content hash on the account tells the circle to fetch GET /api/account/avatar. PNG or JPEG, square-cropped in the browser, sniffed on the way in so a URL or an SVG cannot be stored. Remove clears it. Not Pro-gated.

title: A hub tells a client to sign in and now gives them a way to
details: Opening a real invite link showed the dead end: the page said sign in with the address this hub was shared with, and there was nothing on it to click. The note box that carries the account prompt is hidden from exactly the people that line is written for, and the header sign-in links do not render on this page. So a client could read their broker comps, go to reply, and stop. The line now carries a Sign in or create an account link. A closed hub still says only that it is closed, because signing in cannot reopen it.

title: The proof line no longer says up to 12 comps
details: Nearby saved deals join the table, so a city report can carry far more than the search ask. The desk and the landing both dropped the cap. They still say cited comps, about a minute, every source disclosed.

title: Dark mode reads more clearly, and leftover light chrome is gone
details: Labels on charcoal were sitting at the contrast floor on cards and failing it on slabs. The ink ramp lifts a notch so body copy and workhorse muted text clear AA, without moving the paper or card floor. The toggle now shows a sun once you are in dark, Chrome autofill no longer paints a cream sheet over the field, select chevrons and menus pick up the same card lift, and the form focus ring follows --red so it is visible on a dark cell.

title: A house comps table is compact, and tenancy is gone
details: Residential reports showed CRE tenancy (often empty, sometimes a long NNN string) as a wide canyon before Year Built, and the first handful of rows sat taller than the rest because notes restated beds and year built and wrapped. The house table no longer carries tenancy. Notes stay on one line. Row padding is the same compact height for every row. The prompt stopped asking for house tenancy and stopped dumping beds and year into notes.

title: Sending vault comps into a hub works
details: Every attempt to send a comp from the vault into a hub failed with a generic error. The insert asked Postgres to ignore duplicates against an index that only covers live rows, and Postgres will not match a partial index that way, so the whole send was refused. Duplicates are now filtered before the insert instead: sending the same comp twice is still a no-op, and a comp that was removed can still be re-sent, which is how a corrected price reaches a client. Found by sending a real comp into a real hub.

title: The broker introduction band no longer pitches a signed-in member
details: The band that offers a free opinion of value on a covered market page was written before the call to action below it split into signed-in and anonymous variants, so the two would have stacked: a member on a market with a covering broker would be sold an introduction at the top of the page and offered a CSV of the same comps at the bottom. The band speaks to a property owner arriving from a search engine, so it is anonymous-only now, which is the same line the call to action already draws. It renders on no market today, since no broker has opted into being listed, so nobody saw either version.

title: Vault row delete is a trash icon
details: The red Delete word next to Publish was a second shout on the row. Compact table and spreadsheet now share a quiet trash button: ink until hover, same as removing an import. The confirm still names the action.

title: A house number glued to the street still gets a value
details: The Low / Likely / High hero hid itself unless the address had a space after the street number, so it could skip city-only searches like Boise ID. People type 1210N17th st. That failed the space check, the whole What This Home Is Worth block stayed hidden, and a Residential report with 38 sale comps looked like it had no estimate. The hero now uses the same houseNumberOf helper as the type detector, which already reads a leading run of digits, glued or not. Boise ID and One Wilshire Blvd still skip the hero unless the visitor typed a size or price.

title: An uploaded vault spreadsheet opens in CompNinja
details: After a CSV or PDF import, the vault can open that book as a grid — Open spreadsheet on the comps table, or Open on the import itself. Each cell is an input; leaving it PATCHes that one field through the same route and parsers as the compact Edit form, so a 1.2M still fails instead of storing 1.2. Tab and Enter move like a spreadsheet. A published comp still retracts. The compact Edit form stays for a single-row change.

title: Dark mode chips, inner tiles, and the map follow the charcoal page
details: Estimate and vault badges had no dark pair, so they sat as cream pills; they now have --est-* and --bv-* that keep sienna and purple instead of borrowing the listing or verified tokens. Inner tiles and the Likely ledger cell use --wash-2, which is a no-op in light and a second step in dark. The Carto dark_all basemap is still the provider — a tile-pane filter lifts it toward the page, and Street View and aerials are not in that pane. The Likely tile keeps a red label and drops the full red border, so the accent is a mark not a box.

title: Dark mode cards sit above the page
details: The August 13 lift already raised the floor off near-black. What still read as one charcoal slab was paper, card, and wash sitting too close, with no step between them. Cards now take a dark-only --lift: a 1px inset highlight plus a short drop. In light mode --lift is none, so nothing moves. Print and PNG still strip shadows. Native form controls follow the page via color-scheme. Public-record badges and the hero scatter ticks pick up tokens in dark instead of sitting as cream pills.

title: A house report now reads as a house report
details: Zillow is more useful for residential because it is a listing portal. CompNinja cannot be that, and should not try: no MLS, no listing photos, no homes-for-sale browse. What it can be is the cited fair-price check for a house someone already found. A Residential search no longer opens as a commercial real estate analyst write-up with LoopNet/Crexi lane copy. The model is told to match bedroom count as well as neighborhood and vintage. The comparison card is list price vs Low/Likely/High whenever the listing (or a typed ask) exists, and no longer waits for a Refine size. Year built sits under the hero with last sale and ask. The Analysis tab and its NOI/DCF toolkit stay behind Details until someone types an NOI, so investment SFR still works and a house shopper does not land on hold-or-sell. The size field says Living area. The CTA says Talk to a local agent; the lead is still source bov and we still connect you with a licensed local broker, never claiming to be one.

title: Nearby sales pull the value more than sales across town
details: Distance used to be a table column the map filled in after the pins settled, and the Low / Likely / High treated a next-door sale the same as one nine miles away. It is now a fifth compWeight factor: a free pass inside a mile, then a 4-mile half-life, missing distance still neutral so an unplaced search comp is not punished. The mile figure rides locked_basis (never lat/lng) so a free report's range stays in step with Pro. Saved radius deals stamp it at blend time; comps that already have coordinates get it just before the paywall; once the map geocodes the rest, the hero re-runs.

title: A comp hub now has a shortlist, notes on each building, and comps the client adds
details: Hubs shipped as a way to send comps to a client. They are now somewhere the two of you work. Every comp carries where it stands (not decided, shortlisted, toured, passed) and the CLIENT can move it, because a shortlist only the broker can change records what the broker hopes rather than what the client decided. One line above the table says where the requirement stands, counting only what somebody actually decided. Notes can be filed against a single building and read under that building rather than in one stream, which is the thing an email thread cannot do. A client can add a building they found themselves: it is marked as theirs, never wears the broker badge, and is refused in the vault importer's own words if a price is written as 1.2M rather than 1200000. Two people in a hub at the same time now see each other's comps and decisions without reloading, and a half-typed note survives the other person's activity.

title: The brokers page is two ledgers, not two cards
details: What you get for submitting comps and Pro: the Broker Vault sat as peer bullet cards, so the page still read as a feature list after How it works had already drawn those trades as a statement. They are now two stacked hairline ledgers — Contribute (Credit with the Verified chip, Intros, Profile) then With Pro (Book, Pipeline, Private) — so the vault does not look like it comes with a submitted comp. The one Submit button, the 1031 card, and the compliance line are unchanged.

title: Saved deals within 10 miles join the next report
details: Every search already stored its priced comps, but a later search in the same area only reused them if the model picked them or the visitor clicked Add. Saved deals of the same property type, inside the lookback, with coordinates, and within 10 miles of the subject now fold into the report at serialization so they hit the table and the Low / Likely / High math. A free report turns extras into locked_basis, same as extra search comps. Harvest geocodes new rows before writing them; a deal with no point is skipped rather than guessed as same-city. Cache and market snapshots stay search-only, so a later nearby search still picks up deals saved after the cache write. CORPUS_RADIUS=off restores search-only reports. Vault rows are never read.

title: A signed-in search lands in Portfolio on its own
details: Free and Pro alike keep every report they run, on any device, without pressing Save. The same address updates the existing row and appends a value snapshot. Free My Desk is an address list; Pro keeps the likely-value ledger and sparklines, and upgrading reveals history Free already stored. Caps are 100 and 500, enforced on insert only. The Save button remains as a retry when the auto-save fails or the list is full. The $20 unlock is unchanged.

title: What brokers get is a ledger, not a leftover paragraph
details: The landing's Brokers block had collapsed to one paragraph that named Private, Credit, and Leads in a single breath, so it still read as Method's leftover. Those are trades, not steps: they now sit as hairline rows with the real Verified · via Your Firm chip on Credit, the same chip the sample report already shows. Method keeps its 3-up. Copy pins (privacy sentence, firm name, /brokers link) are unchanged.

title: Tab fills the example address
details: The search box's rotating e.g. placeholder used to be display-only: Tab jumped to the next field and left the box empty. Tab on an empty address field now types in the current example, without the e.g. prefix, so a visitor can try a real building without inventing one. A second Tab moves on because the field is no longer empty; Shift+Tab is still back. The same shortcut sits on the shared-report lock field. A placeholder that is not an example is never a fill.

title: The signed-in search page is one Research Desk
details: The report form and Market Explorer used to sit as two products on the same page, with a stale 3-6 cited comps line under them. They are now one bordered desk with two chambers: Value a building (the existing form, ids unchanged) and Or read a market. The explorer is a sibling of the form, not a child, so typing a market and hitting Enter cannot submit a building report. The COMMERCIAL COMP REPORTS kicker is back, the proof line is Up to 12 cited comps, and How it works and For brokers share one pointer row. The public landing is untouched.

title: The digest card says when it last actually mailed anybody
details: The digest is driven from outside this process on purpose, which buys a schedule somebody chose and costs the thing every external scheduler eventually does: it stops, and nothing says so. A cron that quietly dies looks exactly like a quiet few weeks, with no error and no bounce, just people not being mailed. The card on /admin now reports when the digest last sent, how many went out, and how many runs are logged, with never run as a real answer rather than an empty space. Previews are counted separately and never set the last-sent stamp, because a card reading last sent two days ago off somebody clicking Preview would report a healthy schedule while nobody had been mailed in a month, which is worse than reporting nothing. A previews-only state says so in those words. The date is rendered in the reader's own timezone rather than sliced off the ISO string, since an evening run in Mountain time otherwise renders as today followed by tomorrow's date and reads as a bug in the dashboard. Pinned by tests in all three states and confirmed by mutation.

title: A search's plan was passed to the analytics log and thrown away
details: Three /api/comps call sites have passed the visitor's plan to logEvent since the Pro tier shipped, and logEvent's row never had a plan field, so the value was built and discarded on every search for months. Nothing failed, and the code read as though do free users search more than Pro ones was answerable when it never was. It is the same silently-inert shape as vault_beta missing from getSessionUser's narrowed return, which is the second time this exact class of bug has landed here, so the fix comes with a pairing test: every dimension a logEvent call site passes must appear in logEvent's row, read out of server.js on both sides, so adding one at a call site fails the build until it is recorded. The column rides along in migration 026 rather than a fourth migration, since it is the same table and the same unrun deploy. /admin gains a Searches by plan table: anonymous, free, or the paid plan name. Rows logged before today carry no plan and show as unknown rather than being dropped, so the table still totals to the Searches tile.

title: A signed-out /desk lands on the sign-in door, not the marketing page
details: Under the account wall, asking for /desk without a session redirected to the homepage, which answers somebody who already has an account by telling them to go read about the product. It now redirects to /?auth=signin, a door the wall already exempts so the account modal has somewhere to live. The wall's actual rule, that a personal workspace never renders anonymously, is unchanged, and so are the 302 and the no-store; only the destination moved, and ACCOUNT_WALL=off still serves /desk as the app so the rollback lever stays exact. It surfaced because the watchlist digest's only call to action is see them all in your desk: a reader signed in on that device was always fine, which at a 90-day session is most of them, but a new phone or cleared cookies dead-ended the email on marketing copy. Any future mail linking to /desk inherits the fix. The account-wall test that pinned the old target now pins the new one, plus a second case proving the target really serves the app, because a redirect to a door that bounced back would be a loop that looked exactly like the bug it replaced.

title: The digest can be run from the page you already have open
details: The digest route is deliberately manual, because a timer inside the process fires at an hour nobody chose, again after every deploy restart, and twice the day this runs on two instances, and all three end with real people mailed the same comps again. But manual meant curl with an admin key, which is a feature nobody runs. /admin now carries a Watchlist digest card: Preview builds every email, sends none and marks nothing, so the copy can be read before anyone gets it; Send now confirms first and says the send cannot be recalled. Preview is the primary button and Send is the quiet one, because a dialog on the safe action trains people to click through the one on the unsafe action. The refusals show their reason rather than a status code, since no database and no outbound mail configured are different problems with different fixes. One property is load-bearing and now tested: opening /admin must not send email. Every other card on that page fetches its data on load, so the obvious way to write this one is the wrong way and the mistake would be invisible, the page looking identical while the mail had already gone. Both that and the confirm were checked by mutation.

title: The digest is now tested by actually sending one
details: The watchlist digest deliberately has no file fallback, so with no database it stops at a 503 and every test stopped there with it. The cutoff arithmetic, which markets get marked, the opt-out, and the rule that a second run mails nobody twice were all argued in comments and had never executed. test/helpers/fake-supabase.js is a stand-in PostgREST and Resend, so the run can be exercised end to end: fifteen cases now assert who was mailed, what the body said, and what the run left behind. It caught a real hole immediately, though not the one expected. The outbound-mail guard, the subtlest refusal in the feature, turned out to be untestable in the database-free suite because the database refusal fires first; deleting the guard entirely left every existing test green. It has its own case now, and both it and the cutoff rule were confirmed by mutation, meaning the guard was removed on purpose and the suite was watched to go red. One correction worth recording: the same work looked at first like it had found a live in.() encoding bug in findUsersByIds, and that was wrong. Percent-decoding restores the separator commas for values that contain none, so uuids were always fine. The helper that replaced it is consistency with the market-key idiom, not a fix, and the comment says so. The fake refuses a filter it cannot parse rather than matching everything, because a fake that matches everything reports a user-scoped read as working while it hands back another account's rows.

title: The watchlist can reach out, instead of waiting to be opened
details: watchlist_items and the feed have been live since July and are read only by somebody who already decided to open the app. Every loop in the product is pull. POST /api/watchlist/digest mails each watcher the markets of theirs that have new comps, using the send path that was already built: sendOutboundEmail and the branded letterhead, which has named market alerts as an intended category since the day it was written. The copy and the is-this-worth-sending rule live in the pure watchlist-digest.js, and buildDigest returns null rather than an empty string when there is no news, so nobody can mail a blank digest by forgetting to check. The feed computation is now shared with the page, so the two can never quote different numbers for one market. This is the only thing CompNinja sends on its own initiative, so the refusals are the feature: admin-gated and manually triggered rather than a timer, because a setInterval fires at an hour nobody chose, again after every deploy restart, and twice the day this runs on two instances, and all three end with real people mailed the same comps again. It refuses without a database, and refuses without outbound mail configured, because sendOutboundEmail is a silent no-op when the keys are unset and running blind would advance every high-water mark and delete a digest nobody received. Dry run builds every email, sends none and marks nothing. Markets are marked only after the send and only where there was news. The send cutoff is the later of last mailed and last seen, so the email can never tell somebody what they already saw on screen and an active user quietly stops getting digests without unsubscribing. Unsubscribe is a self-authenticating token link whose GET only shows a confirm button, because mail scanners fetch every URL in an email and a one-click GET would opt people out of mail they never opened; the same link turns them back on.

title: The event log can finally say whether one person did two things
details: analytics_events recorded what happened and nothing about whose visit it was, so it could count signups and count reports and never say whether the same browser did both. That is the question the first broker cohort raises, and the August 6 measurement had to answer it by hand-assembling rows out of Supabase. Two columns fix it (migration 026): visitor_id, an opaque random id in a new cn_vid cookie, and user_id once a session resolves. The id is a random number handed to a browser, not derived from IP or user agent or anything else about the person, so the events stay PII-free; the privacy policy names the cookie. /admin gains a Visitor funnel card reading arrived, hit the sign-in wall, created an account, ran a report, as cumulative sets over distinct visitors so the gap between two lines is a real drop-off. Rows predating the migration are excluded rather than bucketed as one unknown visitor, which would have invented a single visitor who did everything the product has ever seen, and percentages are withheld below ten arrivals where they are noise. The cookie is minted only on document navigations, because a page load fires a dozen parallel requests and minting on whichever arrived first would split one visit across ids that never appear again. Worth knowing for anything else built on the request context: AsyncLocalStorage does not reach a req.on end callback, which is where every route with a body logs from, so a plain run around the handler attributed every GET perfectly and recorded every signup, lead, share and vault import as anonymous. Measured, not assumed, and enterWith does not fix it either. The listener registration is bound instead, and a test pins the POST case specifically.

title: A broker can open their own vault with a code, without a SQL update
details: Granting the vault meant typing 'update users set vault_beta = true' into the Supabase SQL editor, one broker at a time, so handing three brokers a vault at a meeting was a note to run later rather than something that happened in the room. VAULT_PASSKEY is that same grant, self-serve: the broker signs in, opens Have a code, and lands on their own vault. It sets the same users.vault_beta column, so nothing about the grant changed. It stays a separate secret from TESTER_PASSKEY on purpose, because the tester code deliberately excludes the vault and folding them together would open a private-data workspace with an upload endpoint to everyone ever handed a try-Pro code; two codes also mean rotating one does not lock the other audience out. Both redeem through the same route and the same input, since someone handed a code should not also have to know which kind it is, and the response names which door opened so the modal can point a new broker at the vault instead of closing silently. One deliberate change to make room for the second code: the redeem route's idempotency check used to run before the secret compare, and now runs after and asks whether the account holds everything this deployment can give, which is identical behavior wherever only the tester code is set.

title: Market pages work as a research table, not only a teaser
details: The Market Explorer still builds the same 8-comp snapshot, but the page no longer throws away what an analyst needs from it. Cap rate, tenancy and year built render when a comp has them; a http(s) source URL turns the address into a citation; Sales and Leases split instead of mixing $/SF with $/SF/yr; the table sorts; signed-in visitors can watch the market or download the visible rows as CSV. Op-ex, the annual price trend, and a typical-rent band sit on a second ledger row, each omitted rather than invented. Anonymous SEO traffic still sees the valuation CTA. Seeded pages without the new fields look as they did, except Ontario (and any other snapshot with two priced leases) now shows a rent cell derived from comps already on the page.

title: A refund takes the report back, and a payment that clears late still unlocks one
details: Two events Stripe sends were never handled, and both failed in the direction that costs a real customer. A refunded single-report purchase kept its unlock forever: the unlock is a row in report_purchases and nothing ever removed one, so the money went back and the report stayed open. And a payment method that settles after checkout closes (bank debits, some wallets) produced a session that arrives complete but unpaid, logged "no unlock yet", and was never revisited by anything, because checkout.session.async_payment_succeeded is the only follow-up such a session ever gets: charged, locked out, no error, no retry. Now a FULL refund deletes the matching unlock and says so; a partial one deliberately changes nothing and emails instead, because revoking a report the customer still mostly paid for and quietly giving away what was refunded are both wrong often enough to want a human. A refunded Pro invoice matches no unlock and is left alone, since subscription access belongs to the subscription lifecycle events and ending it early on a goodwill credit would cut off a paid-up member. The full-versus-partial rule is pure and tested (stripe.js refundOf), the revoke matches on the payment intent because it is the only field a charge and that table share, and a test now reads the event list out of PRO-BILLING-SETUP.md and fails the build if it disagrees with the switch: a handler for an event the Stripe destination is not subscribed to is dead code that looks alive, so the three new events have to be ticked in the dashboard before any of this runs.

title: Brokers and clients trade comps in a hub, not an email thread
details: Comps sent to a client used to be attachments: three forwards and a reply-all later, nobody could say which buildings were still live. A hub is one shared page per requirement, where every comp is a row rather than a file, and the notes sit beside them. The broker creates one from the vault or straight from a report they already shared, and gets a link per person to send. The client opens it without an account and is only asked to sign in when they reply, so reading costs them nothing. Comps sent from the vault stay out of public records and earn no Verified badge: sending is private disclosure to named people, and publishing is still a separate choice. Each comp is copied into the hub as it was sent, so correcting a price later shows as a new row instead of quietly rewriting what the client already read. Access is per person and can be turned off one person at a time; closing a hub stops new posts and leaves everyone what is already there.

title: A covered market page leads with the broker, not with the comps
details: An owner asking a broker to price their building is the only event on a market page that has cash value to a broker, and it was the second clause of the last sentence on the page. Where a broker actually covers the market, that offer now sits directly under the heading, above the tiles and the comps: the broker firm named, the consent rule stated (nothing about you reaches them until you say yes), one button into the app, and a link down to the numbers for anyone who wants the evidence first. The comps did not move; they became the proof under the offer rather than the whole pitch. It renders on exactly the same condition as the broker card and the closing call to action, so an uncovered market shows none of it, and it never renders on a thin-data Explorer preview, which is noindex, expires in half an hour, and carries its own warning not to rely on it. A framing test, reversible by deleting the block.

title: The market pages stop promising a broker nobody has
details: The loudest call to action on the site biggest public surface offered a no-cost Broker Opinion of Value from a licensed local broker, on all 38 market pages, while the broker card directly above it rendered nothing at all because no broker has opted into any market yet. The promise was fulfillable only by going and finding someone by hand, which is not what the sentence said. It now reads the same list that card reads: a market with a covering broker keeps the full promise and names the city, and every other market sells the report instead, with the source cited on every comp. That costs no extra query, since the page already had the list in hand, and it corrects itself in both directions as brokers opt in or leave. A test pins the two to each other so the sentence cannot drift back outside the condition. The BOV follow-up email also dropped its two-business-day estimate: every one of these is answered by hand today, and a self-imposed deadline that slips is the first impression a real lead gets.

title: A forwarded report now asks the reader for their own building
details: A shared report link is the only page the account wall lets a stranger through to, which makes it the one surface that reaches people who have never heard of CompNinja. It greeted them with the generic signup card, and, worse, a line under the report telling them to enter an address above, while the card sat exactly where that field would have been: the single instruction on the page named a control the reader could not see. The card now names the report they are reading, credits the sending firm when the report already carries that firm letterhead, and offers a field for their own address. What they type rides through signup and is waiting in the search box on the other side, prefilled and focused but never submitted, because creating an account is not permission to spend a billed search on their behalf. A cancelled signup drops the address, the same rule every other pending action here follows. The status line now says whichever of the two true things applies, and it is recomputed by the same function that decides whether the card is showing, because the report renders before the server has said whether this visitor is walled out at all.

title: Outreach that leads with the finished report, not a link to make one
details: node outreach.js takes one market and property type, picks the buildings worth writing about out of the comp corpus, runs a real report on each, publishes a public share link, and writes a draft message per building. The ask stops being sign up and try it and becomes here is your building, tell me what is wrong with it, which is answerable in one line by somebody who knows the market. It sends nothing and has no mail path at all: it writes text, and the decision to send stays with the person whose name is on the message. Nothing is billed without --confirm, and the plan it prints first names every target and the estimated cost, read from the live provider rather than assumed. The same command with --warm-only runs the searches and stops, which is the cache pre-warm for a shortlist somebody is about to be shown: bounded to a list on purpose, since the general monthly refresh was measured and rejected on 2026-08-13. Two bugs surfaced the first time it read the real corpus rather than a fixture, and both are now pinned by tests: the same warehouse appeared twice because one row carried a ZIP and the other did not, and the target order was alphabetical rather than recent because deal dates are stored as display strings, where Sep sorts above Nov and every 2026 deal sorts below every 2025 one. Targets are also held to a higher bar than the corpus itself, since a bad row here costs a real message to a real person: provenance better than estimate, an address that proves an individual property, and no unit designator, which would address a tenant rather than an owner.

title: A saved property now says what its market did while you were away
details: The desk already showed what a property valuation did between two RUNS of its report, which only changes when the owner comes back and re-runs it: a record of visits rather than a reason to make one. The comp corpus, meanwhile, fills up from everybody else searches, so the market a saved building sits in keeps moving whether or not its owner ever returns. Each saved property now carries one line comparing its market median $/SF since that property was last checked against the equal length window before it, drawn entirely from comps already harvested. No search, no cost, nothing to schedule. It refuses to speak rather than guess: under three sale comps on either side there is no line, a window shorter than a month has no line, and an absence longer than a year is compared over the last year with the line saying so. It is deliberately a MARKET statistic and says median $/SF out loud, never that the building is worth more, because that would be a search nobody paid for, and it is styled in plain grey rather than the green and red the property own valuation change uses. The portfolio read batches one corpus lookup per market and type, and any failure serves the portfolio exactly as before with no line at all, because a page a member opens to see their own work must never break over a footnote.

title: The comp map now reaches the PDF and the PNG
details: The map was the one exhibit that never left the browser: it was dropped from Print / PDF and skipped by the image export, so every report a broker sent a client had the comp table and no map. Both exports now carry a flat version of the same map, built from the same pins and numbered to match the table. It is always the light street basemap rather than satellite, because satellite prints as a dark rectangle the pin numbers disappear into, and the exports are already pinned light for the same reason. Private vault comps are left off it, exactly as they are left out of the table and the CSV. If the map cannot be built (no connection, tiles blocked) the exports drop it and succeed as before, rather than printing an empty box.

title: The hero shows the county's assessed value next to the range
details: The first report had no public-record number about this exact address to read against the sales range, so a wrong size box could mint a headline like the $795,000 Boise trailer with nothing on the page to contradict it. The county's total assessed value now rides the same subject-size lookup that already opens assessor pages — no extra search — and lands as a County assessment row in the approaches table, never as Low/Likely/High and never as the cost approach. When it sits more than 25% outside a dollar headline, the same outlier rule as the table chips says the size box or the comps deserve a second look. Whole parcel or nothing. Not harvested. Not in the summary.

title: A listed house is no longer valued without the list price the size lookup already saw
details: A 1994 Rosedale house listed on Zillow at $1,250,000 ($454/SF, at the neighborhood median) came back as $1,650,000. Size was right — 2,752 SF from the listing. The comps were the expensive tail ($486–$653/SF) and a +5.5%/yr trend was applied in a market whose sold prices were falling. The $1.25M ask was sitting on the same page the size was read from and never entered the report. Three changes. The size lookup now also reads the current asking price and the year built, shown as evidence under the approaches the same way last sale is, never as a fourth headline figure. VALUATION.askFit flags a gap of more than 25% between that ask and the estimate on the trust line, so a $400k miss cannot hide behind the generic residential MLS disclaimer. And vintage is a fourth compWeight factor — free pass within 15 years, then halving per further 15 — so a 2024 teardown-rebuild does not price a 1994 resale at full weight. year_built rides locked_basis so a free report's range still matches Pro.

title: The vault takes a screenshot of a comp table, not only a PDF
details: Brokers were being asked for a spreadsheet or an exported PDF, which is not usually what they have. A CoStar table on screen, a photo of a printed comp sheet, or a cropped screenshot from a colleague all now go through the same door: the file is read by the extract vendor, the deals come back as the same confirm table, and nothing is stored until the rows are imported. PNG, JPEG and WebP are accepted alongside PDF. That list is the intersection of what both search providers read rather than the union, so a file that imports today cannot start refusing after a provider switch. The file type is decided by its bytes, never by its name, so a renamed spreadsheet still cannot reach the vendor. iPhone HEIC photos are refused by name with what to do instead, since a generic unsupported-file line would send a broker looking for a fault in their comp sheet.

title: The homepage asks for a building and shows one sample report
details: The account-wall landing was a how-it-works page: Create a free account, then the same Rancho Cucamonga sample twice, then Method. It now has an address field in the hero, one full sample exhibit, and a proof line (up to 12 comps, about a minute) instead of a stat strip. Brokers is one block with the Verified chip, not a second Method row. The typed address goes through sessionStorage into the search box after signup, never in the URL.

title: Dark mode is charcoal, not near-black
details: The page was slate-950 with near-white text (16:1) and read like an IDE invert. Paper lifts to #121826 and body ink dims to #C9D3E0 (11.7:1). Same cool slate, no layout change, light mode untouched. Print and PNG stay light.

title: An empty vault is the real vault, not a numbered onboarding page
details: Day one used to be two cards, with Your book and Your pipeline hidden until a spreadsheet landed, so the pipeline table shipped yesterday was invisible on an empty account. The empty vault is now the same two decks. The trust line shows zeros. Each empty body is a short invitation: upload closed deals, or watch a market. Add comps and Log a BOV stay closed. The watch-market form sits in the pipeline body until a lead or BOV exists, then collapses under Markets you watch. Watching a market on day one no longer hides waiting leads.

title: The vault pipeline is one table, from a new lead through won or lost
details: Leads and the BOV tracker described one flow in two sections 500px apart, repeating the same four columns, with nothing on screen connecting an intro request to the engagement it opened. They are now one table with a stage column. A lead is a New chip whose only action is requesting an introduction; a BOV keeps its status select and Remove. The four tiles became a five-cell stage strip plus a note for this year and the win rate. Coverage collapses under Markets you watch, and logging a BOV is the deck action behind a closed panel, matching Add comps. No new endpoint: the browser already had both payloads.

title: A mobile home was valued at $795,000 because the size came off a bike shop
details: Reported live: a trailer at 6728 W Fairview Ave listed on Zillow at $52,000 came back as $795,000, with a photo of the wrong building. The comps were right — the model found eight manufactured homes at $61-158/SF and said so in the summary. The size box was wrong. The confirm dialog's footprint estimate takes the biggest OSM building within 120 m of the geocoded point, and on a commercial strip that was Bob's Bicycles, 10,064 sq ft, 81 m away: 10,100 SF x $78/SF = $795,000 exactly. The map's photo snap scores footprints the same way, so one heuristic produced both symptoms. Three fixes. A footprint must now PROVE the address (addr:housenumber + addr:street) before it can be measured or photographed — the same filter detectPropertyType has used since the Phoenix Mandarin Buffet bug, which the size estimate and the photo never adopted; at Fairview 38 footprints prove #6728 (the trailers, several tagged static_caravan) and the bike shop proves nothing. An address naming one unit of a site (Trailer 51, Apt 3B, SPC 12, #45) gets no footprint size and no photo at all, because the geocoder drops the unit and no footprint near the point can be shown to be the subject's. And VALUATION.subjectSizeFit now flags a subject size that every sized comp contradicts: the report already whispered '8 comps are a different size class', which blamed the comps for a gap the size box had caused, and it now names the figure to doubt and how far the range is extrapolated. fpSize and bldgCache are bumped to v2 so browsers holding the wrong answers re-ask.

title: /healthz names the model that is actually running
details: Asked whether a live report had run on Gemini 3.7 Flash, the only way to answer was a git argument: MODEL is a startup constant an env var can override, and a provider's defaultModel moves with the code, so reading the repo proves what the source says rather than what production serves. /healthz already reported the provider; it now reports the model beside it. (The answer was 3.6 Flash — the 3.7 switch is sitting on an unmerged branch.)

title: Vault PDF extract no longer looks like a search outage or an empty table
details: Gemini extract now asks for 24k output tokens and maps usageMetadata including thought tokens. A vendor failure on extract returns the spec copy at 502 and does not trip UPSTREAM_HEALTH. Truncation (max_tokens / MAX_TOKENS / incomplete) is a 400 instead of We could not find a deals table. The model is no longer asked for lat/lng. Returning brokers see the vendor disclosure on the drop zone.

title: The vault header matches the rest of the site, and its forms finally look like forms
details: The workspace kept a short Search / My Desk / Vault / Brokers bar after every other server-rendered page grew an Explore menu and an account circle, so leaving My Desk for the vault still read as having been signed out. It now lifts the same chrome (desk:false, so My Desk is not drawn twice) and keeps Vault as the current page. First-run no longer parks the empty leads inbox under the two quiet cards; the coverage form still lives in step 2, and the inbox only returns if a watched market already has owners waiting. Add-comp, BOV, identity, and the inline edit row share one grid instead of a wrapping stack of labels, and the column mapper names sample values as chips above a ruled action row. Visual only — same IDs, same two decks, still one file input and one relocating coverage form.

title: Comp and market searches now run on Gemini 3.7 Flash
details: The default search model moved from gemini-3.6-flash to gemini-3.7-flash. Comp reports and Market Explorer share the same provider default, so both pick it up. MODEL still overrides if set.

title: The broker vault looks like a finished workspace
details: The page kept the two-deck structure, the trust ledger, and the statement tables, and raised everything around them: Inter is loaded, the header sticks, the masthead has a private-workspace kicker, figures sit in lightly shadowed panels, forms stack their labels, the comps filter is a toolbar, tables are framed, coverage is pill chips, and the footer matches the rest of the site. First-run stays two quiet cards rather than a coloured empty state. No route or entitlement change — it is the same book, drawn as a product a broker would hand a colleague.

title: Vault PDF import for table exports
details: A broker can drop a CoStar/ARGUS/CMA PDF onto Build your own comp set. The file is sent to the extract vendor with no search tools, never stored, and the rows land only after a confirm table. Spreadsheets are unchanged.

title: Dark mode across the site
details: Follows your system setting, with a toggle in the header to override. Covers the app, the report, My Desk, the vault, and every public page. Print and PNG export stay light on purpose, so a client deliverable still looks like one.

title: The per-account vault grant reached the database but not the code
details: Migration 023 was run and the grant was set on a real account, and the vault still refused to open. The session user object is deliberately narrowed, which is what keeps a password hash away from callers, and the new flag had never been added to it. So entitlements asked for a field that was not there, read it as false, and every granted broker resolved to no vault while every request succeeded and nothing was logged. The function's own comment warns about exactly this and it still happened. Found by granting it to an account and looking, which no unit test could have done: they hand the flag straight to the decision table, on the far side of the missing plumbing. The pairing is now pinned by a test that reads both sides out of the server, and the schema verifier gained checks for this column and for the tester flag from migration 022, neither of which it had ever looked at.

title: Brokers get a path off the landing page, not just an FAQ row
details: Every visitor lands on the same page, and until now it spoke only to owners: a broker arriving there met one FAQ answer and a link inside the Explore dropdown. That is a poor showing for the audience these relationships are the better acquisition lever with. The page now states three concrete trades, private book, credit by name on published comps, and introductions to owners asking for a valuation in markets you watch, then points at the brokers page. It reuses the method section's own layout so it needed no new styling. Separately, the vault's coverage note stopped assuming the reader knows markets can be earned, and now just says what happens.

title: The vault's headline median names its type instead of showing a dash
details: Declining the figure outright fixed the wrong number but cost every mixed book its headline: most real books span property types, so the largest slot on the page would have read as a dash more or less permanently. The ledger tile now narrows rather than declines. It quotes the median of whichever type holds most of the priced sales and names it, so a mixed book reads '$79' above 'Industrial, 2 of 4 sales'. The reading strip and the table footer still decline, and the difference is the point: those two seal the rows on screen, where a dominant-type median would describe a subset the reader can see they did not filter to, while the tile describes the whole book. Both surfaces still read the one psfStats helper, so neither can quote a figure the other contradicts. Ties between types break on the type name rather than on the order the rows arrived in, so the same book cannot name a different type on a second load.

title: No more headline $/SF median across mixed property types
details: A book holding industrial, office and retail reported a single median of $117/SF, the largest figure on the page and one that described no building in it: dollars per square foot are not comparable across property types, so a median mixing them is an artifact rather than a statistic. The ledger tile, the reading strip and the table footer now all decline the figure when the rows they summarise span more than one type, and say how many types and that filtering brings it back. Filtering to a type restores it immediately, and the market cards underneath were already segmented correctly, so no real number was lost. Counted over priced sales only, so an unpriced lease in a second type cannot silence a median it could never have moved.

title: An import now reports what was stored, not what was read
details: Re-uploading a book the vault already held said 'Imported 16 comps' after saving none. The insert ignores duplicates against the database, but it asked for no confirmation back, so the route could only report how many rows it had parsed. It now asks for the stored ids and counts those, and the page states the two facts separately: what landed, and how many rows the vault already had. Rows repeated inside a single file stay a third, separate count, because a broker re-uploading last month's export is doing something entirely normal and none of it is an error. Being wrong in the reassuring direction is the failure that matters here: a broker told their deals landed does not go looking for them.

title: The gut check now appears on the first import instead of the next page load
details: Market benchmarks are fetched per market-and-type bucket, so a brand-new vault has nothing to ask for and the fetch returns early. The caller marked them loaded anyway, so a broker who imported their book into an empty vault got no gut check for the rest of that session, and only saw one if they happened to reload the page. Found on a clean-slate run against the real corpus, and it is the actual reason the panel looked like it was failing in thin markets: the benchmarks were fine the whole time. The flag now stays unset until there is a bucket to ask about, so the reload that follows the first import is the one that loads them.

title: A broker states the name their published comps are credited to
details: Publishing a comp promises credit to your firm by name, and there was nowhere to say what that name was. A broker who came in through the vault had no profile, so the credit quietly fell back to whatever they typed in the signup form, and that personal name was then copied into the firm field and shown publicly as their company. Nobody chose it, so nobody could correct it. The vault now names the credit before any publish and offers one form to set it, publishing refuses with a message that opens that form instead of a dead end, and the credit reads the stated profile only. Stating a name is deliberately not a public listing: the row it creates is private, so a broker who wants a public profile page still opts into that separately.

title: The mapper now reads a real brokerage export without hand-fixing
details: Measured against the first real broker file: 4 of its 11 meaningful columns needed manual mapping, and one suggestion was actively wrong. All four are fixed. "$/SF" normalizes to bare "sf" and was the sole claimant of the size alias, so the mapper suggested importing $68.11 as a 68 sq ft building; a rate-shaped header (isRateHeader, tested on the raw string) may now claim nothing by alias, while an exact name like "Price Per Unit" still maps. "Cap Rate (%)" left an underscore stub after the symbols stripped and missed its own exact match; normalization now trims those. "Trans", "Bldg SF", RBA and GLA joined the alias table. And an explicit no-value price ("Undisclosed", "N/A") now reads as an empty cell instead of losing the row to the 1.2M error, which is what the template promised all along; pending prices ("TBD", "call for price") are still refused, and shorthand still gets the write-it-out advice.

title: vault_beta: hand a specific broker the vault without a subscription
details: Broker onboarding had no door: the tester passkey deliberately excludes the vault, ADMIN_KEY also unlocks the dashboards, so a real broker's only path in was paying on day one. users.vault_beta (migration 023, run it before flipping any flag) is the narrow alternative: set per account by hand, revoked the same way, no shared secret. It grants the broker surfaces only, so reports stay free-tier; it cannot switch a dark deployment on; and it is independent of billing on purpose, so a beta broker's book stays reachable with no subscription to lapse. Rules live in entitlements.js with the rest of the decision table.

title: First real vault book through the funnel: badge, distances, and import summary fixed
details: Walking a realistic 12-row broker CSV through the whole funnel surfaced three bugs, all fixed with tests. Blended vault comps showed 7,508-mile distances: a building with no stored location was joined as latitude 0, longitude 0 (Number(null) is 0), the same Null Island trap the export path fixed a day earlier; the join now lives in pure, tested blend-comps code. The "From your vault" badge never rendered because TIER_WEIGHT had no broker_vault key, so tierOf answered null; the key now exists at full weight, which leaves the valuation unchanged. And a mapper import wrote its summary, including the line-numbered skipped rows, into the closed Add comps panel; the panel now opens, so a dropped row is never silent.

title: Gemini 3.6 Flash is now the default comp-search model
details: Measured on the 12-target eval through the real pipeline: better on every scored metric than Claude Sonnet 4.6 (valuation possible 82% → 100%, priced sales 4.8 → 5.3, provenance 0.73 → 0.77, aggregate-padding rate 19% → 8.5%), while running 1.6x faster (56s vs 87s) and 3.9x cheaper ($0.092 vs $0.36 per report). Rollback is a single env var, SEARCH_PROVIDER=anthropic — no code change, no redeploy. Requires GEMINI_API_KEY on a paid-tier Google project: a free-tier key runs the model but 429s on every grounded search.

title: Multi-provider comp search (Anthropic + Gemini)
details: The Anthropic search call is now behind a pure provider interface (search-provider-anthropic.js, search-provider-gemini.js), selected by SEARCH_PROVIDER (default anthropic, no fallthrough on an unrecognized value) — server.js owns all I/O and branches on the provider's capabilities, never its name. On the 12-target eval, Gemini scored cheaper and faster than the current Anthropic model with no accuracy regression, so this lays the groundwork for switching the default once real traffic confirms it.

title: The summary can no longer claim verified comps the table does not show
details: A reviewer reported a report whose summary described verified comps while every badge in the table read Estimate, News or Listing. Root cause: "verified" was in the comp shape the model fills even when we had offered it no broker comps to match against, so it awarded itself the badge - measured live at 4 of 5 comps on a market with zero broker submissions. The badge was always safe (enforceVerifiedFlags cleared them) but nothing revisited the prose the model had already written around them. Two fixes: the field is now only present when broker comps were actually offered, so there is nothing to over-claim; and scrubUnearnedVerifiedClaims (pure, tested) rewrites the verified word family in summary, value_drivers, market_trend, price_discovery and per-comp notes whenever the finished report carries no verified comp. It fires only at zero, because with even one real badge the word is accurate and rewriting it would lose information, and it rewrites rather than deletes so the required honesty caveats survive.

title: The vault gets an edit, a delete, an add, and a way out
details: Until today the vault had no way to fix a mistake, no way to add a deal between bulk uploads, and no way out. The only delete was by import id with every comp in it cascading, so a broker who spotted one wrong sale price had to delete the entire spreadsheet and re-import it to fix a typo. Recording Tuesday's closing meant authoring a CSV by hand. And nothing exported a broker's own data, which is the question asked before a first upload, not after it: what happens to my book if I cancel. All three are closed now. PATCH and DELETE /api/vault/comp fix or remove one comp, every field editable including address and price, since restricting the editable set would miss the case that motivates the feature. POST /api/vault/comp adds one by hand through the same row parser the CSV importer uses, so a hand-typed comp faces the same rejections a spreadsheet row does. And GET /api/vault/export.csv writes the whole book, paged past the dashboard's 1000-row display cap, so the button that says export all comps means all of them. Two rules worth remembering. Editing or deleting a comp that has already been published retracts it from the public record first, so a broker correcting a price does not leave the old, wrong number sitting out there; republishing the corrected row is a deliberate second act, not automatic. And the export carries more than the template's own columns: it appends every per-type field actually in use, clear heights and units and lot acres among them, plus the coordinates from the comp's linked property, because a plainer export would re-import a book with its specs gone and its private addresses sent back out to a third-party geocoder. No migration: upload_id was already nullable, so a hand-added comp just leaves it unset.

title: The 1031 guide gets its own card on /brokers
details: Owner-directed: the guide was a fine-print link inside the submit CTA. It now has its own card below that CTA with a bordered Open the 1031 guide button (not red, the submit door keeps the loud button) and one plain line: A plain guide to the 45 and 180 day deadlines. Send it to your client. The CTA's Or run a free valuation alt link is cut, it only led back to the home page.

title: Apartment communities and retail centers are called properties, not buildings
details: Follow-on to the house-is-not-a-building fix. Multifamily and Retail were still falling through to "building", which is wrong for the two types that most often are not one building: a garden apartment community and a strip or anchored center. Both now read property, so the hero says "What This Property Is Worth". Multifamily is deliberately not "apartment building" or "apartment community" - the type spans duplexes and 300-unit communities and neither phrase is true across that range, while property is also the unit the report already prices on. Retail is property because building fits only a single-tenant pad and center only an anchored center. Industrial and Office keep building, because those genuinely are one. Condos and townhomes need nothing: they have no type of their own and ride under Residential's home, which is already right for them.

title: Reports now say what the property itself last sold for
details: A Bensalem report was shown to a reviewer who pointed out the property had sold a year earlier for $12.45M and the report never mentioned it. It was not a search failure: nothing in the prompt ever asked. The report now carries subject_last_sale (date, price, source link) and renders it as one line under the valuation approaches: "This building last sold for $12,450,000 in Aug 2025. That is $185/SF." It costs no extra search, because the assessor and listing pages the subject-size lookup already opens are the same pages that carry the sale history, and the model is told to read it off those rather than spend a search of its own. Deliberately a line of evidence and not a fourth figure in the ledger: a years-old price shown big reads as a current valuation. It is also told to work the sale into the summary, where it outranks the market-level read. The value is normalized server-side (no date means no line at all, and a non-http source URL is dropped) so nothing model-written reaches the page unchecked.

title: The lookback hint stopped claiming your own override was our advice
details: "Recommended for Industrial" sat under the Lookback dropdown and was written once, when the property type resolved, then never touched again. Changing the window to 6 months left the label still saying the recommendation, so the form asserted something false about whatever the reader had just chosen. The hint is now recomputed from what the control currently says, and disappears the moment you change the window: it shows "Recommended for Industrial" only while the window really is the recommendation. It is a caption for the default, not standing advice, so once you have made your own choice it has nothing left to say. Fixed a second case found while testing: both startup restores (a ?type= deep link and the remembered last type) set the type without touching the hint, so a returning visitor whose last search was Residential got a Residential form under "Recommended for Industrial".

title: A house is no longer called a building
details: A residential report led with "WHAT THIS BUILDING IS WORTH" and told the owner to "edit Building Size above", next to a form field actually labelled Property size. The report and the form now use the right noun per type: home for Residential, property for Land, building for the four commercial types. It covers the value hero's heading, the basis line under it (which now names the form's own label rather than a second hardcoded one), the sales, income and cost approach explanations, the no-size fallbacks, the details hint, the size helper and the footprint-estimate note. Land drops the footprint sentence entirely rather than rewording it, since a parcel's size does not come from a building footprint.

title: The map says which comps it could not place
details: A comp whose address will not geocode simply produced no pin and said nothing, so the map showed fewer comps than the table and the reader was left to work out which ones were missing and whether the report had dropped them. A line under the map now names them: "Comps 1 and 2 aren't on the map, we couldn't match those addresses to a location. They're still in the table below and still counted in the valuation." The second half is the load-bearing part; a missing pin must never read as a dropped comp.

title: Residential comps stay in the neighborhood
details: A Gurnee house came back with comps miles away while Zillow showed five on its own streets. The generic radius rule is written for commercial assets, where a buyer really will weigh a warehouse two towns over, and its "widen it in a smaller market" license is what let residential searches reach. Residential now overrides that rule outright: same subdivision or roughly a mile, same side of any boundary a buyer would notice, and an explicit instruction that 3 comps from the subject's own streets beat 8 that include homes miles away. Reaching further is allowed only when the immediate area genuinely has fewer than 3 sales, and has to be disclosed in the summary.

title: The export counter no longer reads as a cap on running reports
details: "4 exports left this month" sits in the report toolbar and was read as "you can only run 4 reports". Running reports is unlimited on every plan; only the downloads are metered. The counter now says which of the two it is counting ("4 downloads left this month, reports are unlimited"), and the plan comparison table leads with a Reports you can run row so the unlimited half is stated rather than inferred.

title: Free tier now itemizes 10 comps, up from 4
details: FREE_MAX_COMPS raised in entitlements.js as a step toward the owner's longer-term direction of dropping prices and eventually making comp reports free outright, with Pro growing into more features rather than gating the core report. Every place the old number was hard-coded in prose moved with it: the pricing modal subtitle and comparison table, both plan-card strings, and the public /how-it-works FAQ (also read by Google's FAQPage JSON-LD).

title: Brokers page: the broker's payoff first, in bullets
details: Owner-directed rework of /brokers. New hero (Your comps, your name, on every report that uses them) with a two-sentence plain sub. Two cards, three bullets each: what submitting earns (with the report's actual green Verified badge shown inline, not described) and the Pro vault told in the vault page's own verbs. The dangling Get introduced mailto is gone; the one action is the Submit door below. Upgrade to Pro hides itself for members via the shared entitlements hydration, and also when billing is off so it cannot dead-end.

title: /brokers no longer 404s under a query string
details: The route matched req.url without stripping the query, so /brokers?utm_source=x answered 404 - the exact regression the route tests pin for every other page, found by a cache-busting query during the rework. Path-only match now, pinned by a test.

title: The Broker Vault is organized into two decks, and your comps come first
details: The vault had grown to ten sections stacked down one scroll, every heading the same size over the same rule, so nothing said where one part of the page ended and the next began. It now reads as the two things it actually is. "Your book" covers the uploader, your markets and your comps; "Your pipeline" covers leads and the BOV tracker. Four things moved. Adding comps was a full section sitting above your comps table, so a broker with 200 comps opened their own book and was shown an uploader first: it is now the Add comps control on the Your book rule, and the panel opens when you click it, or when you drag a spreadsheet anywhere onto the page. The gut check, the median-by-year chart and the repeat-property list were three bordered panels between the filter row and the data they describe; their three headline figures come up into one reading strip and each one opens the full panel behind it, which moved the comps table roughly 3,200 pixels up the page on a test book. Imports moved under the comps table it explains, collapsed, instead of sitting alone at the very bottom. And the BOV log's add form is tucked under its own tiles rather than splitting the section in half. Nothing was deleted and no numbers changed: the strip's median is the same figure the table's own closing row states, computed once. A first-run vault is untouched, still just the two numbered steps.

title: The vault's Start here panel loses its heading, and step 1 says whose comp set it is
details: Two copy changes on the broker vault's first-run screen. The "Start here" heading over the two numbered steps is gone: a 1 and a 2 under two instruction headings already say where to start, so the line was announcing a panel that announces itself. And step 1 now reads "Build your own comp set" rather than "Build your comp set", which is the whole point of the vault said in one word: the set is the broker's, not ours, and nothing in it is ever read into CompNinja's public records. Nothing else on the panel moved, and the gap the heading used to sit in is unchanged, because the steps block's own top margin collapses into the section's.

title: The property-type guesser now records when it guesses wrong
details: /admin has shown how OFTEN the type autofill fires since it shipped, and never once whether it was right. The two ways a visitor overturns a guess, the Undo link on the note and the change door in the confirm dialog, both threw that away silently, so a detector quietly setting the wrong type on every warehouse in a city would have looked identical to one working perfectly. Both paths now log it, and the tile carries a corrected percentage beside the applied one: the same denominator, and the one number on that page where lower is better. Three deliberate exclusions. A correction is filed under the type the DETECTOR asserted, not the one the visitor moved to, so it is comparable per type with the applied count it answers. Overturning a REMEMBERED type is not counted at all, because that is the visitor's own earlier pick about that address and changing their mind is not a detector error. And a correction never enters the attempts denominator, or one wrong guess would dock the rate twice, once for being wrong and once for the row saying so. The rate is deliberately not clamped at 100%: the counts are independent tallies over one capped row window, so a figure above it means unpaired rows, which is worth seeing rather than rounding away.

title: The landing page draws the report as you scroll
details: The landing page and /how-it-works now animate as you move down them, and the motion is made of the product rather than laid on top of it. Reaching the sample report sweeps its ink rules out from the left, counts the Low, Likely and High figures up to their values, and deals the five comp rows in one after another; the stat strip counts to 12 and to 100% as it arrives, and the three Method steps land in sequence. The comp figures themselves never animate: that exhibit's whole pitch is that the arithmetic checks out, so every number in it appears correct and stays correct. Three things it deliberately does not do. It does not fade the headline, which is the largest thing on the page and therefore what its load speed is measured by, so decoration nobody has scrolled to yet cannot slow down the one thing everybody sees. It does nothing at all for a visitor whose system asks for reduced motion. And nothing on the page is hidden unless the script that animates it is actually running, so with JavaScript off, broken, or still arriving, the page renders whole rather than blank: this is the site's front door and its search-engine surface, and no animation is worth risking either.

title: Vault: three-line cards, folded fine print, one market form
details: Owner's restructure of /vault's Start-here view. Both cards now lead with a short line and three bullets; the required-columns and privacy fine print folds into collapsed disclosures (Required columns & privacy details, How markets work). The market-adding form moved up into step 2 and is ONE relocating node: applyFirstRun moves it to the top of the leads section once the vault has content, since step 2 hides then and a broker with a full book must still be able to add a market. The leads section is display-only, with new description and empty-state copy. Hero shortened to "Your own private comp data."

title: Leaving the home page no longer looks like being logged out
details: MARKET_BAR carried three links and nothing else, so every server-rendered page (all 38 market pages, /markets, /brokers, /1031-exchange, /terms, /privacy) dropped Pricing, My Desk and the account circle the moment you left index.html — reading as a silent mid-browse logout. The bar now ships auth-shaped slots hidden in byte-identical HTML and a small script hydrates them from /api/config + /api/account/me after paint, so the hour-long crawler caches on market pages survive untouched. The circle mirrors the full home-page menu: email, vault, upgrade, billing, sign out. Pricing links through the /?pricing=1 door (the /?submit=comp idiom — a fragment dies at the account wall).

title: Explore menu: Pricing first, 1031 Guide added
details: Owner ordering — Pricing, Brokers, Markets, How it works, 1031 Guide — applied to all three headers (index.html, MARKET_BAR, /how-it-works).

title: Broker page rewritten: one door, BOV named, a home for the vault
details: One Submit a comp CTA instead of two, the BOV card finally says the words Broker Opinion of Value, the Verified explainer cut from five sentences to two, and a new For members card links the Broker Vault and pricing.

title: The single-report unlock is one click from the report
details: The locked-comps strip now shows Unlock just this report — $20 next to See all comparables. It was two clicks deep and rendered last in the pricing modal. Hidden on shared reports and when billing is off; straight to checkout otherwise.

title: Search form slimmed: market note gone, Details for comps
details: The optional market-note field is removed from the form (a hidden input keeps saved searches hitting the cache they paid for). Your property details is retitled Details for comps and its hint now leads with why the fields exist: they steer comp selection. A broker signpost strip joins the how-it-works pointer on the landing page.

title: FAQ catches up with the paid tier, and brokers get answers
details: The free-and-no-subscription answer predated the Pro launch; it now describes free vs Pro vs the one-off without naming amounts. Two new entries: what submitting comps earns a broker, and what the Broker Vault is.

title: The vault template now carries its own rules, and they are true
details: Everything a broker needed to know about filling in the comp template lived in one cell: the notes column of the single example row. The first edit deleted it. It was also wrong, telling brokers to strip dollar signs and commas that the importer already strips. The rules now ride in the file as lines beginning with #, which the importer skips, so they survive whether the broker deletes them or leaves them: which four columns are required, the six property types, the two transaction words, the date format and how a slash date is read, what the number fields really accept ($1,250,000 and 45,000 SF and 6.25% are all fine, 1.2M is not), the coordinate pair that keeps a private address off third-party geocoders, and the twelve optional per-type columns that were accepted all along and mentioned nowhere. There are three examples instead of one: a priced sale, a lease, and a sale with an undisclosed price, the two cases the first-run panel promises are welcome and the old template demonstrated neither of. Every example carries a # in its address cell, so the file we hand a broker can no longer plant a fake comp in their own book of business; typing an address over the # is what turns a row on. Skipped # lines are counted and reported back rather than dropped quietly, and a test now fails the build if a new per-type field is added without the template telling brokers they can bring it.

title: The vault's two first-run steps say what to do, not what they are
details: Step 1 was headed "Bring your own comps" over a five-line paragraph explaining what a private comp set is, where it shows up, and the four places it never goes. Step 2 was headed "Or just tell us where you work". Both are now plain instructions, "Add your comps" and "Add your markets", and step 1's paragraph is gone: it was the longest block on a panel whose whole job is to get a broker to their first upload, and it argued a case before anyone had asked the question. What survives under step 1 is the line that actually removes friction, that only four columns are required and undisclosed deals still count. The privacy promise itself is not lost, only moved off the empty-state panel: the trust line above the workspace states it the moment a vault has anything in it, and the publish flow states it again at the one point where it can be acted on. The panel's own "Start here" heading went with them, along with step 2's "Nothing to upload": a numbered 1 and 2 under two instruction headings already say where to start, and the reassurance was answering a worry the step no longer raises.

title: The missing divider in the landing page's stat strip
details: On the landing page (and /how-it-works, which serves the same body) the four-figure stat strip drew a rule after "Free" and after "~1 min" but not between "Up to 12" and "~1 min". The two-column phone layout only needs a rule after the 1st and 3rd cells, and the four-across breakpoint never added the 2nd, so one gap in the row was blank and the strip read as two pairs rather than four figures.

title: The property type moves out of the grey band and under the address
details: The search form's settings row sat above a filled grey strip carrying a size hint and the property-type sentence.
