It was the only filled row in an otherwise white card, so the page's one band of grey landed on its quietest text and read as a rule cutting the card in half. The strip is gone. The type sentence, its inline picker and the OpenStreetMap detection note now sit directly under the address, which is where they belong: each of them describes the building the address just named, not the settings they were sitting beneath, and the card is a row shorter for it. The size line that shared the strip is retired rather than moved, because the size field moved into Refine earlier the same day and Refine states the same fact beside the actual input, so the form was saying it twice. The footprint-estimate note survives and still announces itself while Refine is collapsed; it is a block now rather than an inline span, so it stacks above the type sentence instead of running into it.

title: Refine takes your own cap rate, and the income approach reads it against the market's
details: The Refine section's third cell held "Price max", the upper bound for the asking price. That max earned its slot when the price also lived down there; once the price moved onto the form itself, a lone "max" was a control that only made sense if you remembered the field it belonged to. It is now "Cap rate (%)". Enter it alongside your NOI and the report adds a second income-approach line, your income at your rate, sitting right beside the same income at the market's cap-rate range, so you can read your own assumption against the market's instead of only being told what the market thinks. It also seeds the DCF's discount and exit-cap defaults, and it revives a case that used to render nothing at all: when a search comes back with no market cap-rate range and too few priced sale comps, your own rate now carries the valuation. A single rate gives a single figure and is deliberately not widened into a fake range. Like the NOI beside it, the cap rate never leaves your browser. Reports saved before today keep showing their asking-price range.

title: The vault takes the broker's own spreadsheet
details: Until now a vault upload had to use our exact column names, so a CoStar or MLS export whose first column is "Property Address" was rejected outright with an instruction to go copy the data into our template. That is homework, and it stood between the vault and its first real book of business. An upload now opens a matching screen: your column, our field, and two or three real values from that column so a wrong match is visible rather than silent. It also closes two quieter failures. Only four fields are required per row, so a file carrying "Sq Ft" instead of size_sqft imported perfectly happily with every size null, every price per square foot missing, and no explanation anywhere. Any file with a column we do not recognise now asks, and the screen names the columns it is going to ignore. And a column headed only "$" used to disappear from that screen altogether: stripping it down to letters and numbers left nothing, so it was never listed, never offered as something to map, and never even named as a column being skipped. A file with a "$" price column now gets the same matching screen as any other unrecognised column instead of quietly losing its prices. Files already in our template import with no extra step. A confirmed mapping is remembered, but only ever as a pre-selection on a screen the broker still confirms, so a stale mapping can never quietly import the wrong thing. The suggestion rules keep the module's old promise not to guess: a field is pre-selected only when exactly one column claims it, so a file with both "Sale Price" and "Consideration" leaves the choice to the person who knows.

title: Focus and Lookback lead the search form's third row, ahead of the optional asking price
details: The three-cell row under the address read Asking price, Lookback, Focus, putting the one optional field of the three first and ahead of the two everyday controls every visitor sets. Reordered to Focus, Lookback, Asking price: a pure DOM move, every id and its JS wiring untouched, so nothing about how the fields work changed, only which one a visitor's eye and tab order reach first.

title: The Market Explorer stops demanding one exact phrasing
details: It used to accept only "industrial Boise ID", so a full state name, a zip code, an ordinary word like market or in, and the way most people name a property type all dead-ended in a hint row at the very top of the funnel. It now reads full state names including two-word ones, resolves a five-digit zip to its city, understands warehouse, apartments, multi-family, office building, shopping center and their neighbours, and ignores filler words. The state is resolved before filler words are dropped, which matters more than it sounds: eight state abbreviations are also English words, so stripping "in" first would quietly lose Indiana. Nothing auto-runs and the parsed market is still spelled out on the button before anything is searched, so a wrong guess is visible rather than expensive. The parsing moved into its own tested module, which is the first time any of this logic has had test coverage.

title: The valuation reconciles like an appraisal instead of reading like a paragraph
details: Under the value range, the classic sales comparison, income and cost approaches were a wall of prose with each indicated value buried mid-sentence, so the one thing worth seeing at a glance, whether the approaches agree, took reading two paragraphs to find. They now read as an appraiser's reconciliation: each approach is a row with its evidence on the left and its indicated value in a right-aligned serif column, in the same statement vocabulary the comp table already uses. With a size and an NOI entered you can now see sales comparison and the income approach stacked against each other and tell instantly which comes in higher. There is deliberately no closing total sealed under a double rule, which is how this site marks a final figure everywhere else: the value ledger directly above is already that conclusion, and sealing the same number a second time would state it twice in one card. An approach with no computed figure, the not-run and not-modeled lines, spans both columns and reads exactly as it did before, so the display degrades to prose rather than showing an empty cell where a number belongs. On phones the row stacks, because a nowrap money column at that width squeezed the evidence into a fifteen-line ribbon. Rode along: three pieces of copy still sent people to a section called Your property details, which was renamed Refine when the search form was rebuilt, so they now point at a control that exists.

title: A one-in-a-hundred test flake could abort a deploy
details: CI run #244 failed on a two-line HTML copy edit and went green on a re-run of the identical commit. The raw log named the test: the share-privacy regression in test/routes.test.js, which publishes a report containing a private comp at "742 Off-Market Secret Rd" and then asserts the string "742" appears nowhere in the payload GET /api/shared hands back. That sweep is the right paranoia for a privacy leak, but it is only sound while every byte of the payload is fixed test data, and it was not: POST /api/share stamps generatedAt from its own clock when the browser does not send one, so each run put a fresh 13-digit epoch millisecond in the payload, and roughly one run in a hundred produced a millisecond containing "742" (the failing run landed at 05:33:36.742Z). This is not cosmetic: npm start runs the suite as a prestart gate, so the same 1% could stop a real Render deploy and leave the previous build serving. Fixed by removing the clock rather than loosening the assertion: the test now sends its own fixed generatedAt, which is what a real share always carries, so the payload is byte-identical on every run (verified across 30 consecutive shares and 10 consecutive runs of the file). A new assertion pins that value as a tripwire, so a future change that re-stamps the server clock fails on the first run instead of quietly re-arming the flake. No product code changed.

title: The asking price takes the search form's third slot from the building size
details: The size was occupying a prime slot on the form while being answered automatically twice over, from public records on the server and from the OpenStreetMap building footprint during the confirm dialog, so most visitors were looking at a field they never had to touch. The slot now belongs to the asking price, which is the one optional input that lights up a report surface that is otherwise dark: the market comparison card hides itself unless it has both a size and a price, so until now nobody who skipped the collapsed section ever saw their own $/SF against the market's, or the over-or-under verdict that goes with it. Size moved into Refine and was reunited with its max as a single range, the shape it had before the price took the slot, and the price max moved down beside it with a note saying it pairs with the price on the form. All of the size machinery works unchanged from its new home because every part of it addresses the field by id and never by position: the per-type relabelling to Lot size or Property size, the footprint estimate landing while the section is collapsed, the markers that clear a machine-written size when the address changes, and the saved-report restores. The label reads Asking price rather than Your price on purpose, since a bare your price invites the number someone paid years ago and a historical figure would make the comparison card announce a nonsense verdict against today's market; it also had to be short enough to sit on one line in a cell with 184 pixels of usable width, which the old two-line label was not.

title: A limited-data market preview stops spending the free search
details: When the Explorer finds too few priced sales to publish a market page, it shows a temporary preview that lives 30 minutes and does not survive a redeploy. That still counted as the one free search an account-less visitor gets, so they could spend their single allowance on a link that was already gone. Only a permanently published page counts now, matching every other empty-handed outcome (too little data, daily cap, upstream failure), and because the allowance survives, re-exploring that market is free and instant from cache and simply rebuilds the preview. Previews are also logged as their own analytics event, carrying whether the search was billed or served from cache, so the thin-market rate is finally visible rather than hiding inside the ordinary search count. Note this is a latent fix: the account wall currently blocks anonymous searches before this code runs, so it matters when the wall is rolled back.

title: The value hero shows the comps behind the number
details: Under the Low/Likely/High ledger there is now a hairline number line with one gray tick per sale comp, each at its own $/SF, a light tint marking the Low-to-High span and a red mark at Likely. Confidence stops being asserted and becomes visible: ticks bunched around the red mark show why a range is narrow, and a scattered row honestly shows a soft market, which is exactly what the trust line underneath could only claim in words. The axis spans the comps rather than the range, because the range is the middle 50% of them and about half the comps sit outside it by construction. It draws only when the ledger above is quoting the same unit (so multifamily gets it in $/unit, land in $/acre) and only above four comps, where the range stops being the raw spread. Screen, print and PNG export all carry it; nothing is stored or sent.

title: The Market Explorer remembers what you asked for through signup
details: When the free-account gate interrupts a typed market search, the search now resumes automatically the moment the account exists, instead of dumping the new member back on an empty Explorer to retype it. Same one-shot pending-intent rules as the portfolio save and checkout: dismissing the modal cancels it, and it can never fire on a later unrelated sign-in.

title: The vault page says what it is
details: The /vault screen led with a red all-caps "Broker workspace" kicker over a heading that read "Your vault", so the only red thing above the fold was a label nobody needed and the page never named the product it is. The kicker is gone, the heading is now "Broker Vault" (matching the browser tab and the way the plan card and the desk refer to it), and the description drops its trailing promise of comps "sortable and filterable by property and by market", which described controls sitting in plain view a screen below it. The first-run panel lost its intro line too ("Two ways to get something out of this today. The second one takes about ten seconds and needs no spreadsheet."): it counted and rated the two steps sitting directly beneath it, which announce themselves perfectly well as a numbered 1 and 2, one headed "Bring your own comps" and the other "Or just tell us where you work" with "Nothing to upload" already on it.

title: The search form goes quiet (Direction N)
details: The comp input form was carrying twelve pieces of text before the red button — three hint lines, two inline links, the type sentence, a split size range, a disclosure, and a footnote — each earned individually, collectively reading as clutter. Redesigned to the owner-approved Direction N from the design system: the address now takes the full top row alone in the largest text on the form (17px, still above the iOS zoom floor), the three everyday settings (size, lookback, focus) share one calm row of three equal cells, and every hint plus the property-type sentence merged into a single quiet strip beneath them. Nothing was hidden that wasn't already: the size max and the market note joined price and NOI in the existing disclosure, renamed "+ Refine", and the explore-a-market link moved down beside "View a sample report" where the other secondary actions live. All the dynamic machinery survived the move verbatim — the type picker, the OSM-detected and remembered-type states with their aria-live announcement, the footprint size estimate swapping in for the standing size sentence via the same CSS adjacency rule, and the Pro gating on the explore link. One deliberate deviation from the mockup: the "Recommended for <type>" line stays under Lookback, because it explains a window the type change just moved. Also: a Residential subject's size field is labeled "Property size (SF)" again instead of "Living area (SF)".

title: Plainer hero and Market Explorer copy
details: The signed-in hero now says "Find out what a property is worth, with comparables to prove it." in place of "Know what the building is worth before you make the call." — a plainer ask that keeps the one claim no other valuation widget can copy (the number arrives with cited evidence), and "a property" stops assuming the reader owns the building, which brokers and buyers don't. The Market Explorer section promises "We'll build the report" instead of "the page", and its intro dropped two lines of self-explanation: the "(about a minute)" aside and the "Standing market pages, separate from the property valuation above" note, an internal distinction no visitor asked about.

title: The city check learns Ft. Worth and Mt. Vernon
details: GeoNames spells out Fort and Mount the way it spells out Saint, so "industrial Ft. Worth TX" was refused as an unknown city (live-verified) while "Fort Worth" sailed through. The Market Explorer's city check now expands a leading Ft/Mt abbreviation the same way it already expanded St. Also corrected a stale comment claiming the search cache makes a re-explore free for 7 days (the TTL has been 30 days since 2026-08-03), and CLAUDE.md now documents the city check so the three-variant rule doesn't get simplified away.

title: Market Explorer checks the city is real before billing a search
details: A typo'd or nonexistent city ("industrial Bosie ID") now gets a friendly error instead of spending a billed search and potentially publishing a misspelled market page. Keyless Zippopotam check with a punctuation-variant retry; fails open if the service is down.

title: The building size field stops truncating its own instructions
details: Its placeholder read "auto from recc" on the home page, which looks like a typo on the most-seen screen the site has. The box is the 1fr column of the search form's 2.2fr/1fr grid and then splits again into two number inputs around a "to", so "auto from records" needed 135 pixels of a 124 pixel box and clipped mid-word. Measured across widths it was worse than it looked: at the two-column breakpoint the box is about 69 pixels of usable text, where the second input's "max (optional)" clipped as well, so no descriptive placeholder could ever have fitted there. The placeholders are now simply "auto" and "max", with roughly double the room to spare at the tightest width, and the sentence they were failing to carry moved to a standing hint line under the field: leave it blank and we'll pull the size from public records. That fact was previously stated only inside the collapsed property-details section and in a placeholder that vanished the moment anyone typed. The hint and the footprint-estimate note are made mutually exclusive in CSS rather than JavaScript, because four separate places already toggle that note and none of them should have to know a second element exists; a welcome side effect is that the note now replaces a line instead of adding one, so the form no longer shifts when an estimate lands.

title: A building-footprint size no longer poses as a lot size on Land searches
details: The confirm dialog's footprint pass estimates a BUILDING's square footage (footprint × levels) into the size field while the visitor reads the modal. Its own Land guard checks the property type when the estimate starts — which worked when the type dropdown was set before submitting, but type-at-verification moved the pick INTO the dialog, so the guard now usually runs before there is a type to check. Result: pick Land in the dialog and the building-derived estimate stayed in the box, relabeled Lot size (SF) with the footprint note still under it, and rode the billed search as the parcel's size — the value hero then multiplied land $/SF by a number that was never the lot. The moment a type change resolves to Land, a machine-written size is now dropped the same way an address change already drops it (same provenance markers, same helper); a size the visitor typed is theirs and survives, whatever the type. Verified in a browser: the Land pick clears the estimate and its note, an Industrial pick keeps the estimate and sends it with the search, and a typed size rides a Land search untouched.

title: Outbound email wears the letterhead
details: The last unbranded surface a customer touches. Every customer-facing email — share invites, BOV follow-ups, broker confirmations, password resets, market alerts — now carries a branded HTML part: the wordmark over the red rule the printed report already uses, the body set cleanly with bare URLs turned into links, and a brand-contact footer. Built by the new pure email-shell.js from the same plain text each call site already sends, so the text remains the source of truth and the fallback part; no email's copy changed, and plain-text clients lose nothing. Table layout, inline styles, system fonts, and no images, so the letterhead survives Outlook and image-blocking clients — the wordmark is text on purpose. Owner-facing notifications stay deliberately plain. Six new tests pin the contract: every word of the text survives, hostile text cannot become markup, and the public contact address appears while the owner's personal inbox never does. This closes the design-system list: the touch icon it also carried turned out to have already shipped with the favicon work.

title: My Desk becomes the owner's book
details: Directions K and L from the design system, approved together. The desk opens with a ledger line that answers the daily question first: how many properties, what everything is worth combined (on the warm emphasized cell), which way the book moved since the last checks, and how many markets are watched. The portfolio's boxed card grid becomes a statement table that closes on that same combined total under the double rule — one sum feeds both, so they cannot disagree — and each row finally SHOWS the value-snapshot history the product has been saving on every re-run: a bare gray sparkline with the latest point in red, no axes, no animation. The watchlist feed becomes a briefing: each watched market is a ruled section with its median and trend beside the name, new comps as quiet statement rows, the red N-new label as the only accent, and a you're-caught-up line to close. Every desk section head (Portfolio, Watchlist, Broker, Shares, Branding, Vault, Plan) now sits on an ink rule instead of floating as a gray label, so the page reads as one document. All arithmetic is client-side over data the existing APIs already return; no server change, no migration, and opening the desk still costs nothing.

title: One pixel of curvature stops separating tiles from cards
details: The radii half of the consistency audit. The report's value tiles and highlight tiles sat at 5px inside 6px cards, and the loading skeleton spelled the same 6px as .375rem — the kind of almost-right that reads as unfinished without anyone being able to say why. All three join the 6px frame tier. The audit's original claim that nine rounded-md controls also needed to move turned out wrong on inspection: they are all cards, and rounded-md IS the 6px frame tier, so they were already canonical and stay. Every other radius tier (3px badges, 4px deep CTAs, 8px app controls, 12px modals, full pills) was confirmed deliberate and untouched.

title: One warm gray scale, everywhere on light paper
details: The grays half of the consistency audit. index.html carried two unrelated gray systems: the design system's warm ink scale and, interleaved with it on the same screens, roughly 180 uses of the cool blue-tinted Tailwind slate utilities that predate the redesign — most visibly on modals and inputs, which bordered cool while every report surface bordered warm. Every cool gray moved to its warm twin (slate-900/800 to ink, 700/600/500/400 down the ink scale ending at the AA gray the accessibility pass already chose, borders to the frame and hairline tones, hover washes to the paper wash). The dark bookends — modal backdrops, the footer, the logo tile — keep slate deliberately, per the token comment's own rule, and the token comment now documents the swept recipes. The internal dashboards already ran this scale as CSS tokens; the public app now matches them.

title: The comp table and report tabs work by keyboard, and the last tiny buttons grew up
details: The sortable column headers were click-only: no way to reach them by keyboard, no announced sort state, and the little triangle read out to screen readers as a stray character. Each header now contains a real button, so Enter and Space sort, the active column announces ascending or descending, and the triangle is marked decorative. The Market Report and Analysis tabs likewise carried no semantics beyond a red underline; they are now a proper tab strip, with the selected state announced and the arrow keys switching between them. And the remaining under-sized touch targets got real hit areas: the export toolbar row, the All Sales Leases filter, the vault's delete-import control and its publish toggle, none of which moved a pixel of layout. Three small companions rode along: the 1031 deadline widget now announces its computed dates to screen readers, the rotating example addresses in the search field darkened to pass the contrast floor, and the signup prompt reached from a market page's Explore link now says up front that browsing whole markets is part of Pro while free reports work on any single address, matching the notice that already appears after signup.

title: Four small corrections to the new property-type picker
details: Cleanup pass on the type-at-verification work, all four found by review rather than by anyone hitting them. The type picker under the address field could be left open while something else resolved the type behind it, so it sat there highlighting the old value while the line directly above it said something newer; any re-render of that line now closes it, because every path that redraws it has already answered the question the picker was asking. Clicking the picker also lit the address field's red focus ring, since the picker lives inside the address cell and the ring fires on anything focused within it; the ring is now scoped to the cell's own input. That scoping carries a trap worth recording: Chrome stops matching :focus once the browser WINDOW loses focus but keeps matching :focus-within, so writing the two halves of the rule with different focus notions made them disagree exactly then and stripped the ring off a legitimately focused address field. Both halves now use the same notion. The status line also gained a polite live region, because the type can change without the visitor touching anything, when map data resolves it or an address's remembered type is recalled, and that line was the only thing saying so, silently, to a screen reader. Last, My Desk's Refresh valuation set the property type without re-rendering the type-specific detail inputs, so a refresh could run with the previous type's fields on screen; it now syncs them the way every other programmatic type change already did. Verified in a browser: the ring appears for the address input and the size input and not for the picker buttons, an open picker closes when a remembered type lands, picking still applies the type, its recommended lookback and its detail fields, and Land still relabels the promoted size field.

title: The pricing modal becomes a rate card with a $0 anchor
details: Directions I and J from the design system, approved together. The two boxed plan tiles and the separate single-report strip become one ruled rate-card ledger in the report hero's own geometry: a FREE column anchors the left edge and says plainly what $0 already buys — the same value range Pro sees, which comp-gate's locked_basis makes literally true — so the paid cells read as an upgrade from something real rather than a paywall. Pro sits on the warm emphasized cell, Founding keeps its seat counter, prices set in Georgia like every other number on the site. Behind a quiet Compare-plans toggle, the full Free-vs-Pro comparison renders as an itemized statement whose bottom line is the price, sealed under the double rule; its figures restate entitlements.js (4 comps, 3-year window, 5 exports a month with a free account). The three Stripe buttons kept their exact data-plan values and ids, so checkout, the founding show/hide, and the contextual $20 strip all work unchanged.

title: The market pages' Explore link stops dying silently for free accounts
details: Every market page carries an Explore this market link into the Address Explorer, which is a Pro feature. For anyone without Pro the link was a double failure. First, during page boot the app briefly believes the pre-Pro defaults before the server's answer arrives, and in that window it consumed the link's one-shot intent and fired a doomed market search straight into a 403, invisibly. Second, a visitor who followed the link and created a free account, exactly what the page asked of them, landed on a plain search form with no sign of what they clicked or why nothing happened. The boot race is closed with an explicit did-the-server-actually-answer flag, so the link's intent is never spent on a guess: a Pro account still gets the panel opened and prefilled, and a deployment with the paid tier off still gets the old free-for-everyone behavior. And a signed-in account without Pro now gets a plain note that the Explorer is part of Pro, with the pricing panel one click away and a reminder that free reports work on any single address, with the property type from the market page already filled in. The note names no market and interpolates nothing from the URL.

title: The landing stat strip stops implying nothing is ever charged
details: The first tile said Free / Every report, two scrolls above an FAQ describing the $129 Pro plan and the $20 single-report unlock. Every report is genuinely free to run, but next to paid tiers that wording read as denying them. It now says Free / To start, the wording the approved front-door design card carried; the other three tiles were already made honest in the same day's audit (Up to 12 comps, ~1 min).

title: Lost visitors get a page instead of a bare Not found
details: Market pages are indexed by Google and explorer-generated pages come and go, so arriving on a dead slug is a normal event, not an edge case. It used to be answered with an unbranded white page reading Market not found, with no link anywhere. Every visitor-facing miss, a dead market slug, an expired explorer preview, a delisted broker profile, and any mistyped address, now renders a small branded page with the site header, a route back to a free valuation, and a link to the live market directory. The status stays 404 so crawlers still drop the URL, the page is noindexed, and the machine surfaces are untouched: API paths and non-GET requests keep their plain text bodies, and the admin routes keep denying their own existence.

title: The landing stats stop selling the wrong product in both directions
details: The stat strip promised 3 to 6 cited comps and a 40 second search. Both were wrong opposite ways: the search asks the model for up to 12 comps and dense markets deliver them, while the measured wall clock is 40 to 70 seconds of report writing alone, with a full search landing around a minute or more. A visitor timing their first search saw the product take double what the page promised, at the exact moment it was supposed to be proving itself. Now says up to 12 comps and about a minute.

title: A phone and accessibility pass over the whole app
details: Four small defects, each felt by every visitor on the wrong side of them. Tapping any input used to zoom an iPhone in and leave it zoomed, because iOS Safari does that to any input under 16 pixels; the address field, the market filter, the vault filters and the 1031 date boxes are all 16 pixels now. The muted gray used for every secondary caption and table header measured below the accessibility contrast floor on every light background; it is now a slightly deeper gray that clears the bar everywhere while keeping the calm look, with the footer left alone because it already passed on navy. Escape now closes whichever modal is open, through the same path as that modal's own cancel button; before, it was a dead key in most modals, and pressing it with the pricing modal open silently closed the report underneath while the modal stayed up. And the per-comp Exclude control, the primary action in the phone card list, had a tap target the height of its own text; it now has a real hit area without moving a pixel of layout.

title: Exports are named after the building, and an empty report offers a human
details: Every CSV used to download as market-comps.csv and every image as market-comp-report.png, so a broker who exported five properties got five indistinguishable files carrying a retired product name onto their clients' machines. All three formats now share the Excel export's rule: compninja followed by the property address. And a search that finds no comps used to end in a bare No comps found; it now says what actually works, trying a longer lookback since thin markets usually do have sales further back, and offers the free Broker Opinion of Value through the same lead flow as the hero button, which is the site's best outcome arriving at the visitor's worst moment.

title: A test fixture that only existed on one machine was silently blocking every deploy
details: The new public-pages test asserted against /market/industrial-boise-id — a market that lives only in a git-ignored local file on the machine that wrote the test, not in the committed seed. The suite passed there and failed on Render's fresh disk, and since the deploy now runs the tests before the server starts (the prestart gate added the same day), every deploy after that test landed was refused: production quietly served an hour-old build while two pushes in a row reported success. Nothing external says a deploy was blocked rather than slow, which is how it went unnoticed until a routine post-deploy check timed out; the Render dashboard's Events tab had the answer. The test now derives its market from the committed seed file, so the fixture exists on every machine that has the repo — which is the hermeticity the test's own header comment already promised. The deploy skill now records both lessons: a successful push proves nothing about the deploy, and a fixture leaning on a git-ignored file will pass locally and fail the gate.

title: Market pages speak the report's language: a ledger strip and a statement table
details: Directions G and H from the design system, both approved by the owner on claude.ai/design, applied to every market page in one pass since they all render from one function. G: the four boxed stat tiles become one ruled ledger line — hairline dividers, the median $/SF emphasized on warmer paper with the red label — the same geometry the report's value hero and the vault's book line already use. The old Comps window tile is gone rather than restyled: it set a whole date range at display size, which wrapped into two ragged lines on the live page, and the snapshot line above already states the same window at text size. H: the comps table trades its grey web header for the statement treatment — an ink rule under the header, and a closing median row sealed under a double rule. That closing figure deliberately quotes the page's own headline statistic rather than recomputing it, so the median cell at the top of the page and the row at the bottom of the table can never disagree; the table now visibly proves the number the page leads with. Scoped so the brokers page, the vault, and the markets directory keep their own table styling. Verified against a real boot at desktop and phone widths: ledger stacks with bottom hairlines, no horizontal overflow, table still scrolls in its own container.

title: The brokers page's Submit a comp button led nowhere
details: Both copies of the Submit a comp call to action on /brokers pointed at /#submit-comp, and under the account wall that could never work: the wall decides what the homepage serves on the server, and a URL fragment is never sent to a server. So a logged-out broker clicking the single most important button on the broker page landed on the marketing page, where there is no submission form and no such anchor, and nothing happened at all. Since broker-contributed comps are the entire verified-comp layer, this was the acquisition path for the site's best data quietly failing in silence. The link is now /?submit=comp, a query the wall can actually see, added to the same one-value allowlist that already lets the signup and sign-in doors through. No account is required to reach the form, which matches the endpoint behind it, because a broker contributing a comp is exactly the visitor who does not yet have a reason to hold an account.

title: The pricing FAQ said there was no subscription, and said it to Google too
details: The cost answer on the landing page still read "Nothing. Reports are free and there is no subscription. We only ask for your contact details when you export a report." All three claims had stopped being true: Pro sells at $129 a month, a founding annual plan at $990 is live, a single report unlocks for $20, and the account wall asks for an email before the first report rather than at export. The reach was wider than the visible page, because that one array feeds both the FAQ accordions and the FAQPage structured data, so a search result could answer a question about this product by denying the product. The answer now states the free tier honestly (a full report, no card, four itemized comps, three years back) and then names the paid options, with the numbers taken from the same places that charge them.

title: Every public page now offers a way in, and the market CTA carries the market
details: None of the pages that visitors actually arrive on from Google, the 38 market pages plus the market directory, the brokers page, the 1031 guide and both legal pages, carried a single sign-in or create-account control anywhere in the header. A returning customer landing on a Boise industrial page had nothing to click, and a new visitor's only route was the body call to action, which was itself a bare link to the homepage: under the wall that answers with the landing page, so someone asking to value their building was handed another marketing page and had to find Create account a second time. The shared header now carries both doors, and swaps them for My Desk and Run a report once a session cookie is present, the same rule and the same caching contract the landing page uses, so a member is never told to create an account they already have and no cached copy outlives a sign-out. The market page's primary button now carries the property type the visitor was reading about, and the app honours it over the type remembered from their last visit. One new test file pins all of it, including the header on every page in both states.

title: The front door leads with the report instead of describing it
details: Directions E and F from the design system, both approved by the owner on claude.ai/design. E: the hero on /how-it-works (which is also what a logged-out visitor gets at the root while the account wall is up) was a column of text beside an empty half-row, with the product itself below the fold. A compact report now sits in that empty half: the address, the value ledger, three badged comps, and the median. It stacks claim-first below 900px. F: the sample exhibit further down was a layout no report has ever produced, and it predated the ledger and statement table that shipped this week, so the one place a visitor saw the product misrepresented it. It is now a faithful miniature of the real thing: title block with a ruled meta strip, ink-ruled sections, the ledger, and the comp table closing on its double-ruled median. The illustrative figures were also made arithmetically honest, which they were not before: the median is the true median of the five comps shown, the Likely value is that median times the building size, and Low and High are the size times the cheapest and dearest comp. Anyone who checks the numbers on a page whose whole argument is showing its work now finds that they hold.

title: Market page headings say what people search for
details: The 38 market page <title>s moved to "Industrial Comps in Dallas, TX" on 2026-08-06 because that is the phrase owners and brokers type; the <h1>s were left saying "Industrial Property Values in Dallas, TX". Google weights both, so every market page was giving a mixed signal about its own subject. marketTitle() now returns the same string as marketPageTitle()'s base, which aligns the h1, the JSON-LD name, the breadcrumb leaf and /markets' hasPart entries in one change. The related-markets links are unchanged on screen ("Industrial - Dallas, TX") because the string replace that trims them was updated in step; that needle is a silent dependency, so a route test now pins both the h1/title agreement and the trimming. The cost is real and was weighed: "property values" reads more plainly as a heading than "comps", but consistency with the title is worth more than the nicer phrase.

title: The vault dresses like the report: a book ledger and statement tables
details: Vault A and Vault B from the design system, both approved by the owner on claude.ai/design. A: the trust line — the broker's proof that their book stays private — stops being a sentence in a gray box and becomes a ruled ledger strip in the report hero's own cell geometry: Comps, Priced sales, Median $/SF, and Published, with serif figures and green spent on exactly one cell, Published, because zero staying zero is the number the page exists to prove. B: every table header on the page now closes under an ink rule, and the comps table seals with the median $/SF of the current view under a double rule — the same figure the market cards and the year chart lead with, so the three views read against each other; it hides when the view holds no priced sales rather than ruling off a blank. The Publish control becomes the statement's badge chip, green only once published — the deliberate act, not the default. Markup and CSS plus two small script additions; every behavior — sorting, filtering, publish confirms, the first-run page — is untouched.

title: The printed report becomes a document, not a webpage on paper
details: Directions C and D from the design system, both approved by the owner on claude.ai/design. C: the report header prints as a proper title block — the box dissolves, the address sets large in the display face under the red kicker, and the meta chips flatten into a ruled strip stating property type, size, window, and date. D: every report card's rounded web border dissolves on paper and its heading becomes an uppercase micro-label sitting on an ink rule, so the page reads as one continuous ruled analysis document; only the value ledger and the statement table keep their frames, as the exhibits they are. Print and PDF only — the screen and the PNG export are untouched. Two long-standing print flaws fixed on the way: the market-position chart printed empty when the report was printed before the chart had ever been scrolled into view (its entrance animation left every mark at opacity zero, and the print rules that force cards visible never reached the chart's own marks), and the 'Enter an NOI to unlock the analysis tools' prompt — an instruction to click things — printed as noise.

title: The property type is now chosen at verification, never silently defaulted
details: Forgetting the property-type dropdown used to mean a confident Industrial report on an office building, because the dropdown defaulted to Industrial and nothing forced a look at it. The dropdown is gone from the form. The type now resolves at the address-verification step: the existing OpenStreetMap detection pre-fills it when the building's own map data names it, a per-address memory recalls what you ran last time, and when neither decides, the confirm dialog asks with six tap-to-pick buttons and refuses to run until one is chosen. A status line under the address always says what will run and offers a one-click change, which is also how a rendered report gets re-run under a different type. The freed slot in the form went to the building size field, promoted from the collapsed details section, because a typed size skips the model's records lookup and directly cuts search cost. Model-side type detection was considered and rejected: the prompt, cache, corpus and purchase records are all keyed per type before the search starts, so detection would need an extra classification call of roughly two to three cents and three to eight seconds per search, against zero for asking at the moment the visitor is already confirming the address. Costs and generation time are unchanged; the admin type-autofill tile now also counts dialog picks.

title: The landing page stops telling signed-in visitors to create an account
details: The how-it-works landing content is linked from inside the signed-in app, and it rendered the same chrome for everyone: Log in and Create account buttons, which to a member mid-session read as having been silently logged out. The page now checks for the presence of a session cookie and swaps that chrome for links back into the app — My Desk and running a report — while anonymous visitors keep the signup chrome exactly as before. Presence is the wall's own cheap rule: no database read on a page that renders synchronously, and a forged cookie buys the sight of different buttons and nothing else, because every real gate stays server-side. The signed-in variant is served with a no-store cache header so a cached copy cannot outlive a sign-out. Live-verified both ways: anonymous keeps the signup chrome and canonical, a cookie'd visit shows the desk link. (Shipped in a test-infrastructure commit by accident of timing between parallel work sessions; this entry documents it after the fact.)

title: A building's square footage stops following you to the next building
details: The size box is filled in for you in two places: the confirm dialog estimates it from the building's footprint, and a finished report fills in the size it looked up from public records. Neither was ever cleared when you moved on to a different address, so the next search valued the new building at the previous one's square footage. Worse, because the estimator only ever fills an EMPTY box, the new building's own footprint estimate was suppressed on top of that, and nothing on screen changed, which is what made it invisible. Caught while testing a thin market: a Calabasas office report's 152,400 SF rode into an Agoura Hills search picked straight off an Address Explorer chip, where the building is actually 61,700 SF, so the size driving the value was wrong by two and a half times. An automatically filled size is now tagged with the address it was looked up for and dropped the moment a different address is submitted, which also clears the way for the new building's own estimate. A size you typed yourself is left alone: it is yours, the same way a property type you picked survives an address edit.

title: The deploy gate can no longer be failed by two test runs racing each other
details: Since this morning, npm start runs the whole test suite before the server will boot, which quietly made a new demand of the suite: it now has to pass while ANOTHER copy of itself may be running, because every session's dev-server restart triggers one. It could not. The route tests boot real servers on ports counted up from fixed numbers, and a boot accepted whichever process answered the health check on its port — so when two runs raced, one run's test could adopt the other run's server, configured differently, and fail an assertion about wording or routes that its own server would have passed. This was reproduced deterministically by parking a stray server on the first fixed port: the suite adopted it and failed two tests. Two changes close it: every test server now asks the operating system for a free port instead of counting from a fixed base, and the health check now carries a per-boot identity token the server echoes back, so a test accepts only its own child and a foreign responder is ignored rather than adopted. Verified by running two full suites concurrently, repeatedly, with a decoy server still parked on the old fixed port: green throughout, where the decoy alone used to break the run.

title: Thin-market reports stop spending comp slots on rate-less lease listings
details: Two real searches in a row (Westlake Village industrial, then Calabasas office) came back unable to value the building: the value estimate is computed only from sale comps carrying a price and a size, and both reports had filled most of their rows with lease listings that did not even state a rate while priced sales sat one search away. The mixed-search prompt now says so explicitly: secure at least three priced, sized sale comps before spending searches on leases, treat a rate-less lease listing as the least useful row in the report, and prefer an older priced sale (disclosed in the summary, as the window rule already requires) over an unpriced listing. Verified against the exact failing case: the same Calabasas office search that returned one priced sale and four rate-less leases now returns two priced sales, enough for the value range, including an in-window sale the old prompt never found. Cached reports are untouched; the rule only shapes new searches.

title: The report parser and the purchase key move into tested modules, and drift now fails the tests
details: The rest of the roadmap's extraction list is done. Everything that turns the model's raw text into a report — the JSON parse with its salvage rescue, the em-dash scrub, the compact comp encoding and its re-expansion — now lives in report-parse.js with tests pinning each behavior, and the identity a $20 single-report purchase is keyed on lives in report-id.js. The part a changelog reader should care about: the browser and the server each build that identity string separately, and until today only a pair of warning comments kept them in agreement. A new test now compiles the browser's actual key-builder out of index.html and proves both sides hash to the same key, so if a future edit ever makes them drift, the test suite fails immediately — instead of the failure mode the comments warned about, where a bought report quietly stops matching itself and the buyer's exports start counting against their free allowance.

title: The homepage is a page again
details: Since the account wall shipped, an anonymous visit to / answered a redirect to /how-it-works, the root URL was dropped from the sitemap, and Search Console confirmed Google had never crawled the redirect's target. So the strongest URL the site has - the one every brand search and every typed-in domain points at - was a detour to a page the index didn't hold. The root now renders the landing content itself: a logged-out visitor gets the full how-it-works page at / with a 200, a signed-in member still gets the app, and nothing about enforcement moved an inch (the wall was always really enforced at /api/comps, and still is). While the wall is up, /how-it-works serves the same content and declares / as its canonical, so the two URLs pool their signals instead of splitting them; the sitemap lists / and drops the duplicate. Turning the wall off still restores the pre-wall site exactly, including /how-it-works as its own page. One knock-on effect paid for the whole change: every market page's Get my free valuation button points at /, and until now an anonymous visitor who arrived on a Boise comps search and clicked it was bounced through a redirect to a generic explainer. Now the button lands on a real page. /desk still redirects - it is a personal workspace with nothing to show a logged-out visitor - but its target is the new front door at / rather than /how-it-works.

title: The Address Explorer marks which addresses answer instantly
details: Some explorer addresses already have a report in the 30-day search cache, which means clicking one costs nothing and answers in about a second - but nothing told the visitor which ones. Cached rows now carry a small Instant mark. The cache is keyed by an opaque hash of the whole request, correct for correctness and useless for the question which addresses have a recent report, so the address itself is now recorded alongside each cache entry: two nullable columns from migration 020, written by a separate best-effort update after the main cache write. Separate on purpose, and the reason is a scar rather than a preference: an unknown column in the main insert would quietly divert the whole cache to the ephemeral fallback file, which is the exact shape of the corpus outage that once went unnoticed for weeks. This way the deploy and the migration are safe in either order, and the worst a missing column can do is keep the badge dark. The badge is a nudge, not a contract - the real cache hit still requires the visitor's request to match exactly, and the explorer's deterministic flow is what makes that the common case. When it misses, the failure is one ordinary billed search, invisible to the visitor.

title: A red build can no longer replace a green one in production
details: Render deploys whatever lands on main, and CI has always been advisory: a red X on GitHub meant fix it now, but the broken code was already live. Worse, during GitHub's seven-hour Actions outage this week, four branches merged with no verdict at all - the checks were not failing, they were never being asked. The gap is now closed at the one chokepoint that does not depend on GitHub: npm start runs the whole check suite before the server will boot. A deploy whose syntax check or tests fail exits before listening, Render marks the deploy failed, and the previous green version keeps serving - even when Actions is down, which is precisely when the old setup was blind. The checks are the same fast, dependency-free suite CI runs (they finish in about two seconds, and the test harness clears every environment key that matters, so production credentials cannot change what they prove). Proven both ways before shipping: a deliberately red test blocked the boot entirely, and the green suite booted straight through. The owner's usual local launch by full node path is untouched - this rides the npm start path Render uses.

title: The comp table closes like an audited statement
details: Direction B from the design system, approved by the owner on claude.ai/design: the table header now ends under a strong ink rule, and the table itself closes with a median row sealed under a double rule — the accountant's mark for a final figure. The row shows the median $/SF of the full valuation set (the same statistic the chart's median line and the value hero read, locked comps included, curation respected), in the label and again under the $/SF column since the wide table scrolls. It hides on a leases-only filter and lives in its own tfoot so sorting never moves it.

title: A report that can't compute a value now offers the search that can
details: When fewer than two priced sale comps come back, the value hero shows dashes and explains why — and until now it stopped there, leaving the visitor to work out that a wider window focused on sales is usually the fix. That is exactly what solved a real case today: a Westlake Village industrial building at the default 24-month Sales & leases search returned four leases and one priced sale, so no estimate rendered; the same address re-run at 60 months, sales only, returned five priced sales and a full value range. The no-estimate message now carries one quiet button that runs that re-run — same address, type and building details, window widened to 60 months (or to the free tier's 36-month ceiling, which is as far as those accounts can look), focus set to sales only. It goes through the ordinary search path, so the cache, the free-search gate and the confirm step all apply unchanged, and because a re-run is a billed search it only ever fires on the visitor's own click, never automatically. The button stays away from the cases where it isn't the fix: a shortfall the visitor created by excluding comps (restoring one is free), a report that can already be valued per unit or per acre, someone else's shared report, and a search that was already sales-only at the widest window the account allows.

title: Market pages now open a door into the Address Explorer
details: Every market page's closing CTA gains a second link: "No specific address? Explore <city> <type> properties". It points at the explorer deep link that has existed since the explorer shipped but that nothing public ever linked to. The href is the one form the account wall never redirects, so the same static link serves everyone: an anonymous visitor gets the signup modal with the explorer input already filled in behind it, and a signed-in Pro member skips the modal and lands with the panel open and fetching that market's list. A route test pins the encoded link on a live-served market page.

title: The market key gets its own tested module, and learns to read Canadian addresses
details: marketOf(), the parse that turns a freeform address into the "City, ST" key the comp corpus is filed under, moved out of server.js into market.js with 19 tests pinning it — the same pure-module treatment the entitlement and gating rules already have. The parse is load-bearing: the corpus write side and read side must agree on it byte for byte, and until now nothing but a warning comment guarded that. One behavior change rode along, straight off the roadmap: Canadian addresses used to collapse to the literal key "Canada" (Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal would all have shared one corpus bucket the day non-USD reports are ever harvested); the parse now reads provinces like states, so "Toronto, ON, Canada" keys as "Toronto, ON". US addresses key exactly as before, which the tests prove.

title: The value hero reads as one ruled ledger line
details: The report's Low / Likely / High tiles are now a single bordered ledger row: hairline dividers between the three cells, the figures set in the site's Georgia display face, and red spent in exactly one place — the LIKELY label, whose cell sits on a slightly warmer paper. Picked as Direction A from the new CompNinja design system on claude.ai/design, where the owner compared variants before anything shipped. On phones the ledger stacks with bottom hairlines; the PNG, print, and CSV exports are untouched because the change is markup and CSS only.

title: The Address Explorer fills the form instead of firing the report for you
details: Clicking an address in the explorer used to submit the search immediately, so the confirm-property card popped up before the visitor had done anything but click a suggestion — it read as the site running off on its own. A click now just pastes the address into the form (and still snaps the property type to match the list it came from), the panel stays open so a different address can be swapped in, and the status line says what to do next. Running the report is the visitor's own click on Run a report, which goes through the ordinary confirm step: the map check still appears, so you always see the pin before the search is spent. Verified end to end against a local boot: click fills the field with no modal, submit shows the map card with the matched address.

title: A private comp's address stops being handed to a third party
details: Every comp on a report gets a map pin, and the pin is found by sending the address to a geocoder. That was fine when every comp came from public records, and stopped being fine when a broker's own vault comps started appearing in their reports: the address of an off-market deal was leaving the broker's own browser and going to OpenStreetMap's public geocoder, along with their IP, purely to place a dot on a map. Two things changed. A private comp that already knows where it is is no longer geocoded at all, which sounds obvious but was not true: the map deliberately re-geocodes every comp, treating whatever coordinates it arrived with as a rough first guess to be improved on, which is the right behaviour for a public comp and the wrong one for a private one. And a private comp that does still need locating now goes only to our own proxy, which asks the US Census, a government service with no account and no advertising business behind it. It never falls through to the third party. The cost is honest and accepted: a private comp the Census cannot place gets no pin rather than an approximate one, which is the same rule already applied to building photos, where showing the actual property or nothing beats showing the house next door. A refused lookup is deliberately not remembered, because the address cache is shared with ordinary public comps and remembering it would deny them a fallback they are still entitled to. Nothing about public comps changed. This is the display half of a two-part change agreed with Owen; the other half lets a broker put coordinates straight into their upload, at which point their addresses stop being sent anywhere at all.

title: A broker's private address stops needing to leave the building to draw a map pin
details: A private vault comp was geocoded by address, from the broker's own browser, on every report that included it. So the address of an off-market deal left in a URL query string and reached the US Census geocoder, and on a miss OpenStreetMap, with the broker's IP attached, purely to place a dot on a map. The vault's whole pitch is that nothing in it is ever read out, and a broker reasonably reads that as covering the address of the deal and not only its price. This is the storage half of the fix, and it deliberately does nothing on its own: the map still geocodes every comp unconditionally, so until the display guards land these coordinates are stored and ignored. That was the agreed shape of the work rather than an oversight, because both halves are useless alone and neither had to wait for the other. Coordinates now live on the building, not the deal. Two sales on one property share one location, and storing it per deal would keep two copies free to disagree, which is the drift this repo puts warnings on elsewhere. Brokers supply them in two optional spreadsheet columns that many CRM and MLS exports already carry, which means the honest version of this feature contacts nobody at all. Import-time geocoding, where the server would look up the ones nobody supplied, was deliberately not built: it is where a rate limit and a retry policy would have to live, its remaining privacy gain over this is second-order, and with no real vault uploads in existence the question it answers cannot be measured yet. The column that would record it is declared anyway so that adding it later is a code change rather than another migration. Three things were harder than they looked. The spec said to reuse the existing number parser, which rejects negative numbers, so it would have refused every longitude in the United States including the one in the spec's own worked example. Coordinates cannot ride on the comp row at all, because there are no coordinate columns on that table and an unknown column makes PostgREST refuse the entire upload rather than the one field. And they cannot travel in the property upsert either, because that upsert replaces the columns it is given, so a broker's second import — the one where they did not bother filling the columns in again — would have silently wiped the coordinates their first import supplied. They are written by a separate patch that only ever fills a building with none, which also means a location is never quietly overwritten by a re-import.

title: CI can be started by hand, for the days GitHub cannot start it itself
details: GitHub had a seven hour Actions outage today. For most of it, pushes and pull requests were simply not creating test runs at all: GitHub was throttling the webhooks that carry those events down to about fifteen percent to keep the rest of the system alive. The tests were never failing. They were never being asked. Four branches merged into the live site during that window with no result recorded, and since every merge to main deploys automatically, code shipped unchecked, not because a test went red but because nothing ever ran. What made it worse is that no result looks almost exactly like a result nobody has got round to yet. The gap this exposed is that the only way to ask for a test run was to push something, which is precisely the mechanism that had stopped working. There is now a Run workflow button on the Actions tab that works on any branch. It is a direct request rather than a webhook, so it keeps working when pushes are being dropped, and it is also the way to get a verdict on something already merged without inventing a pointless empty commit to trigger one. It adds a way to start the checks and no way to skip them. Everything from today was verified by running the same four checks locally instead, which takes about two seconds, and all of them passed.

title: The vault is a dashboard now, not a list of rows
details: A broker with 400 comps learned nothing from 400 rows. /vault now opens on their own markets: one card per market and property type showing the median $/SF, how many comps and priced sales sit behind it, the years covered and anything they have published. Clicking a card filters everything below it, and clicking it again clears it. Under the filter sits a median-$/SF-by-year chart and, where a broker has transacted on the same building more than once, that property's own deal history. Three things were fixed on the way that were not the point of the task but mattered more than some of it. The page was asking the API for its default page size of 200, so a broker with 400 comps was being shown half their vault and the header said 200 with nothing to suggest anything was missing; it now asks for the whole book and says so out loud if there is more than a thousand. Filtering used to go back to the server on every change, which cannot work once there is a rollup, because the browser would only ever hold the slice it was already looking at; it is now instant and costs no round trip. And the repeat-property grouping matched on street address alone, which on the first realistic test book merged a Boise building and a Meridian building at the same house number into one property with a three-deal history that never happened; it groups on market and address, and names the market on every row. Every $/SF on the page comes from the stored per-square-foot column, which is written for sales only, so a book of leases shows its comp count rather than a number invented by dividing rent by size. A price trend is only drawn when there are priced sales in at least two years, and says why when there are not. An empty vault looks exactly as it did before: the dashboard hides itself, and a first-time broker still lands on the uploader with nothing in the way.

title: The first five minutes in the vault
details: A broker who had just paid opened their vault and found a count of zero, an uploader, and three empty tables. The only way forward was to download a template, map their book of business into it, and come back, which is homework with no visible reason to do it. The one thing they could have done immediately sat at the bottom of the page under a heading about something else. An empty vault now opens on two steps instead. The first explains what uploading actually buys: your closed deals become a private comp set that appears inside your own valuation reports and moves the number on them, and is never exported, shared, published or shown to another broker. It also says the part that removes the most hesitation, which is that only four of the ten columns are required and price is not one of them, so deals with undisclosed prices still count. The second step needs no spreadsheet at all: name the markets you work and you start seeing owners in them asking for a valuation. That takes about ten seconds and works on a completely empty vault, which means nobody has to do the homework before getting anything back. The zeros and the empty tables are simply hidden until there is something to put in them, because a header row with nothing underneath reads as a broken page rather than a new one, and there were three of those stacked up. The privacy promise that the counter used to carry is now said in words in the panel, so it is not lost. One case is deliberately not treated as a first run: a broker whose import was rejected, or who has deleted every comp out of one, has been through the door already, and greeting them with Start here would read as their work having been thrown away.

title: Three server strings were still selling a plan that cannot be bought
details: The one-product decision landed in the code on 5 August and in the site's words on 6 August, but three strings in server.js were missed by both because they live in 403 bodies rather than in any page. All three said the lead inbox or the private vault was "part of the broker plan", which is a product that was removed from the checkout map and whose Stripe price was deleted, so anyone who read it would go looking for something they cannot buy. Two of them are unreachable in practice: the vault page now catches its own 403 before the generic error render, so the server's wording never reaches the gate, and the /api/vault routes are only reachable behind a page that already refused. The third is not. The lead inbox has no 403 branch of its own, so vault-page.js renders the server's string verbatim into the leads panel, which makes it product copy that happened to be written in a place where product copy is not usually reviewed. It now says Pro, like the other three places, and carries a comment saying it reaches the screen so the next person editing it knows what it is. The comment above the gate named the removed plan too and no longer does.

title: The site said there were two products. There is one.
details: The vault was built as a separate broker subscription, and then the decision was made that there is one subscription with the vault as part of it. The code changed on 5 August; the words did not, so the site was still describing a product nobody can buy. Three places now say the same thing. The Pro box gained a line for the private vault, which is the whole point of the decision: a subscription that quietly includes the largest thing built this month was selling the smaller half of itself. The plan card on your account says it too, because a paying member who never learns they have a vault is the clearest way to still be running two products after deciding to run one. And the vault's own locked screen said it was part of the broker plan and pointed at the brokers page, which sent anyone who read it looking for a plan that does not exist, and at a page about earning a Verified badge, which is free and unrelated; it now says Pro and points at your plan. One thing is now said out loud that was not being said at all: the vault closes when a subscription ends, and a broker who uploaded their book of business and then finds the door shut deserves to know nothing in it was deleted. Nothing is. The only ways vault data is ever removed are the broker deleting an import themselves, and deleting the account. The handbook was stale here in four separate ways, still describing the removed plan, its deleted Stripe price, a rule that has since been reversed, and a vault it called not built which has been live for two days.

title: A broker's own vault comps show up inside their own report
details: Comps a broker uploads to their private vault used to just sit in the vault. They now appear in that broker's own valuation reports alongside the public ones, badged "From your vault" and counted in the number at the top — on a sample report the two private sales moved the likely value from $8,250,000 to $8,375,000, which is the whole point of the feature: your own deals should move your own valuation. This is the display half; the server half that fetches them and fences them off is a separate change. The badge is deliberately not the green Verified one. Verified is a public claim, earned by vouching for a comp in the public records and taking visible credit for it, and a private row has earned none of it — "From your vault" states where the row came from instead of asserting anything about it. Private comps are ordinary comps in every other respect: they sort, filter, curate and pin on the map like the rest, which is what let the whole feature land as styling rather than as plumbing. Where they are not ordinary is on the way out. They are stripped from the CSV, the Excel file, the saved PNG and the printed page, because those are the files a broker hands to a client (a shared link is stripped server-side, which is the stronger guarantee since it never trusts the browser). That leaves the exported table shorter than the one on screen while the valuation above it still counts every comp, so all four exports now say so in plain words rather than leaving a gap that reads as lost data. A broker with an empty vault sees no line, no badge and no change at all.

title: Every market page title was being cut off in Google, and the cut part was the useful part
details: Measured against the live site: all 38 market pages carried titles of 68 to 82 characters, and Google renders about 60. So every one of them was truncated mid-phrase in search results. The two longest pieces were also the two doing the least work. The date range, '(Dec 2024 - Jul 2026)', spent roughly 22 characters on something nobody has ever typed into a search box, and the '| CompNinja' suffix spent another 12 on a brand with no search demand yet. What got cut was the tail of the part actually carrying the query terms. The wording was wrong too: 'Property Values in' is not a phrase people search, where 'comps', '$/SF' and 'cap rates' are exactly what owners and brokers type. Titles are now '<Type> Comps in <City>, <ST> | $/SF & Cap Rates', which lands between 44 and 57 characters across all 38 pages and drops the whole clause rather than cutting mid-word if a longer city name ever arrives from the Explorer, which generates these pages on demand. Dropping the brand is a deliberate trade and not an oversight, worth revisiting once brand searches actually appear in Search Console. marketTitle() is untouched and still supplies the on-page heading and the related-market link text, where there is no length budget and the plainer wording reads better; the comps window it used to advertise is still on the page as its own tile. Three other pages were over the limits too: how-it-works had a 199-character description and a title, 'How CompNinja Works', addressed to people who already knew the name, which under the account wall is the first thing every anonymous visitor and every brand search now sees; brokers and the market directory both had descriptions past the 160 Google renders. Verified by booting the server and re-fetching all 43 sitemap URLs: zero titles over 60, zero descriptions over 160, and no page doubling the brand suffix, which is a mistake this pass made once and the check caught.

title: The market pages stop being a black box: Search Console can verify the site
details: Thirty-eight market pages sit in sitemap.xml and they are the whole organic acquisition strategy right now, but nobody could see whether Google had crawled a single one of them. analytics_events only ever records people who already arrived and did something, so a page that is never indexed and a page that is indexed and ignored look identical from inside the app: zero. Search Console is the view that distinguishes them, and the site had no verification of any kind, no meta tag and no file. It does now, driven by GOOGLE_SITE_VERIFICATION, which takes either the google<token>.html filename Search Console hands out or the bare token, since the one place this is ever typed is a Render env field. The FILE method rather than the meta tag, and the reason is the account wall: meta-tag verification fetches the property root, and under ACCOUNT_WALL / is a 302 to /how-it-works, so a tag placed there would never be seen and verification would fail without saying why. The file has its own route, reached before the static handler's allowlist can care about it, and the wall never touches it. A DNS TXT record does the same job and is better where there is registrar access, covering every subdomain and surviving any redirect rule; the two do not conflict. Unset, the route does not exist at all. Set but malformed, startup says so rather than answering 404 forever while the property quietly fails to verify. And the env var stays set for good, because Google re-fetches the file and unverifies the property when it stops answering.

title: Market pages show which brokers cover that market
details: The first step of the connection hub: a property owner looking at Boise industrial can see who works Boise industrial. A market page slug already IS a (market, property type) pair - industrial-boise-id - which is the identical key broker_coverage uses, so this belongs on the pages that already exist rather than on a directory of its own. The rules live in the pure, tested broker-directory.js because both of them are about a real person. TWO CONSENTS, NOT ONE: broker_coverage records which markets a broker wants LEADS from, which is a working preference and not permission to publish them; broker_profiles.public is the opt-in, it already existed, and it is false by default. Reading coverage as publication consent would put every broker who ever configured a lead inbox onto a public web page they never agreed to, and it would look completely fine. The public flag is enforced twice, in the query and again in the module, so a bug in either one alone cannot publish somebody, and only a literal true counts - the string true, the number 1 and an empty object are all rejected by test. NO CONTACT DETAILS: a listing carries name, company and a link to the profile page the broker opted into, never email or phone. The existing findBrokersForMarket carries both but feeds an owner-facing email and never reaches a browser; routing here is owner-mediated by design and a public directory is the reverse of that. It is an allowlist rather than a delete, so a column added to broker_profiles later cannot appear by default. Cached in-process with stale-while-revalidate exactly like MARKET_CREDIT, because market pages are cached SEO pages that render synchronously and must never wait on a database call; any failure keeps the previous map and the section simply does not render. It renders nothing at all today because no broker has yet signed up, opted public or set a coverage market - all three tables are empty - and a no-brokers-yet placeholder would advertise an empty network on a page whose job is to look like a market worth being in.

title: Broker comps get a property dimension, the indexes to slice by it, and a reporting view
details: Migration 016. The brief was to store broker comps in the shape reporting tools expect, with clean links to property, market, broker and date. Three of those four were already clean after 013: broker is a real foreign key to users, deal_date is a real date, and market is canonical text written by marketOf() and byte-identical to comp_corpus.market. The gap was property. address_key had been written on every row since 013 and read by nothing at all - no index, no table, no foreign key - and it is the one dimension a broker actually slices by, meaning everything I have done on this building. So 016 adds broker_properties, one row per building per broker, plus a nullable property_id on broker_comps, an idempotent backfill, the indexes the slicing needs, and a broker_comps_reporting view that resolves the dimensions for a BI tool. No market dimension and no date dimension: a market table would duplicate the corpus vocabulary and become a second thing to keep in sync, which this repo already has one of and marks with a warning, and a date dimension earns its place only against a fiscal calendar, which there is not one of. The migration is PURELY ADDITIVE - nothing dropped, nothing renamed - because the vault holds brokers uploaded books and there is no staging database to rehearse against; a test asserts that and fails the build if a destructive statement ever appears. property_id is nullable on purpose so that migrate-then-deploy and deploy-then-migrate both work with no window where an upload fails.
