The application links properties on write through linkVaultProperties(), which never throws: the dimension is an index onto a broker's book, not part of it, and losing a link costs a join while failing an upload costs a broker their spreadsheet. Two brokers who transacted on the same building get separate property rows, which is the privacy wall rather than a duplicate. The vault API's shape holds through all of it: toApiComp is now a real allowlist, so the four plumbing fields are omitted and a future storage column cannot reach the browser by default.

title: Google now has one CompNinja to point at, not five
details: This started as a request to set up a Google Business Profile and ended somewhere more useful, because CompNinja is not eligible for one. Google requires a business that customers can meet face to face, and names online-only businesses as excluded; since 2026 the default check is a video review looking for signage at the claimed address, stock and equipment inside, and a person present who can confirm they run it. There is nothing to film. The two obvious workarounds are worse than doing nothing: the registered agent address is a virtual office, which is excluded by name, and a home address would fail the same video review, and a listing created against the guidelines is suspended rather than merely rejected, which is far harder to undo than never having applied. What an online-only business gets instead of a map pin is a brand entity, and the site barely had one. Five server-rendered page types each described the company from scratch, or not at all: the only mention of an organization anywhere was a bare name on the how-it-works page, with no logo, no legal name, no contact address, and no identifier tying any of it together. Every page now carries one canonical Organization node, with the CompNinja LLC legal name, the logo, and the public info@compninja.co address, and the market pages, the markets directory, the brokers page, the broker profiles and how-it-works all reference that single node by id rather than restating it. The contact address is deliberately the public one and never the owner's personal inbox, and there is no sameAs list, because that field means profiles the business actually controls and inventing one would be a fabricated claim in public structured data. Add real profile URLs there when they exist. Verified against a real boot on all four reachable page types: the structured data parses, the identifiers line up, and nothing inlines a duplicate organization any more.

title: Blended comps: a broker's own vault comps inside their own report
details: A broker uploads private comps into their vault and until now they just sat there. They now appear inside that broker's own valuation reports alongside the public ones, flagged private:true and rendered as "From your vault", and they feed the valuation math because valuationComps() already reads includedComps(). The server half only: the display half is separate. The load-bearing rule is that blending happens at SERIALIZATION and nowhere else, mirroring the rule comp-gate.js already follows in the other direction. The cache write, harvestComps() and maybePublishMarketSnapshot() all keep seeing the public report; private comps enter inside the gate() closure, which is the single funnel every exit routes through. Blending any earlier fails silently in two ways: before the cache write, one broker's private book is served to the next visitor who searches that address, because search_cache is keyed by property and not by user; before the harvest, the comps enter the public corpus permanently with nothing alerting anyone, since that write path swallows its own errors by design. POST /api/share was the least obvious exit and is now closed too: it accepts the report FROM the browser, and a broker's browser holds a blended one, so the server strips private comps rather than trusting what it was handed. A vault comp deliberately claims no public provenance: not verified, which is a public claim earned by vouching in the public records, and not the enum default, which normalizes to estimate and would stamp a real closed transaction as guesswork. It carries source_type broker_vault instead. An empty vault returns the very same report object with no private_count key at all, so a non-broker's response is byte-identical to before the feature existed. Rules live in the pure blend-comps.js, 17 tests.

title: The broker vault page moves out of server.js into vault-page.js
details: renderVaultHTML was a 475-line block sitting in the middle of server.js. It is a web page, so it belongs to whoever owns the front end, but living inside server.js meant editing it was editing the server file — which made two of the four vault tasks collide with the server work by accident rather than by design. It now lives in vault-page.js, following the same pattern as broker-vault.js, broker-leads.js, comp-gate.js and the other extracted modules. Nothing about the code changed in the move: the rendered output was compared byte for byte across seven boot payloads (no boot, empty, the 401/403/503 refusals, an empty vault, and a populated vault including an XSS attempt in a comp note) and is identical in every case. Two dependencies came to light that a call-site scan alone would have missed, CN_LOGO and MARKET_CSS, which are the site's shared chrome used by seven other server-rendered pages. They are passed in as an argument rather than copied, because a second copy would drift from the first — server.js already carries a keep-the-two-in-step warning about exactly that hazard. The data is still resolved in server.js by vaultReadPayload, which owns the entitlement gate; this file only decides how that data is drawn, and a read that happened here would be a read outside the gate.

title: One subscription: every Pro member gets a private vault
details: The broker tier shipped on 2026-08-05 as a second plan, broker_monthly, modelled on the Ecosystem Plan sections 2 and 3 as a superset of Pro. The owner has decided against two products: there is one subscription, and the private vault is a capability of it. So broker_monthly is gone from the checkout plans map, STRIPE_PRICE_BROKER_MONTHLY is deleted rather than left unset, and canUseVault now tracks pro exactly. Nobody loses access, because that plan was never sellable: its Stripe price was never set, so checkout answered 503 for it and no subscription row in the wild can carry it. One rule reversed deliberately and the test that pinned it now pins the opposite: the vault used to fail closed on any plan name we could not recognize, which was right when an unnameable plan might have been a second product, and is wrong with a single product, because it would leave a paying customer holding a subscription that silently withheld half of what it sells. The vault still closes the moment a subscription lapses, still stays shut on a dark deployment, and is still not something a one-off report unlock can buy. The privacy wall is untouched: which accounts may open a vault is an entitlement question, what may be read out of one is enforced by separate tables read by separate functions.

title: CompNinja is account-only, and How it works is the front door
details: A new visitor used to land on the app itself and get one free search before being asked for an account. The funnel now sits at the front of the visit instead: an anonymous visitor is sent to /how-it-works, which explains the product and gained Log in and Create account controls in its header, under its headline and on its closing call to action. It also lost the red How it works label above that headline, which was redundant once the page stopped being somewhere you navigate to and became the place you arrive. The search form itself is replaced by a signup card until you have a free account. One lever runs all of it: ACCOUNT_WALL, on by default, which also forces GUEST_SEARCH_LIMIT to 0 rather than trusting two settings to agree, because a wall that is up while the API still hands out a free search is the one inconsistent state that would look correct in testing from either side. Setting ACCOUNT_WALL=off on Render reverses the whole thing in an environment edit with no deploy, and the startup log says loudly which state it is in. Two deliberate exemptions: a shared report link stays public, because that is the entire point of sharing, and it now renders with the signup card above it so a shared link becomes a funnel rather than a leak; and the ?auth= links from the front door serve the app, because the account modal lives only in index.html and would otherwise be unreachable behind a redirect loop. The routing decides on the presence of a session cookie and never on a validated session, because that check reads the database and this route runs on every page view; a forged cookie buys the sight of a locked form and nothing else, since the search itself is still refused server-side. Because Google no longer reaches the app, the product's WebApplication structured data moved onto /how-it-works and the sitemap stops listing a URL that now redirects. The accepted trade is real and worth writing down: all anonymous traffic now meets a signup form, including people arriving from a market page or a shared report, and the signup_gate events on Analytics are how that gets measured rather than guessed.

title: CI goes green again after the account wall
details: The boot smoke test fetched / and required the word CompNinja in the response, which had been a fine proxy for "the app renders" right up until the account wall shipped. With the wall on, which is the default and the intended state, an anonymous GET / answers 302 to /how-it-works; curl was not following redirects, so it received an empty body and the grep failed. CI went red on main for a healthy build, and every branch cut afterwards inherited the failure, which is exactly the noise that trains people to ignore a red X. The request now follows the redirect, so the assertion is the one that actually matters, an anonymous visitor lands on a rendered CompNinja page, and it holds identically whether the wall is on or off. Verified both ways locally against a real boot.

title: ADMIN_KEY tolerates stray whitespace, like every other secret
details: ADMIN_KEY was the only secret in server.js read without .trim(), and it locked the owner out of every dashboard for an hour. The value had been saved in Render with a trailing newline, because pressing Enter in that textarea inserts a character rather than submitting the form. secretMatches compares exact bytes, so the stored key was secret-plus-newline while the login box sent secret, and the two could never agree. What made it nearly undiagnosable is that the failure is invisible from every angle: Render does not display a stored value back to you (its edit boxes come back empty by design), the character renders in no UI, an HTTP header cannot carry a newline at all so the header path was structurally impossible to satisfy, and a wrong-whitespace key fails identically to a wrong key. DNS, the custom domain, two suspected services, a blueprint override and a failed deploy were all investigated and cleared before the actual field was inspected in the browser. Now trimmed at the constant, matching STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY, RESEND_API_KEY and the rest. Four route-level tests pin it, one server boot per whitespace form (newline, space, leading space, carriage return), each asserting the clean key authenticates through the header path the login box actually uses, and that a genuinely wrong key is still refused so trimming cannot decay into accepting anything. Deliberately route-level rather than a unit test on a helper: trimming the constant is only half of it, what has to hold is that the ROUTE authenticates, and a test against a trim helper would have passed all along.

title: Market pages can update themselves again
details: All 27 curated market pages were stamped 14 July and could never move: the publisher that refreshes pages from ordinary searches skipped any market a curated page owned, and reads always preferred the curated copy. Since that date is also what the sitemap reports to search engines, the pages were visibly ageing with no way out. A newer snapshot can now replace an older one, but only when it is at least as well evidenced, so a quiet month returning three sales can never overwrite a page built on twelve. Nothing extra is searched or billed: it reuses the data a search already paid for. The page, the directory card and the sitemap date are now read through one path, so they cannot disagree about which snapshot is showing.

title: The market directory can be searched
details: /markets listed every market as a card grid with no way to narrow it, which mattered more once the account wall made it the only market-finding page a signed-out visitor can reach. It now has a filter that matches on city, state or property type, and understands the words people actually use: warehouse finds industrial, apartments finds multifamily, and California works as well as CA. Several words narrow rather than widen, so warehouse texas lands on one market. Enter opens the first match. Nothing is searched or billed, the whole list is already on the page, so it works with no account and costs nothing.

title: Stop telling new visitors they used a free search they never had
details: With the account wall up the free-search allowance is zero, so nobody gets one. Five places still said "You have used your free search" anyway, including a hint under the search box that appeared on the very first page load, before the visitor had done anything. Every anonymous visitor on the site was reading it. The wording now depends on the configured allowance: at zero it simply asks for the free account, and where a free search really was spent it still says so. The two account prompts also stopped keeping their own copy of the sentence and now show whatever the server sent, so there is one place to change it rather than three that can drift.

title: A slow search is no longer killed while it is still working
details: A report search could fail with take too long and was stopped even though the search was alive and running, and the owner was billed for it anyway. The cause was the idle watchdog, a fixed 30 second limit on going without a single frame from Anthropic. That is too tight to be safe: a report runs around seven web searches, and while those execute there can be a long quiet gap with no output, so a perfectly healthy search was being stopped mid-flight. Raised to 90 seconds. The number comes from the asymmetry rather than a guess: set too tight it aborts a live, already-paid-for search and shows the customer a failure, while set too loose a genuinely stuck call merely takes longer to give up and is still capped by the per-call deadline of roughly 260 seconds, which never stopped guarding it. So the cost of being loose is bounded and cheap and the cost of being tight is a failed customer search plus the bill. This is the same kind of fixed constant that was already outgrown twice as a whole-call deadline, at 100 and then 150 seconds, each time turning live calls into errors. It is now tunable from the environment, so it can be moved on Render without a deploy. Verified with a stubbed upstream that opens a stream and then goes silent: the watchdog now waits the full 90 seconds, still fails cleanly instead of hanging, and still names itself in the log.

title: Live progress while the Market Explorer builds a page
details: Building a new market page takes 30-60 seconds and used to show one frozen line. It now streams the same live progress a valuation search does, rendered compactly in the search dropdown: the real searches running, sales found, and a progress bar. Two visitors exploring the same market at once still share one billed search, and both now watch it happen, including one who joins after it started. A market page that already exists, or a cached search, still answers instantly as an ordinary response with a real status code.

title: A failed search now says which deadline killed it, and gets counted
details: A report search can die two very different ways, and until now they raised the identical error with nothing to tell them apart, in the message or in the log: the call genuinely ran past its whole derived budget (around 260 seconds for a full search), or upstream went silent for 30 seconds and the idle watchdog stopped it. Those have opposite fixes, a budget too small versus a watchdog too twitchy, and the second one aborts a call that was alive and already billed, so guessing wrong costs real money. The Render log now names which fired and how long it had been waiting, and says plainly when the call may have been alive. The visitor still reads the same single plain sentence. Second gap closed at the same time: a failed search left no trace at all, because search events were only logged on the success and cache-hit paths, so the failure rate was literally unknowable and the first question anyone asks about a reported failure, how often does this happen, could not be answered. Failures now log a PII-free search_failed event carrying the timeout cause. Verified against a stubbed upstream that opens a stream and goes silent: the watchdog fires at 30.0s, names itself, the visitor gets a clean error rather than a hang, and the event lands with the right cause. That test also caught a crash in the first version of this change, a variable referenced outside its scope in the catch, which would have turned every failed search into a server error.

title: The Market Explorer no longer bypasses the free-search cap
details: Building a new market page runs the same billed search a report does, but it carried no free-search check, so a visitor who had used their free search could keep triggering searches from the homepage. It now spends the same single allowance, and asks for a free account once that is used. Browsing a market page that already exists stays free.

title: Test runs can no longer reach the live API
details: The .env loader treated a deliberately-cleared setting as unset and put the real value back, so the test suite was booting servers with live credentials instead of the blank ones it asked for. Two test runs billed real searches before this was caught.

title: Intro requests get a surface that survives a dropped email
details: The broker lead inbox stored every introduction request in lead_intro_requests and emailed the owner — and that email was the only owner-facing signal, so a dropped one made the request invisible, the exact failure mode the corpus-health alarm exists for. /api/stats now reads the table alongside the analytics events and /admin renders a Broker intro requests card: total count plus the dozen most recent with broker email and the lead's market and type (owner-facing, so that PII is fine — it is exactly what the email already carries; analytics events stay PII-free). Fails safe like the corpus-audit panel: a read failure says Unavailable and breaks nothing else, and a server without Supabase says so honestly rather than showing a fabricated zero, since the table has no file fallback. aggregateStats also gains the missing lead_intro branch (totals.leadIntros), and the route test now pins the surface to the response so the wiring cannot silently drop out. Verified in a browser against a live local server: all four card states render correctly and broker-supplied text is escaped (an injected script tag renders as inert text).

title: Broker lead inbox: anonymized BOV demand, owner-mediated introductions
details: Paying brokers see market/type/size/date of BOV requests in markets they cover (earned from approved comps or chosen), get emailed on new ones, and can request an introduction the owner still makes by hand. Lead PII never reaches a broker; the allowlist is pinned by a test. broker_profiles now follows user_id, so an email change no longer orphans a profile. Migration 015.

title: One logo lockup across every page
details: Chasing the vault's missing logo turned up a wider split: the header mark and wordmark sat 10px apart on index.html and every public page (the market family, /markets, /brokers, /how-it-works), but 12px on the internal dashboards, which use a --s4 spacing token there. The home page is the reference, so the five dashboards (/hq, /admin, /dev, /contacts, /vault) moved to 10px rather than the other way round — unifying toward the token would have left the flagship page as the odd one out and made the site less consistent, not more. The value is deliberately literal rather than a token: the logo/wordmark gap is a fixed brand relationship shared with index.html and MARKET_CSS, not a page's spacing scale, and a comment on each says so. Verified by measuring the rendered header on all nine pages in a browser: mark size, gap, wordmark size and tracking now come back identical on every one.

title: The Analytics tile strip gets the same durable dividers
details: Completes the HQ hairline fix from earlier the same day, which had left a known hole: /admin's ten-tile strip was the original of the pattern HQ copied, so it could lose a divider on a scaled display in exactly the same way, and the previous entry said so rather than quietly leaving it. Its dividers are now 1px borders on the tiles instead of 1px grid gaps showing the container's cream background through, because a gap is empty space whose width can round to zero on fractional device pixels while a border always paints at least one. The row-start rules follow the column count, which for this page steps 1, 2 and 5. Two things fall out that HQ did not need. Because the rules key off the column count rather than the tile count, the long-standing constraint recorded above this CSS, that the number of tiles must divide the column count, is retired: a partly-filled last row is now plain white instead of the grey block that appeared when a tenth tile was added while the grid still assumed nine in three columns. And nothing about the strip's appearance changes when every row is full, which is the case today. Verified by reading computed border widths across all ten tiles at all three breakpoints: tiles 1 and 6 start rows at five across and carry no left border, only the second row carries top borders, and no tile has a doubled divider.

title: A missing hairline between two HQ tiles
details: The owner reported no divider between the Dev hub and Contacts tiles, and the CSS said there should be one: the grid was drawn as /admin's hairline mesh, meaning a 1px gap between tiles with the container's background showing through. The catch is that a gap is empty space rather than a painted thing, so its width is free to round to zero. Four equal columns in a 1024px measure land on fractional widths (242.75px each), and once Windows display scaling at 125 or 150% is applied, individual gaps round away while their neighbours survive, which is why one hairline vanished rather than all three. Dividers are now 1px borders on the tiles themselves, and a border always paints at least one device pixel. Because a border has to know which tile starts a row, the rule changes with the column count: stacked, every tile but the first gets a top border; two across, the second tile of each row gets a left border and the second row gets a top border; four across, only left borders. Verified by reading the computed border widths at all three widths, so no tile is missing a divider and none has two. Worth knowing: /admin's tile strip is still built the original way and can lose a hairline the same way on a scaled display.

title: HQ stops being a dashboard dressed as a document
details: The owner said the page still looked off, and comparing the three internal pages side by side named it: the house has two page idioms, and HQ had borrowed the wrong one. /dev is a document, a narrow column of spined rows, and it works because each row is a bold title plus a paragraph that fills the measure. /admin is a dashboard, a tile grid with the label above the figure, and it works because numbers are tiny objects that have to sit close together to be compared. HQ had dashboard content in /dev's document layout, so each row was a two-glyph number stranded in a full-width ruled space; measured on the live page, the content filled less than half the width its own hairlines spanned, and those rules then underlined the emptiness. The four tools are now tiles on /admin's hairline mesh at /admin's 1024px measure, which removes the void by construction rather than by decoration. Second fix, the same pass: the loudest things on the page were the three CSV links at the bottom, the least important content on it and the only red, while the four tool names, which are the page's entire reason to exist, were set in ink with no affordance and read as inert labels. The names now carry an underline at rest and go red on hover; the CSV links are demoted to match. Third, a sentence above the grid answers the question the page is opened to ask ("56 searches this week, up from 28. 7 signups and no new leads. Nothing sold yet."), assembled from whatever resolved so a failed source drops its clause, and with the money claim gated on the billing tables actually answering, because "nothing sold yet" is a claim and an unreadable database must not be allowed to make it. Fourth, the Updated and Refresh stamp moves out of the Downloads block, where it had been sitting under the treat-a-copied-link-as-the-key warning and reading as a caption for it, up beside the sentence where it means what it says. Three smaller things fell out: the Tools heading is gone, since four labelled tiles do not need a heading announcing they are tools; the standfirst no longer describes the page's own layout; and the old adjacency where 0 leads this week sat one line above 1 lead all time is retired, because the week's leads now live in the sentence and the tile keeps the standing total.

title: The corpus now gets audited for structural integrity
details: Nothing had ever measured whether the rows in the comp corpus are sound, even though broker verification, corpus-first retrieval and the in-report records offer all build on them. A new Corpus integrity panel on Analytics reports five structural findings per row: a source link that does not name the property, a badge stronger than todays rule would grant, one source cited by several different addresses, a date that will not parse (so retrieval can never surface the row), and a missing price. Measured against the real corpus first, which changed the design: roughly half the rows cite hosts that hard-block automated reading (LoopNet, CityFeet, PropertyShark and CommercialSearch all refuse), so an audit built on fetching each page would have reported a bot-detection rate and called it accuracy. Every check is therefore structural, costs nothing, calls no model and fetches no page. Blocked hosts are reported as context and deliberately never affect the score, and unreachable rows stay in the denominator so the number cannot be flattered. The panel is explicit that this measures citation quality rather than accuracy, and that it is not the 90% gate. Report-only for now: no row is changed, no badge is downgraded and nothing is withheld from retrieval, because the scale of the problem should be known before any of that is decided. The first run against the local corpus put 20% of 134 rows fully clean, with the standout being one listing search page cited by six different comps. One real cleanup rode along: the badge-enforcement rule moved out of server.js into the new pure module, so the live normalization and the audit share one copy instead of two, and the rule is under test for the first time.

title: Your building sits at the top of the comp table, like an appraisal grid
details: The comparison card and the chart's You marker both positioned the subject against the market in aggregate, but the grid itself never showed it, so there was no reading across from your building to the comps on the same columns. A pinned Your property row now sits above the comps carrying whatever is known: address, size, price, the derived $/SF, and any per-type specs entered in the subject-details form, with a dash where a building you own has no answer (it has no sale date, no transaction type, no source). It is deliberately its OWN tbody and deliberately NOT a member of currentComps, because that array feeds the valuation, the chart, the map pins, curation, the exports and, upstream, the corpus harvest, and the subject is not a transaction. Sorting only ever rebuilds the comps tbody, so the row cannot drift out of position. NOI is unreachable from the renderer by design: it is private finance and this row travels in the print and PNG exports. The whole row hides when nothing is known beyond the address, since a line of dashes under a Your property label is worse than no line. Editing size or price now re-renders the table too, which it previously never did.

title: Every comp says how good a comparable it actually is
details: compWeight has always decided which comps a free visitor sees and how much each one moves the value range, but the only part of it ever visible was the size double-dagger, so "why is that comp carrying so much of the number?" had no answer anywhere in the report. A new sortable Match column reads Strong, Fair or Weak straight off that existing weight, and its tooltip names the three factors in the order the weight multiplies them: "sold in the last 6 months, similar size, verified source." Labels rather than the raw number, because it is a relative ranking and printing 0.63 would invite arithmetic it cannot support. It sorts by the underlying weight, not the label, so Strong never sorts alphabetically below Weak. Being the first column computed at render time rather than stored on the comp, it needed three small pieces of plumbing that each fail silently when missed: the empty-column prune skips derived columns, the phone cards stop dropping them as empty, and both exporters ask for the value instead of reading it, or Match would have shipped as a blank stripe down every CSV and XLSX.

title: A stat tile that says something the report did not already say
details: Comps Found duplicated the count already sitting in the chip beside the table header, and exclusions are spelled out in the curation note either way, so the tile spent a quarter of the stat row restating a number twice over. It now reads Median Comp Age. The gap that fills is real: the Lookback tile beside it says how wide the window was, but nothing said whether the window actually returned recent deals, so a 24-month search that came back with nothing newer than 22 months looked identical to one full of last-quarter sales. Reads the full comp set including the locked rows, matching the tiles either side of it.

title: The site footer reads as three short groups, not one ten-item tower
details: Ten links stacked in a single column had made the footer the tallest block on the landing page, and gave a reader nothing to scan by. Same links, same colors, same type: they now sit under Explore, Company and Follow, and the contact address moves up beside the disclaimer where it reads as contact rather than as a heading for the list. The footer's height drops by roughly half. The site keeps three separate copies of this footer (index.html, MARKET_FOOTER for the market and broker pages, and the one inside /how-it-works), so all three changed together; the two server-rendered copies share one pair of CSS rules and carry only the links they already had, which is why they get Explore and Company but no Follow group. The group labels reuse rd-lab, the micro-label token the rest of the site already uses, so this introduced no new type styles, and the two new Tailwind gap utilities were confirmed present in the vendored build before shipping.

title: The comp table finally says how far away each comp is
details: Location is the largest price driver in real estate, and the report conveyed it only as dots on a map you had to eyeball. Every pin is already geocoded in the browser, so a Distance column costs one haversine per comp and no network call: it sits behind Address, sorts like any other column, rides along into the CSV, XLSX, print and PNG exports because they all map over the same column list, and a line above the table reads "Located comps sit 0.4 mi to 2.1 mi from your property." On a fresh report the coordinates arrive a beat after the first paint, so the column starts pruned and fills itself in when the map's geocoding pass settles; saved and shared reports have their pins already and show it immediately. Excluding a comp updates the range, matching the map, which only ever plots included comps. Deliberately display-only: compWeight is mirrored in comp-gate.js so a free report's value range matches a Pro one exactly, and the server has no comp coordinates to mirror with since the model stopped returning per-comp lat/lng in July, so a distance term in the weighting would silently desync the two copies. Whether proximity should move the number is a separate decision, not a side effect of showing it.

title: The $/SF a comp shows and the $/SF it counts as no longer disagree in silence
details: Older comps are indexed to the report date at the market's annual trend before they enter the valuation, so a 2025 sale listed at $122/SF could actually carry $131/SF into the range with nothing on screen saying so. The table keeps showing the raw reported figure, because the audit trail must not move, but where the indexed figure differs the $/SF cell now wears a § whose tooltip gives both numbers and the trend that separates them. Sales only: lease rates are never indexed. It joins the † for a recomputed $/SF and the ‡ for an off-size-class comp, appending to either rather than overwriting, so a cell that is both recomputed and indexed explains both, and the hero's trust line now names the marker the way it already names the ‡. Nothing about the math changed; this closes the one place where the number in the table and the number in the valuation could differ without disclosure, which is a bad thing to have in a product whose whole pitch is proof.

title: Comp-table columns nobody filled stop taking up space
details: The Cap Rate column rendered on every report but was blank on nearly every comp — zero of the 186 comps across the 27 live market pages carry one, and only 15% of the local corpus does — because a cap rate needs a published NOI, which owner-user sales, leases, listings and public records never disclose. Rather than delete the column (cap rates genuinely appear on institutional Multifamily and NNN Retail deals, where they matter) or replace it, the table now prunes any column no comp in the report populates; the per-type spec columns, which come back patchy on thin markets, get the same treatment. Address, Date, Type, Price / Rate and Source always render so the table keeps its shape, and the phone cards, exports and locked-row placeholders all follow automatically since they map over the same column list. Curation re-prunes: a corpus-added comp carrying the report's only cap rate brings the column back, and removing it takes it out again. Everything server-side is untouched — the prompt still asks for cap rates, brokers still submit them, the corpus still stores them, and the market-level cap-rate range that powers the income approach and DCF defaults is a different field and was never in question. Verified in the browser on the sample report both ways, header and body cell counts staying aligned.

title: The vault header carries the CompNinja logo like every other page
details: The vault page shipped with a bare wordmark: no cut-card mark beside it, so its header did not match /hq, /admin, /dev, /contacts or the market pages, all of which render CN_LOGO before the words. It was the only page in the site missing the mark. Added the same shared constant, the same .brand svg sizing rule (28x28, no shrink) and the aria-label its siblings carry, rather than styling anything new — the logo has one definition and this page now uses it. Verified by measuring the rendered header against /dev, /hq and /admin in a browser: mark size, gap, colour, wordmark size, tracking and casing are identical on all four. /brokers sits at a 10px gap because it belongs to the market-page family with its own spacing token; that difference predates this and was left alone.

title: The vault opens in one paint — no more spawn-in
details: The morning's loading-line fix made the wait legible, but the owner rightly still called it a glitch: the title painted, then a second later the whole workspace spawned in, because the page could not render anything below the title until a client-side fetch of /api/vault came back. The data now travels WITH the page: GET /vault resolves the viewer's vault server-side and bakes the same payload /api/vault would return into the HTML as a boot object, so the browser renders title, trust line, table and imports together in the same paint, with zero fetches on load. One function, vaultReadPayload, now produces the answer for both the API route and the page, so the gate can never drift between them, and its entitlement check runs concurrently with the user-scoped reads (rows only ever leave through the post-gate 200 branch) to shave a serial database hop. If the payload cannot be built the page ships without one and falls back to fetching exactly as before; the loading line from this morning remains as that fallback's state. The page stays no-store, which now matters more — it carries the signed-in viewer's own rows. Verified locally on all three boot outcomes: anonymous and non-broker gates render in the first paint with zero /api/vault requests, and a 200 payload renders the full workspace — counts, sorted table, published-button state, imports, filters — likewise fetch-free.

title: An explored address always runs under its own property type
details: The Address Explorer builds its list for whatever property type is selected when Find addresses runs, but clicking an address submitted the search with whatever the dropdown said at click time. Change the type while the panel sat open and you could run an Office search on a warehouse from an Industrial list; with too few priced sale comps of the wrong type, the value estimate rendered blank. Nothing corrected it, because the OSM type detector only fires when an address is typed by hand, never on the explorer's programmatic fill. Each listed address now remembers the type its list was built for, and clicking it snaps the dropdown back, along with the type's recommended lookback and its subject-detail fields, exactly as if the visitor had picked that type themselves, before the search fires. Verified in the browser: list built under Industrial, dropdown moved to Multifamily, click; the search ran as Industrial with the 24-month window and Industrial detail fields restored.

title: HQ answers "is it growing", not just "what happened"
details: Every headline count on /hq stood alone — 44 searches this week meant nothing without knowing last week was 10 — and the one metric the guest gate exists to move, signups, appeared nowhere at all. The searches figure now carries the prior 7-day total in parentheses on the same line, report unlocks show this week against last, and a second week-scoped line under Analytics reads the signup funnel: signups, leads, and how many anonymous visitors hit the sign-in gate, all from events already being logged. Two more gaps closed while in there: pending broker comps were an action item filed as a grey footnote, and now render as a neutral ink attention line above the tools (not red — red stays reserved for failures) linking to the review queue; and the documented live-but-unbuyable trap — PRO_ENABLED on with PRO_AUDIENCE still set, where the public cannot reach checkout and every page looks healthy — now fires a red alarm line, instead of announcing itself only in startup logs nobody tails. A quiet Updated-time-plus-Refresh stamp at the bottom means a tab left open no longer passes off stale numbers as current.

title: The vault no longer opens on a half-rendered flash
details: Clicking Your vault painted just the title and a bare footer, then the whole workspace popped in with a layout jump once /api/vault answered — which for a signed-in broker is a chain of database reads (session, entitlements, then the comps and imports), long enough to read as a glitch. Both panes below the title started display:none with nothing standing in for them. The gate pane now opens showing a quiet Loading your vault… line from the very first paint, and the fetch's three outcomes each replace it — the workspace, a sign-in note, or the broker-plan note — so the wait reads as loading instead of breakage. Verified locally: the served HTML carries the loading line, and the signed-out path swaps it for the sign-in gate.

title: The Verified badge can no longer be claimed by a comp no broker vouched for
details: attachVerifiedAttribution only ever ADDED attribution, and it returned early when no broker comps had been offered — so a "verified": true the model invented passed straight through into the report and then into comp_corpus via harvestComps. Found live: 15 corpus rows badged verified against one broker submission ever, mostly Boise and Eagle addresses nobody had submitted, including aggregate-shaped ones like "Eagle, ID 83616 (built 1999, 1,173-5,333 SF)". The rule is now absolute and lives in broker-vault.js so npm test covers it: a comp is verified if and only if it matches a comp we actually offered, enforcement runs even when the offered list is empty (the case the early return skipped, and the one every bad row came through), and clearing a badge also strips any verified_by beside it so no broker is credited for someone else's row. Same principle as the source_type enforcement a few lines above — prompt rules are requests, normalization is a guarantee — and it matters more here because the badge is what the broker tier pays brokers IN. Unearned badges are logged when cleared, which is the only visible signal the prompt rule is being ignored. Existing data repaired: the 15 rows kept their comps and lost the badge. 9 new tests.

title: The publish button: a broker can put one comp into the public records, for credit
details: Ecosystem Plan §4, the one sanctioned door through the privacy wall. A broker flips a single comp in their vault to public and it is credited to their firm by name in every report it appears in; everything not flipped stays private, and publishing is never a default. Implemented as a COPY into comp_submissions — the table fetchVerifiedComps already reads — so a published comp inherits the entire existing verified pipeline (offered to the model as a trusted candidate, the green Verified badge, citation counting, and inclusion in the broker list surfaced on BOV leads for that market). No public query gains a read on broker_comps, which is precisely why this is a copy rather than a published filter on a shared table. Two conversions are load-bearing and silent when wrong: the transaction must be capitalised, since fetchVerifiedComps filters transaction=eq.Sale and a lowercase copy would simply never be offered; and comp_submissions stores its numbers as text. Publishing requires a price, a size, a date and a street-numbered address — an unpriced comp is fine to keep but cannot support anyone's valuation — and it requires a name to credit, refusing rather than posting anonymously and letting the broker discover later that they got nothing for it. Unpublish deletes the public row, tracked by a stored id (migration 014) so that retraction actually works rather than depending on an address match. The confirm dialog says plainly what publishing cannot undo: reports already delivered keep the comp. 11 new tests.

title: A Broker vault card on My Desk, above Plan
details: The account menu was the vault's only entrance, and a menu behind an avatar is easy to miss — it was, the first time. My Desk now carries a Broker vault card with an "Open your vault" button, placed above Plan because a broker opens their vault far more often than they look at billing. Same entitlement as the menu link (canUseVault) plus a signed-in check, since the desk's account-backed areas are hidden signed out and a card there would offer a page that answers 401. An anchor rather than a button, so middle-click and open-in-new-tab work on what is a real page. Every class reused from the existing Plan card and the nav — verified against the vendored tailwind.css, so no rebuild was triggered.

title: The vault has a way in: "Your vault" in the account menu
details: Until now /vault existed and nothing linked to it, so a broker who paid could not find it. The account menu is the right home — it is per-account, and the vault is the one place a broker's own data lives. Shown off /api/config's canUseVault rather than any plan test, so it appears for a broker subscription and for comped admins and for nobody else. Deliberately not gated on billing being live, matching the exception the billing card already makes: comped admins get the vault on a deployment with no Stripe keys, which is the only way anyone internal renders the broker UI at all. Verified both directions in a browser — the link appears the moment admin access is claimed and disappears the moment it is dropped. Every class reused from the sibling menu items, so no Tailwind regeneration was needed.

title: The vault page: brokers can now upload a spreadsheet and see it organized
details: GET /vault — the broker workspace, wired to the vault API. Drop or choose a .csv, see what imported and what did not (with the line numbers Excel shows), then sort and filter the result by market and property type. Imports are listed as batches so a wrong file is one click to undo. Server-rendered and self-contained like /hq and /admin: its own inline CSS on the same token set, no dependency on tailwind.css, and nothing added to index.html — which is half a megabyte and the likeliest place for two parallel sessions to collide. The page holds no secrets and does no gating of its own; everything comes from /api/vault, so opening the URL without a broker subscription renders a shell and a note. The header line reads "N comps · 0 published · visible only to you", which is the tier's trust proof made checkable — a broker hands over their book of business because they can watch that number stay at zero, not because the terms promise it.

title: Broker vault v1: a private comp store brokers upload into
details: The server half of the paid broker tier's core promise — upload your comps, get them back organized. New tables (migrations/013-broker-vault.sql, run before deploying) and four routes under /api/vault, all behind one gate: signed in, then canUseVault, then a working database. That last refusal is the opposite of the rest of the app on purpose: everywhere else a Supabase failure falls back to a local file, but Render erases its disk on every deploy, so a broker's uploaded book of business would silently vanish days later. The vault has no file fallback and refuses instead. Import validation lives in a new pure module, broker-vault.js, which rejects rather than guesses — "1.2M", a bare number where a date belongs (Excel's serial), and day-first dates all come back with a spreadsheet line number instead of being stored as a best effort, because a wrong number in a broker's own records is the one error nobody catches. Privacy is enforced structurally: broker_comps is a separate table read by separate functions, never a private flag filtered in the corpus queries, because that read path swallows its own errors and a missed filter would leak silently. 44 new tests (150 total). No UI yet.

title: Broker tier billing rails: a plan that is Pro plus a private vault
details: Ecosystem Plan v1 step 2 begins. A new broker_monthly plan rides the existing Stripe rails as a superset of Pro — unlimited comps, the ten-year lookback, unlimited exports, branding and the Explorer all arrive by the ordinary Pro route — and adds one capability on top: canUseVault. Modelled as a subscription plan rather than a role column on users, so vault access lapses with the card instead of outliving it; subscriptions.plan has no CHECK constraint, so no migration was needed. The two rules worth knowing: an unrecognized plan name opens no vault (stricter than pro, which is governed by status alone — a private data store is the wrong place to err generous), and a dark deployment opens no vault either, even though PRO_ENABLED=off grants every other capability, because "pre-Pro behavior" restores what visitors used to have free and the vault never existed. Ships dark: STRIPE_PRICE_BROKER_MONTHLY is unset until pricing is settled, so checkout answers 503 "that plan isn't configured" and the tier becomes buyable with one Stripe price and one env var, no code change. 16 new tests; design spec and the vault contract in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-05-broker-tier-design.md.

title: A housekeeping skill catches drift before it piles up for weeks
details: Earlier the same day, a single session had to reconcile five separate kinds of drift at once: stale merged branches, an unverified migrations log, a corrupted devlog, and stale claims in CLAUDE.md, none of it owned by anything, all of it accumulated silently. .claude/skills/housekeeping turns that into a repeatable checklist: branch and worktree hygiene, migrations vs APPLIED.md, devlog integrity, docs vs. reality, CI health, open PRs, and working-tree cleanliness, each marked as either safe to auto-fix or something that needs the owner's call. Verified against this actual repo before shipping, and the first real run earned its keep: it found a genuinely stale merged branch (deleted), and it also caught a bug in the skill itself before any damage was done, the devlog check as originally written would have flagged EVERY normal em dash and emoji as corruption and 'fixed' clean text into garbage. Rewritten to match CI's exact mojibake pattern instead of 'any non-ASCII', which also surfaced that CLAUDE.md's devlog rule was describing a policy (ASCII-escaping) nobody actually implemented; corrected to describe what the CI guard genuinely enforces.

title: The shared-checkout survival rules are now a skill, not a memory
details: This repo is routinely worked by two Claude sessions in the same checkout at once, plus a human collaborator pushing straight to origin/main, and every hard-won rule for surviving that (never git add -A, read the whole diff not --stat, devlog.json is a guaranteed collision and must be rebuilt not patched, PowerShell mangles git patches so use Bash, foreign hunks can ride along even through a filtered git apply --cached) lived only in one Claude session's private memory, invisible to a fresh session, to Owen, or to anyone reading the repo. .claude/skills/shared-checkout now carries the checklist: always-before-staging rules, the patch recipe for a file someone else is mid-editing, the devlog rebuild recipe, a never-without-confirmation list, and a common-mistakes table. Verified against a live scenario (foreign uncommitted file sitting in git status, none of it yours) before shipping; the test surfaced one real gap, no rule existed for the most common case of an untouched foreign file, which the skill now states explicitly: leave it exactly as it sits, stage only your own paths, and say what you left behind.

title: HQ reads like a dashboard instead of a list of sentences
details: The owner said the page looked off, and measuring it showed why: nothing was broken, the typography just had no hierarchy. Every tool name rendered red, because the link inherited the page's red anchor colour where the Dev hub's matching column is ink, so four red serif words in the margin out-shouted the numbers they labelled. The figures were whole sentences set at one size, so the numerals never lined up and four rows read as four similar paragraphs. And each row's supporting facts were a single chain of five items joined by dots, mixing this-week figures with all-time ones. Now the numeral is set on its own at figure size in serif (the same treatment the Analytics tiles already use) with its unit words alongside, so all four numbers share a left edge and scan as a column; the tool names are ink and turn red only on hover, matching the Dev hub; and the facts split into two lines, one scoped to the figure above it and one for standing totals. Two real defects fell out of the pass: a data source that failed rendered as a bare dash indistinguishable from a rendering fault, and now says which source is unavailable; and the broker-review note blamed a missing database even when the read had simply failed. The page title also expands from HQ to Headquarters, following the same pattern the Dev hub uses, and the standfirst stops calling this the internal desk, which collided with the customer-facing My Desk.

title: HQ warns before the daily search cap bites
details: The two alarms HQ already carries fire after something breaks; the daily spend cap is the one failure that announces itself in advance, and nothing surfaced it. HQ's alert strip now adds a red line once today's billed searches pass 80% of DAILY_SEARCH_CAP, and switches to plainer wording at the cap itself, when visitors start receiving 429s until midnight UTC. The line links to the Render dashboard, where the cap is raised. Below the threshold nothing renders, keeping the healthy page silent. Reads the same in-memory counter the cap itself enforces, including its lazy midnight reset, so the warning can never disagree with the gate.

title: Unlock the admin pages once per month, not once per tab
details: The internal pages kept the admin key in sessionStorage, which browsers scope to a single tab, so every new tab (and every phone visit) demanded the key again even though unlocking any page had already minted the signed 30-day cn_admin cookie. Every dashboard endpoint now accepts that cookie as an alternative to the key header, and each page silently tries a keyless fetch on load: with the cookie present the page just opens; without it the gate appears exactly as before, with no error message for the attempt. Typing the key anywhere still mints the cookie, so one unlock now covers all four pages in every tab for a month. A pleasant side effect closes an old wart: in a cookie session the HQ download links are plain hrefs, so the admin key no longer rides in CSV URLs where browser history and proxy logs could keep it. Deliberately unchanged: /api/admin-access still requires the real key, machine callers keep the header and ?key= forms, rotating ADMIN_KEY still kills every cookie at once, and the internal search bypass stays header-only so a browser cookie can never widen it.

title: HQ shows money in, not just money out
details: A Revenue row joins the tool list: active Pro subscriptions as the headline, with founding seats taken (of the configured limit), report unlocks all-time plus this week, and any subscriptions sitting in payment grace. The row links out to the Stripe dashboard, where the actual money lives. Counts read the billing tables directly and deliberately ignore PRO_ENABLED, so a dark deployment still reports what has been sold; the tables are DB-only by design, so without Supabase the row shows a dash and says why rather than a lying zero. Next to the searches row's estimated API spend, one glance now covers the whole loop: is anything broken, what did the week cost, what did it earn.

title: The product roadmap now lives in the repo
details: Until now the roadmap was split across Claude session memories, the Ecosystem Plan docx in OneDrive, and the owner's head, so no two collaborators (human or AI) were ever working from the same picture of what comes next. docs/ROADMAP.md consolidates it: broker tier v1 and the branding UI up front, the corpus-density-gated features behind them, the broker-tier phase order from the Chuck plan, a no-decisions-needed engineering track, the open attorney/Chuck questions, and the standing principles (calm UI, CompNinja not Adler, no brokerage claims, the 90% accuracy gate). The /dev ideas list stays the owner's personal notepad, deliberately unmirrored. Update rule is in the file: shipped lines move to the shipped log, priorities get reordered in place.

title: HQ raises the alarms instead of smiling through an outage
details: The front door could show a calm week of numbers while every search was failing site-wide: both smoke alarms (the Anthropic upstream-health banner added after the billing outage, and the corpus-persistence banner from the July freeze) rendered only on /admin. /hq now carries one red line per firing alarm above the tool rows, linking to the full detail on Analytics: a billing outage says search is DOWN outright, transient call failures get softer factual wording with the last status, and a corpus failure names the likely missing-column cause when it looks like one. A healthy page shows nothing at all, no green all-clear noise. Same in-memory sources as /admin's banners, so the two pages can never disagree, and like them the counters reset on restart.

title: Free tier no longer sees the Address Explorer link
details: The landing page used to show free users a locked '🔒 Explore a market — Pro' teaser next to the address field. The owner's call: no teaser on the search form at all. Free users now discover the Address Explorer only through the Upgrade-to-Pro card's feature list in the pricing dialog, where it is already listed as a Pro perk; the link appears on the landing page only for visitors whose plan actually includes it, and it shows or hides immediately when entitlements change mid-session (sign-in, upgrade, expiry). With the Pro tier switched off entirely, the link stays visible for everyone, exactly the pre-Pro behavior. A safety net keeps any click that lands before gating applies routing to the pricing dialog rather than opening a panel it shouldn't.

title: HQ shows the week's estimated API spend
details: The searches-this-week line on /hq now carries the cost next to the counts: est. dollar spend for those same seven days, computed by the exact blended pricing /admin's cost tiles use (corpus-discounted report searches, flat market searches, cache hits free) so the two pages can never disagree. Same caveat as /admin: an estimate from the per-search cost constants, not a read of the Anthropic invoice.

title: Analytics and Contacts join the internal design system
details: The two oldest internal pages still carried hand-set pixel values and literal hex colors from before the Dev hub established the house discipline: one type scale, one spacing scale, one radius, uppercase reserved for the kicker and wordmark, red for interaction only. Both stylesheets are now expressed in those tokens; section headings became serif sentence case, shouty uppercase micro-labels became quiet sentence-case ones, and the contacts filter chips adopted the Dev hub's underlined-link idiom in place of raised pills. Structure is untouched: the tile strip, chart, form grid and contact rows all read exactly as before, and the CRM status tag colors stay, deliberately, as content color-coding. One real bug fell out of the pass: the analytics tile strip's own comment warns that its column count must divide the tile count, and a tenth tile (type autofill) had been added while the grid still assumed nine in three columns, so the last row rendered a grey two-cell block. The grid now steps 1, 2, 5 columns, all of which divide 10.

title: A failed search no longer shows customers our vendor's billing error
details: When the Anthropic API refused a call, the server passed its error text straight to the browser. On 2026-08-04 the Console API credit balance hit zero and every visitor — including anyone who had just paid $39 — saw 'Anthropic API error (400). Your credit balance is too low ... purchase credits': it reads as the customer's own billing problem, names a vendor they never bought from, and offers nothing they can act on. Both leak paths (a refused call and a mid-stream error) now show our own copy instead — 'Comp search is temporarily unavailable, the team has been alerted', or a 'we're unusually busy, try again in a minute' line for rate limits — while the real error goes to the log, to a red banner at the top of /admin naming the cause and its fix, and, for billing failures, to one alert email. Errors we write ourselves, like 'The search took too long and was stopped', still reach the customer unchanged. Note for the record: API credits are prepaid against the Console org that owns the key, and no Claude Pro or Team subscription, comped or otherwise, funds them.

title: The valuation stops dying for want of one number
details: The Meridian Walgreens test showed the two ways a report starves: a $4M comp with no square footage (useless to the math), and no square footage for the searched building itself. Both are now attacked. The prompt tells the model that a priced sale comp without a size is worth one dedicated search to complete, because completing two or three priced comps matters more than finding one more; on the re-tested Walgreens search the priced-comp count went from one to six and the value range rendered. And while the visitor reads the address-confirmation dialog, the browser now measures the building's footprint on OpenStreetMap and pre-fills the size field with a clearly labeled, editable estimate; on the Walgreens it measured 14,500 SF, which is exactly a standard Walgreens box. That fill also makes searches faster and cheaper, because a search that already knows the building's size skips the two web searches the model would have spent looking it up. The estimate only appears for verified, street-numbered addresses with a building type, never for Land or submarket searches, typing your own number replaces it, and an OpenStreetMap outage is never mistaken for the building not being mapped.

title: Every push now gets tested before Render ships it
details: Render deploys main on every push, and until now nothing stood between a bad commit and the live site: the 90-test suite only ran when someone remembered to run it, and a simple syntax error in server.js would have taken the whole site down at boot. A GitHub Actions workflow now runs on every push and pull request with three dependency-free layers: node --check on all six entry-point files, the full npm test suite, and a boot smoke test that starts the server in a completely bare environment (no API key, no database, no Stripe) and requires /healthz and the home page to answer, proving every optional integration still degrades instead of crashing. The workflow deliberately holds no secrets, so a fork pull request has nothing to steal. Each step was verified locally before committing: syntax checks pass, all 90 tests pass, and the boot smoke passes on a spare port.

title: The single-report unlock is $20 and now buys the whole property
details: Price cut from $39 to $20, and what it buys changed more than the price did. It now grants every Pro capability that can be scoped to a property - all comps, the full ten-year history, unlimited exports, branding - for that address and type, permanently. Previously it bought a snapshot: the same four-to-five comps you could already see, with one more revealed. A real test purchase earlier today unlocked exactly one additional comp, which is not $39 of value and was not $20 of value either. The change that made this possible is that the report id stopped hashing the lookback. While the window was part of the id, buying a 36-month report and re-running it at ten years produced a different id, matched no purchase and came back locked - so granting the wider window was impossible by construction, which is why the ceiling used to sit on the subscription alone. Keyed on address and type, one purchase covers the building at every window. Two consequences worth knowing: exporting the same property at two different windows now counts as one export rather than two, which is the intended reading since the visitor analysed one building; and the Address Explorer is deliberately still subscription-only, because it finds the NEXT property and cannot be scoped to a report without simply being Pro at a one-off price. Timing note: report_purchases held zero rows when the key changed, so nothing orphaned - a later change would need a migration re-keying every existing purchase.

title: A garbled report gets rescued instead of re-searched
details: When the model's report failed to parse, the server used to throw the whole attempt away and silently re-run the entire search: another 90 seconds and another billed call, which is how a 90-second search became the 3-minute-40 wait measured on a real test, and how one Phoenix search burned two full attempts and still showed an error. Now a failed parse is rescued in two steps before any re-search: the server first extracts the report itself from around any stray text the model tacked on (the one failure captured byte-for-byte was exactly that, a complete valid report with junk after it), free and instant; failing that, one small no-search follow-up call asks the model to re-emit the same JSON corrected, at about a seventh of the cost and half the wait of a full retry. The full retry still exists as the last resort, every rescue is logged so the live logs show which layer fires and how often, and the streamed preview from the first attempt stays on screen through a rescue since its comps were real. Proven against faked responses covering all three paths: trailing junk (salvaged instantly), broken mid-JSON (repaired by the follow-up call), and a healthy report (byte-identical behavior).

title: Industrial reports default to a 24-month window
details: The recommended lookback for Industrial moves from 12 months to 24, measured rather than guessed. On a live Phoenix industrial address a 12-month window returned five comps of which exactly one was a priced sale - and the value hero needs two to compute a range, so the report rendered Low/Likely/High as dashes. The same address at 24 months returned three priced sales and a working valuation; a second nearby address at 24 months returned six of six sales priced. Total comps barely moved (five either way, report 6% larger), so the wider window changed the MIX rather than the volume: the same number of comps, but sales instead of leases. That matters because the hero's range is sales-only. The other types are deliberately untouched and still unmeasured - multifamily and residential trade often enough that a fresher window is genuinely better evidence, and widening them on inference could make reports worse. Measure priced SALE comps per window before moving any of them; total comps is not the number that decides whether a report has a valuation in it.

title: HQ: an internal homepage for the admin tools
details: The internal pages had grown into a triangle of hand-maintained cross-links with inconsistent labels, and the three admin CSV downloads were linked from nowhere at all. The new /hq page is the front door: one row per tool (Analytics, Dev hub, Contacts), each with a live headline number pulled from the same readers its own page uses (searches this week with billed/cached split, leads and pending broker submissions, open ideas and the last shipped entry, contact count), plus direct download links for the leads, broker-submissions and comp-corpus CSVs. Same admin gate and calm Research Desk skin as the other internal pages, same shared one-time unlock, same triple-noindex treatment. All four pages now carry one consistent nav: HQ, Analytics, Dev hub, Contacts, Run a report. Any snapshot source that fails just renders as a dash; the page never breaks because one read did.

title: Every database change now lives in a migrations folder
details: The Supabase schema used to be documented only as SQL snippets buried in server.js comments, and whether a given snippet had actually been run on the live database lived nowhere but the owner's memory. That gap caused the July corpus outage: an ALTER shipped in code, was never run, and every harvested comp silently fell into an ephemeral file for weeks. All twelve schema changes now live as numbered files in migrations/, with APPLIED.md recording what has been run in production and a README describing the one-rule routine: new schema change, new numbered file, run it, log it, commit both with the code. server.js keeps a one-line pointer where each DDL comment used to be, the /admin missing-column banner now points at the folder, and the add-comp-field skill's migration step was rewritten to match. No runtime behavior changed; all 90 tests pass.

title: Free reports look back 3 years instead of 1
details: The free lookback ceiling moves from 12 months to 36. The reason is not generosity: at 12 months the free report frequently could not answer its own headline question. The value hero needs two priced sale comps to compute a range, and a 12-month window in dense industrial markets kept returning fewer - a live Phoenix search came back with five comps of which exactly one was a sale, so Low/Likely/High rendered as dashes. A free tier that cannot produce a number is not a teaser, it is a broken demo, and it gives nobody a reason to believe the paid version works. The short window also disarmed the other gate: 12 months often returned four or fewer comps, so the 4-comp limit withheld nothing and the $39 single-report tile - which only appears when something is actually locked - never rendered at all. Widening the window is what gives the comp gate something real to hold back. Not widened further, deliberately: the window is clamped before the search and the model is asked for up to 12 comps regardless of plan, so a ten-year free window would find and write far more comps on every free search, and the comps array is roughly three quarters of report output, which is the cost and wall-clock driver. Pro keeps the full ten years. Note the per-type recommended windows are unchanged, so picking Industrial still preselects 12 months until those are revisited.

title: The model writes comps in shorthand and the server translates back
details: Two-thirds of a report is the comps array, and a fifth of THAT was just the field names, spelled out twelve times over ('price_per_sqft', 'source_type', ...), plus empty fields written out as empty strings. The model now writes each comp under one-to-three character keys and skips fields it has nothing for; the server expands everything back to the classic shape the moment the response is parsed, so every stored report, cached report, export, and API response is byte-shaped exactly as before. The translation is deliberately forgiving: a model that ignores the shorthand and writes full names anyway produces exactly the old behavior. Proven first against a faked response covering the tricky cases, then on two real searches (Industrial and Multifamily): every field came back under its proper name, fill rates matched or beat the old prompts (cap rates actually appeared MORE often), and per-unit pricing computed correctly through the shorthand. Combined with the narrative caps shipped earlier today, a full 7-comp report fell from 6,111 to about 3,100 output tokens, roughly half, which is directly seconds off every search and a real cut in per-search cost.

title: A checkout returns you to the site you bought from
details: A real $39 purchase went through and the buyer never got their report. The cause was that Stripe's return URL was always built from SITE_URL (the canonical domain), while the deployment also answers on its Render hostname - so a buyer who searched on one host was returned to the other. localStorage is per-origin, and localStorage.pendingUnlock.v1 is the only record of which report was just bought, so handlePurchaseReturn() found nothing and the paid report never re-rendered. The money and the purchase row were both fine; only the landing was wrong. The return origin now follows the request. It is a strict allowlist rather than the raw Host header - the canonical site, this service's own Render hostname, and localhost, with anything else falling back to SITE_URL - because trusting Host would turn our own checkout into an open redirect. Verified against spoofed, suffix-trick and lookalike hosts.

title: A bought report stops claiming you have 4 exports left
details: A report unlocked by the $39 purchase has unlimited exports, and the server has always known that - computeEntitlements returns exportsRemaining 'unlimited' once it can see the purchase row. The counter in the report header did not, because it reads /api/config, which takes no report id and so can only ever answer with the free monthly tally. A buyer was told '4 exports left this month' on a report they owned outright. The gated report response now carries the per-report allowance, resolved from the entitlements /api/comps had already computed with that report's id, so it costs no extra lookup. The client reads it and then deletes it, because the report object is saved to history, the portfolio and shares, and a stored entitlement would be re-read as fact long after it stopped being true. Known gap: re-opening a purchased report from history still shows the monthly tally until it is re-run.

title: A thin report stops blaming the missing square footage
details: When a report could not build a value range, it told the reader 'We couldn't find this building's square footage. Enter it and the estimate updates instantly.' That branch is only reachable with fewer than two priced sale comps - the two-or-more case leads with a per-square-foot band instead - so entering the size could not have built a range and the advice sent people, including someone who had just paid $39, after a number that would have changed nothing. The message now names the real blocker (how many priced sale comps actually came back, and that two are needed) and mentions the square footage only when it is also missing. Found on a live Phoenix industrial report that returned five comps, only one of them a sale.

title: Pricing leads with the 10-year lookback, not the comp count
details: The pricing modal sold Pro on itemizing every comparable, which oversold it in exactly the markets where it matters: two searches in dense industrial markets (Dallas and Ontario CA) each returned only four comps inside the free 12-month window, so nothing was withheld and Pro would have shown the same four. The ten-year lookback is what actually surfaces more transactions, so it now leads both the modal subtitle and the Pro bullet list. The $39 tile gained a matching line saying what it does not buy - it unlocks the report as it stands, and the wider window stays a Pro feature - because a purchase is retroactive and deliberately does not re-run a wider search.

title: A $39 report unlock now opens the CompNinja records panel too
details: Buying the $39 single-report unlock left the "From CompNinja's records" panel locked, which was the worst possible place to leave it: that panel's own CTA is what opens the pricing modal, so a buyer could pay and then walk straight back into the same paywall that sold them. The cause was that /api/corpus-comps asked what this VISITOR may see rather than what they may see ON THIS REPORT - it resolved entitlements with no report id, so a purchase could never register. The report's lookback now rides along with the address and type, and the server hashes the same address|type|months id /api/comps derives, so a purchased report resolves as unlocked and the panel opens. The id is still computed server-side and never accepted from the client, so this cannot unlock a report nobody bought, and a client that omits the lookback simply fails closed to the locked count.

title: The report's narrative fields stop rambling
details: The market summary, value drivers, trend line, and price-discovery note were measured at a combined third of a real report's length, and the excess was the same two patterns the comp-notes cap killed last week: restating figures that already have their own column, and the model narrating its own search. All four now carry notes-style caps (three short sentences for the summary, one named factor per value driver, one short trend sentence, two short price-discovery sentences) with the bloat banned by name and the honesty caveats (comps beyond the window, a widened radius, scarce verified data) given a protected slot in the summary. Verified on a real search the same day: the summary went 941 to 559 characters with every caveat intact, and the whole report came in 13% shorter. Reports get several seconds faster to write and slightly cheaper; nothing the reader needs is lost because everything banned already lives elsewhere in the report.

title: One free search per visitor, then a free sign-in
details: Anonymous visitors now get exactly one free report search; the second opens the account dialog with a plain ask: create a free account to keep searching, no card needed. Not a paywall - any free account clears it - but a signup funnel, and a real cap on anonymous API spend. It's tracked two ways and blocked when either fires: a durable ledger keyed by a one-way hash of the visitor's IP (survives cleared cookies; the raw address is never stored) and an essential cn_guest cookie set once the quota is spent (survives IP changes). Cache hits count too, since the funnel is the point, not just cost; a failed search never burns the free one; and admins and the internal seed/Explorer callers bypass it exactly like the Pro gate. The form shows a quiet one-line hint once the free search is spent, a PII-free signup_gate analytics event records each block for /admin, and the privacy policy's cookie section now tells the whole story. Everything is env-tunable: GUEST_SEARCH_LIMIT defaults to 1, any number works, 0 requires sign-in before the first search, and off restores yesterday's behavior from Render with no deploy. Fails open - if the ledger is unreachable the search runs, and DAILY_SEARCH_CAP still backstops the budget.

title: The loading card shows the report as it's being written
details: The longest stretch of a search is the 40-70 seconds the model spends writing the report, and until now the card just narrated it. The card now shows the goods as they stream in: the market summary appears within seconds of the write starting under an 'Early market read' label, and a compact table (address, price, size, date) gains a row per comp instead of the old five plain text lines. Only fields the final report will not correct are shown; per-SF pricing and provenance badges wait for the real render, since the server corrects both after the full parse. Comp addresses are also geocoded during the wait, so the map's pins paint instantly when the report lands instead of trickling in. Comps past a free visitor's plan still stream as anonymous locked markers, the finished report replaces the whole preview exactly as before, and all three streaming fallbacks (simulated progress, plain JSON, the buffered-stream watchdog) are untouched. Verified at zero cost against a faked Anthropic stream: summary and table fill in live, a mid-stream disconnect still lands on the error card, and the finished report renders identically.

title: Pro and the $39 unlock are sold as unlimited comps
