details: Both paid surfaces used to promise 'every comparable, itemized, not just four', which described the gate accurately but read like a fixed step up from a number rather than the removal of a limit. They now say what they are: unlimited comps, as many as the search turns up. Nothing in the pipeline changed - entitlements.js has always returned maxComps 'all' for a Pro subscriber and for a report bought outright, so neither has ever been shown a shortened list. The claim is deliberately qualified 'as many as the search finds' rather than promising a count, because the search itself still asks for up to twelve and the anti-padding prompt rule means a thin market honestly returns fewer; promising a number the market has to supply is how a paywall starts lying. The single-report line keeps the past tense, 'every comparable the search found', since that unlock is retroactive to a report already on screen and does not re-run a deeper search. The in-report locked notice also stopped naming Pro: the button opens the one pricing modal, which offers Pro and the $39 one-off both, and which of them fits depends on the report.

title: Admins get Pro comped when they sign in
details: The team was about to be the only group that never sees Pro: with PRO_AUDIENCE gone, everyone internal would be a free user testing a paywall they cannot cross. Signing in on an account now grants full Pro — every comp, a 10-year lookback, unlimited exports — whenever the browser is carrying admin credentials. There is no admin USER in this codebase (ADMIN_KEY is a shared secret, not a column on `users`), so possession of that key is the test. Unlocking /admin, /dev or /contacts now also trades the key for an httpOnly `cn_admin` cookie via POST /api/admin-access, because the dashboards keep the key in sessionStorage and sessionStorage is scoped to ONE TAB — a developer who unlocked the dashboard and then opened the app in a second tab would silently be free again. The cookie carries no secret (it is a signed expiry, HMAC'd with ADMIN_KEY), expires in 30 days, and dies the moment ADMIN_KEY is rotated. Two limits are deliberate: comped Pro requires a signed-in account, since a key identifies a machine and not a person, and it cannot switch a PRO_ENABLED=off deployment back on. A 'View as a free user' button on the plan card drops it again — the paywall is the part of the product the team otherwise never renders.

title: The Address Explorer is now a Pro feature
details: Typing a market and getting back real, street-numbered addresses to value shipped free this morning; it is now part of Pro. Free and signed-out visitors still see the link beside the address field, but it reads "Explore a market - Pro" and opens the pricing dialog instead of the panel. The gate is enforced in two places because one is not enough: the panel is withheld in the browser (the OpenStreetMap top-up runs client-side, so the server can never withhold that half) and /api/explore-addresses answers 403 (so a hand-rolled request cannot lift the corpus list). A 403 arriving at a browser that thought otherwise - a lapsed subscription, a second tab left open - re-syncs the page and opens the pricing dialog rather than quietly filling the panel from OpenStreetMap alone. Cancelling and payment-grace subscribers keep the explorer for as long as they keep Pro. A $39 single-report unlock does not include it, on the same reasoning that keeps the 10-year lookback out of that purchase: it buys one report that already exists, and the explorer is for finding the next property. With PRO_ENABLED unset the explorer stays open to everyone, exactly as before.

title: The $39 single-report unlock is real and can be bought
details: Until now the price existed in Stripe and Render but nothing sold it, and nothing could: /api/checkout mapped the founding plan to the founding price and EVERYTHING ELSE to the $129/mo subscription, so a single-report button would have charged a monthly subscription to someone expecting a one-off. That fallthrough is gone - plans are now an explicit table and an unrecognised plan is a 400, not a charge. Buying one opens a Stripe payment-mode session, the webhook records it against your account, and re-running that search serves the report whole with unlimited exports of it, for good. The unlock is keyed on the search (address + property type + lookback), which is the same key the export tally already used, so a bought report never counts against the free monthly export allowance. The $39 tile only appears in the pricing modal when there is actually a gated report on screen to spend it on. Also fixed on the way: a failed webhook used to stay marked as processed, so a purchase lost to a database blip could never be replayed - it now releases the claim and emails the owner.

title: Search cost recalibrated to a measured $0.36
details: A fresh 12-comp report search was measured end-to-end: 8 web searches, 5,035 output tokens, 45.9k cache-write + 121.9k cache-read input = $0.36, less than half the old $0.75 assumption. The July 30 prompt-caching commit (d75608c) is the difference: each web-search round now re-reads the prompt at the 10% cache rate instead of full input price. COST_REPORT_SEARCH and COST_MARKET_SEARCH defaults drop to 0.36 (Explorer shares the same cached pipeline), so the /admin spend tiles stop overstating API cost, and the P&L Forecast workbook's yellow assumption cells were recalibrated to match.

title: Address Explorer: type a market, get real addresses to value
details: A visitor with no address in hand no longer bounces off the blank form. A quiet link under the address field opens the Address Explorer: type a city and state or a 5-digit zip, and get up to 8 real, street-numbered addresses for the selected property type as clickable entries; clicking one fills the form and runs the ordinary report flow, geocode confirmation included. Addresses come from CompNinja's own comp corpus first (a free database read via the new /api/explore-addresses route, addresses only, no deal data), topped up from OpenStreetMap for markets the corpus hasn't covered. The list is deliberately identical for every visitor, so repeat clicks land on the 30-day search cache instead of billing, and because suggested addresses sit in corpus-covered markets, the first click usually runs the cheaper corpus-assisted search budget. A /?explore=City,%20ST&type=Industrial deep link opens the panel prefilled for market pages and campaigns to use later.

title: The Privacy Policy's copy reads like a policy, not product copy
details: The document restyle earlier today fixed the look; this fixes the words. The chatty headings ('Your private financials stay in your browser') and sentence fragments ('HTTPS everywhere, hashed passwords') are replaced by a conventionally drafted policy: an introductory paragraph naming the contracting entity, eleven numbered sections in the standard order (what we collect, browser-only financials, use, providers, cookies, share links, retention, security, children, changes, contact), and complete sentences throughout. Every fact carried over unchanged: the browser-only financials guarantee, the named provider list, the no-trackers stance, and account deletion from My Desk. The Terms page keeps its existing copy.

title: The legal pages read like documents, not dashboards
details: Terms of Service and Privacy Policy shipped earlier today with every section wrapped in a white bordered card, which made a legal document look like a stack of app widgets. Both pages now flow as plain documents: serif section headings, readable line length, no boxes. The grouped 'The legal terms' card on /terms flattened into proper top-level sections, and the privacy page's combined cookies/sharing/retention card did the same. Every word of the copy is unchanged; this is styling only, via a small legal-page style block in the shared market-page CSS.

title: Repeat searches stay free for a month instead of a week
details: A search result is cached and served free to anyone repeating the identical search; that window was 7 days and is now 30. The cost logic is one-way: a repeat on days 8 through 30 that used to bill a fresh ~$0.75 Anthropic call is now a free cache hit, and nothing else changes. The trade is freshness, not money, and it's a safe one here: reports already use a 12-month lookback and commercial comps barely move inside a month. Everything that deliberately busts the cache still does (approving a broker comp, changing the lookback, size or subject details).

title: The Market Explorer rejoins the page, still on its own errand
details: The full-width white band the Explorer got earlier today is reverted: it sits back inline in the content column under the comp searcher, styled like the rest of the landing page. What stays is the behavioral separation that shipped with the band: an Explorer search never hands off to the comp form. No 'Run a valuation' row, Enter never pastes the query into the address field, and dead-end queries still get their inline hints. The one-line note under the heading stays too, since it is now the only cue that the Explorer builds market pages rather than starting a valuation.

title: Market pages drop their FAQ
details: The rewritten FAQ shipped earlier today lasted a few hours: the owner's call is that market pages don't need one at all. The FAQ card and its FAQPage structured data are gone from every market page; the WebPage and breadcrumb markup stay, and the site-wide FAQ on How-it-works (which the footer already links) is now the only FAQ. The comp map is untouched.

title: Market pages get a comp map and a FAQ that stops repeating the page
details: Every market page's FAQ used to answer 'what is the median $/SF' and 'what are cap rates' by restating the numbers from the tiles two scrolls up. Those questions are gone; the FAQ now covers what the page doesn't already say: where the comps come from and what the source badges mean, what the Verified badge is and that contributing brokers get named credit, how the page stays current, and how a missing sale gets added. The FAQPage structured data follows automatically since one array feeds both. And market pages now have the report's comp map: a 'Where these comps are' card pins each street-addressed comp by geocoding it in the visitor's browser (same Census-then-Nominatim stack and shared cache as the report map), with popups showing the address, date, deal type and price. Submarket-level rows are deliberately not pinned, a rough distance gate drops geocoder mismatches (the first test pinned Ontario, CA in Ontario, Canada), and if nothing resolves the card hides itself rather than showing an empty map.

title: The mobile submit row stopped floating over the page
details: On phones the Run a report / View a sample report row used position:sticky so it would pin to the bottom of the screen while the form scrolled underneath it. The owner didn't like the motion, so it's gone: the row now sits in normal document flow at every width, exactly as desktop already behaved.

title: The Market Explorer stands alone
details: The Explorer section no longer hands anything to the comp searcher: the 'Run a valuation for ...' row is gone from its dropdown, and pressing Enter on a query the Explorer can't parse now shows a quiet inline hint (add the state, pick a type, or a note that the Explorer covers Industrial, Office, Retail and Multifamily) instead of pasting the text into the address form and scrolling the page up. Visually the section is now its own full-width white band with hairline borders, with a one-line note that it builds standing market pages, separate from the property valuation above, so it no longer reads as a second search box in the comp searcher's area.

title: Long searches stopped being billed and then thrown away
details: A search that ran long could end in 'Something went wrong' even though the model was healthy and still writing the report: the server put a fixed 150-second ceiling on every Anthropic call, and a full-budget report (up to 10 web searches, then 40-70 seconds of writing, longer on busy or international markets) can honestly outrun it. When the timer fired, the call was aborted mid-report, the visitor saw the error, and every search and token generated up to that moment was still billed, so the site paid for a report nobody received; the visitor's retry paid again. The same ceiling had already been raised once (100s to 150s on 2026-07-30) for this exact symptom, so this time the fixed number is gone: the deadline is now computed per call from the work that call is allowed to do (its web-search budget and its output-token cap), which keeps it above any healthy call no matter how those budgets are tuned later, about 4 minutes 20 seconds for the biggest report. Genuine hangs are still caught fast: a stream that goes silent for 30 seconds fails immediately, exactly as before, so the longer ceiling only ever runs while the model is visibly still working, and the loading card narrates comps arriving the whole way. Verified at zero cost against a faked Anthropic API: a healthy 165-second report that the old code aborted at exactly 150.0 seconds now completes, and a pathological stream that outruns its own derived deadline is still stopped on schedule.

title: The red Back button is gone; Escape stays
details: The corner Back button shipped, moved to the corner, spread to the markets and broker pages, got hidden on phones, and is now removed outright, all within a few days, which is the log telling us it never quite earned its place. What survives is the useful half: on How-it-works, the markets pages and the broker pages, pressing Escape still returns to the previous CompNinja page when there is one and the landing page otherwise, and a first press still just closes the Explore menu when it is open. The header is back to logo and menu.

title: The back button stays off phones
details: The red corner Back button on How-it-works, the markets pages and the broker pages is now hidden below 640px. On a phone it was sitting in the header row next to the logo, spending scarce width on something the browser's own back gesture already does; wider screens keep it exactly as before (in the corner on desktop, in the header row between 640px and 1140px), and the Escape shortcut still works everywhere.

title: The site gets its legal pages: Terms of Service and Privacy Policy
details: CompNinja LLC is now the named contracting entity across the site. Two new pages, /terms and /privacy, carry the terms that were previously only implied: every valuation is an automated estimate and not an appraisal, CompNinja is not a brokerage, subscriptions cancel anytime with access to period end and no refunds, Idaho law governs. The privacy policy tells the true story of the architecture: private financials (NOI, debt, rent roll, gross income) never leave the browser except into your own portfolio, one essential cookie, no trackers, every service provider named. Every footer now reads (c) 2026 CompNinja LLC and links both pages, and small notices appear at account creation and in the pricing dialog. Drafted for attorney review; the pages themselves don't say so.

title: The back button reaches the markets and broker pages
details: The corner back button and Escape shortcut that shipped on How-it-works now cover every page using the shared explore-page header: the markets directory, each market snapshot, the Brokers page, and broker profiles. Same rules everywhere: the button sits in the page's top-left corner on desktop (in the header row on narrower screens), and both it and Escape return to the previous CompNinja page when there is one, otherwise the landing page, so a visitor arriving from a search result lands home rather than bouncing back out to Google. The header's Run a report link went away on those pages the same way it did on How-it-works; the in-page valuation CTAs and footer link are untouched.

title: Smoother view transitions
details: Clicking My Desk used to swap the whole page in one frame: the home stack vanished, the desk snapped in, the scroll jumped to the top, and the portfolio cards popped in a beat later once they loaded. The desk and the home stack now fade in gently on every switch (including browser Back/Forward), the scroll glides instead of jumping, and the portfolio cards ease in after their fetch. The Explore and account menus in the header and the Market Explorer's results dropdown get the same quiet fade on open, matching the fade the server-rendered pages' menus already had; closes stay instant, and typing in the Market Explorer re-renders without re-firing the animation. Everything respects the reduced-motion setting.

title: The landing page dropped its popular-markets link grid
details: The Market Explorer section on the home page used to end in a hardcoded grid of eleven city links plus an 'All markets' link. That listing is gone from the landing page; browsing markets now happens through the Explore menu's Markets entry (and the footer link), which lead to the same directory. The search box stays, so exploring a new market on the spot works exactly as before, and its intro line no longer points at a grid that isn't there.

title: How-it-works gets a red Back button and an Escape shortcut
details: The page's header used to end with a 'Run a report' link, which is a strange answer to the question most visitors have there: how do I get back to where I was? That link is gone from the header (the footer keeps its copy), replaced by a red Back button with a left arrow in the top-left corner of the page (tucked into the header row on narrower screens). Both the button and the Escape key return to the page the visitor came from when that was CompNinja, and to the home page otherwise, so a visitor who landed here straight from a search engine still ends up somewhere useful. Escape stays polite about the Explore menu: with the dropdown open, the first press closes the menu and a second one leaves the page. Verified locally: button and Escape both navigate back after arriving from the home page, and the open-dropdown case closes without navigating.

title: The value hero never shows blank dashes when priced sale comps exist
details: A real search ('3840 Highway 42 Montana', typed for a building actually in Locust Grove, GA) came back with 5 priced sale comps but no square footage, and the What This Building Is Worth card rendered three bare dashes - a broken-looking report. Now, when sale comps carry a $/SF but the building's size is unknown from every source, the hero leads with the per-square-foot band (Low/Likely/High per SF, comp-median center) and says plainly that entering the size turns it into a total dollar value. Two related guards shipped with it: the pre-search address check no longer fails silent when no geocoder recognizes the address - the confirm modal opens in a warning variant ('We couldn't verify this address', 'Run anyway') so a typo costs one click instead of a wrong-market report - and the modal defaults focus to Edit in that state.

title: The export limit stops being a number nobody counted
details: Free reports were supposed to allow three exports a month. The rule existed and was tested, the table existed, and nothing ever wrote to it — so the tally read zero forever and everyone, signed in or not, had unlimited exports. The limit is now real, and generous: five REPORTS a month on a free account, counted per report rather than per click, so wanting the same analysis as a CSV and a PDF and a spreadsheet costs one rather than three. The table stores a row per report instead of a counter, keyed so a repeat export is a no-op rather than a second charge, which also removes any counter to race on. Exporting now needs an account. The alternative was worse than it looks: leaving anonymous visitors uncounted would have given them unlimited exports while a signed-in user got five, making an account strictly worse to have — the ladder only goes one way now, nothing to five to unlimited. The account also replaces the contact form on the export path, so it is one ask instead of two, and what you get back is a real account rather than a form submission. It is an honour system and is written down as one: every export is produced in the browser, so the server can only be asked whether it may, never withhold the file. Someone with dev tools walks straight past it, exactly as they can past the contact form. Every failure path lets the export through — an unreachable server, a failed read, a bug in the counter — because wrongly blocking a report someone is entitled to costs more than wrongly allowing one. With the tier switched off nothing counts at all and the old contact-form gate is untouched.

title: The landing page dropped its jargon label
details: The small red 'Commercial Comp Reports' kicker above the headline was the one piece of industry-speak a first-time visitor hit before anything explained itself - 'comp' means nothing to a non-broker. Rather than rewording it, it is gone: the plain-English headline ('Know what the building is worth before you make the call') now leads the page, the pitch line and its trust signals stay, and the top of the page is one line shorter. The report's own kicker and the Market Explorer's are untouched.

title: The browser tab stopped promising Free ahead of the Pro launch
details: The tab title and the social-share preview titles all read 'Free Commercial Real Estate Comps' — wording from before the paid tier existed. With Pro on the way, a search result or shared link leading with 'Free' would contradict the pricing page the visitor lands on. All three now say 'Commercial Real Estate Comps'. Google shows the old title until its next crawl of the page.

title: The header nav folds its browse links into one Explore menu
details: The bar had grown to six items (Markets, Brokers, How it works, Pricing, My Desk, Sign in) and was crowding phones - How it works was simply hidden below the sm breakpoint to make things fit. The four browse links now live behind a single Explore dropdown on every screen size, while the two actions, My Desk and Sign in (or the account avatar), stay visible; the dropdown reuses the account menu's exact styling so nothing new was invented visually. Pricing keeps its existing rules inside the menu: hidden until billing is live, hidden again for Pro subscribers. The server-rendered pages (/markets, every market page, /brokers, /how-it-works) mirror the same menu as a no-JS details element with a small close-on-outside-click script, scoped so it can never touch the FAQ accordions on /how-it-works, and anchored to the right edge after the left-anchored version clipped offscreen at 375px. Verified at mobile and desktop widths on the home page, /how-it-works and /markets: one-row header on a phone, menu fully on screen, outside click and Escape close it, FAQ accordions unaffected.

title: A street address could end up stored in the analytics market column
details: Analytics events are meant to be PII-free: each one records a property type, a market as city and state, and an outcome, and the address is used to work out the market and then thrown away. That held for any address written the usual way, and it quietly did not hold for one written without a comma. The market parser walks backwards through the comma-separated parts looking for a US state code, and when it finds none it falls back to the last part - but an address with no commas has only one part, which is the whole address. So a real search for a street address typed without commas was sitting in the market column verbatim. Found by reading the actual rows in the database rather than by testing, because the test addresses used to check this were all well-formed and could not have caught it. A market is now either city-and-state or nothing, enforced in the single function every event passes through, which covers all eight kinds that carry a market: searches, leads, portfolio saves and refreshes, comp submissions, comp reviews, shares and the type autofill. The guard is deliberately NOT in the market parser itself, because that same function is the comp corpus key - rows are filed under it and looked up by an exact match - so changing it there would silently re-file the corpus and pin the hit rate at zero. Nothing real is lost by dropping an unparseable market: it was never a market, and the event is still counted, showing as unknown. One visible side effect: non-US searches used to log their country as the market and now log as unknown, which is more honest than filing a Vancouver search under Canada. Existing rows need a one-off scrub in the database; the parser change only stops new ones.

title: The landing pitch gets out of the way once a report is up
details: The headline and one-line pitch above the search form used to stay on screen even after a report finished loading, sitting above content the visitor came for. It now hides the moment a report renders and comes back when the report is closed or My Desk is exited, so a first-time visitor still gets the pitch and a returning one isn't reading past it.

title: Repeat markets stay on the cheap search path for 75 days instead of 45
details: Corpus-first retrieval cuts a report's web-search budget from 10 to 3 (or 2 with a known building size) when we already hold 4 or more recent priced comps for that market and type - but only while the newest harvested comp was under 45 days old. The 2026-07-30 speed work flagged that freshness gate as the top untested cost lever, and it is now 75 days. The quality exposure is deliberately narrow: the only deals a corpus-assisted search can miss are ones that surfaced during the staleness gap, the report's own fresh searches are aimed at exactly that gap because the model already holds the older comps, and coverage is still filtered to the requested lookback window, so a market whose comps have aged out stops qualifying no matter what the gate says. Expected effect on affected reports is small - most should be indistinguishable from a full-budget run, with the value range moving low single digits at worst - while their cost roughly halves. Judged going forward by the /admin corpus hit rate and spot-checks of corpus-tagged reports; it is one constant to revert. Verified with backdated corpus data against a faked Anthropic API: a market whose corpus was 60 days old took the corpus path (budget 2, with the size memo stacking), and the same market at 80 days correctly fell back to the full 8-search budget.

title: A building's size is looked up once, then remembered
details: When the visitor leaves the square-footage field blank, the search budget carries two extra web searches just so the model can look the building's size up in public records - the single priciest line item in a search after the comps themselves. A building's size doesn't change, so the answer is now remembered: the first search of an address pays for the lookup, and every later search of that address hands the model the known size up front and runs the smaller budget, exactly as if the visitor had typed it (10 searches down to 8, or 3 down to 2 in corpus-strong markets). The visitor's own entry always wins over the memo, and the remembered size still autofills the form as an editable override, so a wrong number is visible and fixable, never silent. Two rules keep it honest. Model-ESTIMATED sizes are never remembered - a guess that quietly becomes 'known' for every future search of an address is how a valuation drifts - only assessor-record and listing lookups persist. And the source is stored verbatim, so the value hero keeps saying 'from public records' only when that is actually where the number came from. Stored durably in Supabase (subject_sizes - the DDL comment sits above the memo code in server.js and must be run at deploy) with the usual file fallback, and applied outside the cache key, so no existing cached report is orphaned. Verified end to end against a faked Anthropic API at zero cost: the first search looked the size up and remembered it, the second search of the same address ran the smaller budget with the size in its prompt and the report still carried the size for the hero, and an estimate-sourced size was correctly never stored.

title: The Development Hub's two halves finally line up
details: The last pass on this page fixed the type scale, the radii and the shouting uppercase labels, and measured all three. It then left the spacing entirely alone: twenty-five different margin, padding and gap values, which is the same defect as twelve font sizes wearing a different hat, and the reason the page still read as slightly arbitrary even with the type sorted. There is now one spacing scale of nine steps and no loose pixel values, with two deliberate exceptions that carry comments saying why: the 104px spine column, which is a fixed measure rather than rhythm, and the negative margin on a changelog entry's hover area, which has to stay the exact inverse of its padding or the highlight sits off the text. Worse, the previous pass claimed something untrue. Its own comment said the Future ideas list shared the changelog's margin column so the two halves of the page lined up. They never did: the changelog was a grid and the ideas list was a flat flex column, so Now, Next and Later sat inline while the dates sat out in the margin. Each bucket is now its own grid on the identical column, which needed a wrapper element around each group because a flat list cannot do it - grid auto-placement puts the second heading beside the first group's rows instead of starting a new one. Measured rather than eyeballed this time: the date column and the bucket headings report the same left edge to the pixel. Red also stopped doing nine jobs at once. It now means interaction only - links, buttons, focus, errors, the active filter - and the changelog's own entries are one dot in three weights instead of three colours, so the content no longer competes with the page's controls. The four remaining loose colours became tokens. One bug surfaced while verifying: the mobile rule sat above the new bucket rule in the stylesheet, so at equal specificity the desktop two-column layout won and buckets never collapsed on a phone. The media query now sits last, with a comment explaining why it has to.

title: The loading card now lists comps as the model finds them
details: Instrumentation settled where a report's 45-80 seconds actually go: the web searches finish in the first five, and the model then spends 40-70 seconds writing the report JSON. That writing stretch was a dead bar creeping toward the right, which reads as a site that might be broken. Now the server watches the streamed text as it arrives, and the moment a comp's closing brace lands it sends the address and price down the existing progress stream, where the loading card lists it as a plain text line - the five most recent, oldest scrolling off. The wait is unchanged; what changed is that it visibly consists of comps accumulating. Two guardrails matter more than the feature. The extractor only ever feeds the progress stream - the report itself is still parsed from the full text at the end, so a scanner bug can cost a progress line but never a report. And the paywall holds during loading: once a visitor has seen as many identified comps as their plan allows, further events are stripped to an anonymous count, so the card says '+ N more found, unlock with Pro' rather than flashing addresses the report is about to withhold. Verified with a live search: comps appeared on the card one by one from about twenty seconds in, and the finished report rendered exactly as before.

title: Reports are a few seconds faster to write
details: Same instrumentation, other lever: since the slow part is the model WRITING the report, the fix is to ask it to write less. Per-comp latitude and longitude are gone from the requested shape - the map has re-placed every pin from real geocoding since the Street View work, so the model was spending tokens on twenty-four coordinates that were thrown away on arrival; only the subject property's coordinates remain, for the map's first paint and the wrong-state sanity check. The market summary is capped at two to three sentences and told to lead with the single thing an owner most needs to know, and value drivers at three. Roughly 250-350 fewer output tokens, which is three to four seconds of writing time on every billed search, at no cost to anything the report shows. Old cached reports still carry their comp coordinates and render unchanged; the map on new reports paints the subject pin immediately and adds comp pins as geocoding resolves them, which was already how pins behaved a moment after load.

title: Two places still promised subscribers what the tier can't do yet
details: The pricing tile was trimmed to sell only what ships — the full comp list and the ten-year lookback — because unlimited exports and report branding are granted by the entitlement rules but neither is actually built. Two other places kept the old wording: the plan card a subscriber sees on My Desk, and the confirmation banner shown seconds after paying. So the claim was removed from the page that asks for money and left on the two that appear once it has been taken, which is the worse half. Both now say the same thing as the tile. Found by looking at a real plan card during the phase-8 test run, not by grepping.

title: A shorter lookback is now served from a cached longer one
details: A 12-month search and a 24-month search of the same property used to be two separately billed reports, even though every comp the shorter window could return is already sitting inside the cached longer one. On an exact cache miss the server now probes the preset lookback ladder (12, 24, 36 months) for a cached longer-window report with the same address, type and knobs, filters its comps down to the requested window by deal date, and serves that instead of paying for a fresh search. Undated comps are dropped rather than passed off as recent: the parent search only promised they fell inside ITS window, and the site's provenance rule is under-claim, never over. The shortcut only fires when the filtered set is still a real report - at least 6 comps, including 3 dated sales when the ask includes sales, because the value hero's range is sales-only and a saleless subset would put a number on top of nothing. Anything thinner falls through to the normal corpus-first search unchanged, and the derived report is never re-cached, so it can't outlive its parent's 7-day TTL. Verified against a seeded cache with no API key in play: the 12-month ask returned exactly the in-window comps with no Anthropic call, while a thin parent and a 6-month ask both correctly fell through to the paid path.

title: A cancelled subscription no longer masquerades as a renewing one
details: Caught live during the phase-8 test run, minutes after the first sandbox subscription was cancelled through Stripe's portal: the app kept saying the plan was active with no cancelling state, even though Stripe showed the cancellation scheduled. The webhook had arrived, verified its signature, and written the row; the Supabase row just said cancel_at_period_end = false. The cause is a Stripe API change: newer API versions report a portal cancel not through the old cancel_at_period_end flag (which now stays false) but as a cancel_at timestamp holding the scheduled end date. The mapper only read the old flag, so every cancellation would have looked like a still-renewing subscription; the subscriber would then hard-drop to free at period end with no warning state in between, and the plan card's cancelling copy could never render. The mapper now reads both shapes. Without the end-to-end sandbox run this would have shipped to live mode unnoticed - the unit tests only encoded the old shape; they now encode both.

title: The type autofill now reports whether it is actually working
details: The autofill is designed to do nothing when it is unsure, which is the right behaviour and also makes it invisible: when the dropdown does not move, there is no way to tell whether OpenStreetMap had no building at that house number, or the building was mapped but untyped, or the lookup never completed because Overpass was down, or it quietly agreed with the type already selected. Those are four very different facts, and the difference matters - one is a data gap you cannot fix, another is an outage you can. That ambiguity is not hypothetical: it hid the across-the-street bug through an entire round of testing, because a rate-limited Overpass looked exactly like honest silence. Every completed attempt now records its outcome, and /admin carries a Type autofill tile showing how often it set a type out of how many tries, broken down by applied, agreed, no match, ambiguous and failed. Races are deliberately not counted - if the visitor picked a type or started a search while the lookup was in flight, nothing was decided, and counting it would dilute the ratio the tile exists to report. What is stored is a market (city and state), the resulting type, and the outcome word, exactly like every other analytics event: the address is used to derive the market and then discarded, so nothing identifying is written. The endpoint takes only an address and an outcome and derives or whitelists everything it keeps, so it can be used to add rows but not to choose what they say. Proven on the first real run, where the tile immediately distinguished a throttled Overpass from a genuine absence of data - which is the entire point of building it.

title: The property-type autofill was reading the building across the street
details: Tested on a real Phoenix address the day it shipped, the autofill set the type to Retail for 1500 W Bethany Home Rd. The building it had actually read was Mandarin Super Buffet at 1501 West Bethany Home Road: odd against even, the other side of the road. The cause is that a geocoded address lands on the STREET CENTERLINE, so a search radius wide enough to reach the property also reaches everything opposite it, and being nearest cannot tell the two sides of a street apart. A house number can, and OpenStreetMap was already returning one in the same response - it was simply never looked at. Now a footprint has to prove it is the searched address before it gets a vote: its house number must match the number typed (ranges like 1500-1510 and forms like 1500A included), and if it names a street, a distinctive word from that street name has to appear in the address too, which stops a cross street carrying the same number from standing in. The check runs as a filter BEFORE the best-building scoring rather than as a verdict on the winner, because checking the winner would let a large wrong-numbered neighbour outscore the correct building and then veto the whole lookup - precisely the Phoenix case. A building OpenStreetMap has not addressed is no longer evidence of anything, which is the same rule the map photos already follow: the actual property or nothing. The trade is deliberate and one-directional - the feature now fires less often, and every time it fires the claim is checkable. Verified both ways: the Phoenix address now declines (no footprint numbered 1500 exists there at all), and 350 5th Ave still resolves to Office off the Empire State Building's own house number.

title: The Development Hub reads like a document instead of a dashboard
details: Same CompNinja palette and type as before - the paper, the ink, the red, Georgia headings over Inter - but the page was assembled rather than designed, and it showed. Three habits were doing the damage: twelve different font sizes, three border radii, and nine competing tiny uppercase labels, so nothing sat in a hierarchy and everything shouted equally. The changelog now reads as a dated document. Each day is one row: the date sits in its own margin column in Georgia with the year dropped beneath it, and that day's entries stack alongside. Entry type is no longer a fixed-width filled pill in a column of its own - it is a small coloured dot and the word in sentence case, red for features, ink for improvements, grey for fixes, so the line stays text. Entry details are held to a 66-character measure rather than running the full page width, which is the difference between reading them and skimming past them. The white cards are gone; sections are a serif heading and a hairline rule, and the type filters are a row of links with the active one underlined instead of a raised segmented control. The Future ideas list shares the same margin spine so both halves of the page line up. Measured after: six font sizes, one radius, and uppercase reserved for the page kicker and the wordmark. Self-contained - the page carries its own stylesheet, so nothing else on the site is touched.

title: A way to actually buy Pro
details: The billing plumbing had no front door: every locked surface in the app fired a placeholder alert saying checkout wasn't wired up. Now there's a pricing modal — Pro at $129/month beside the founding annual at $990, with a live 'N of 50 left' counter — and every locked control in the report routes to it. Buying redirects to Stripe's own hosted checkout, so no card detail ever touches this page. The awkward cases are the ones worth naming: choosing a plan while signed out nudges you to create an account and then resumes the same plan; the last founding seat going between page load and click withdraws that tile and points at monthly instead of dead-ending; and returning from a successful payment waits for the webhook to land rather than telling someone who just paid that they're still on Free. The tile sells only what ships today — the full comp list and the 10-year lookback; unlimited exports and report branding are held back until they exist. Subscribers get a plan card and a link into Stripe's portal to cancel or fix a card. All of it stays invisible while PRO_ENABLED is unset.

title: Test the paid tier without gating everyone else
details: PRO_ENABLED is one global switch, so proving the paid tier against the real site meant flipping it for the whole audience: every visitor's report cut to four comps, and a working checkout put in front of them. That checkout is in Stripe test mode, where the card numbers are published — a stranger could have taken a genuine active subscription for nothing, while a real customer's real card would have been declined, and the row they created would still have been sitting there in live mode. PRO_AUDIENCE narrows the switch to named accounts: sign in as one of them and you see the paid tier, everyone else gets the app exactly as it was, and only listed accounts can reach checkout or the billing portal. Unset, which is the launch setting, it changes nothing. The webhook is deliberately left outside the allowlist — it has no user and has to keep recording events, or the test proves nothing. Being on the allowlist grants nothing by itself; PRO_ENABLED is still the master switch. Leaving it set after launch would ship a product nobody can buy, on a deployment that looks perfectly healthy, so the startup log says so in as many words.

title: A paid-for lookback option that stayed locked
details: 'Custom…' was treated as an infinite lookback, so it sat above every ceiling — including Pro's — and stayed disabled with a '· Pro' label for the people paying for it. The '· Pro' suffix was also append-only, so upgrading mid-session left enabled options still advertising the upgrade you'd just bought. Gating is now reversible in both directions.

title: Any URL with a query string 404'd on the home page and My Desk
details: The static route matched the raw URL against '/' and '/desk' exactly, so anything carrying a query string missed it. Stripe returns from checkout to /desk?checkout=success, which would have 404'd the page someone lands on immediately after paying. Matching on the path fixes that, and incidentally fixes campaign links to /?utm_source=…, which had been 404ing for the same reason.

title: A shared contact book for the team at /contacts
details: Leads, brokers, owners and vendors were living in whoever's phone happened to take the call. There is now an internal rolodex at /contacts, behind the same admin key as the analytics dashboard and the dev hub — unlock any one of the three and all three open. Each entry holds a name, company, role, phone, email, market and free-form notes, plus a category (lead, broker, owner, investor, vendor, other) and a status that tracks where the relationship stands (new, contacted, following up, client, dead). The list filters by category, by status, and by typing into a search box that looks across every field including the notes. Phone numbers and emails are tap-to-call and tap-to-mail on a phone. Any filtered view exports to CSV, built in the browser so the admin key never travels in a URL. Deliberately separate from the site's public lead capture: that still feeds the leads table untouched, while this is the book the team keeps by hand. Saves are one contact at a time rather than replacing the whole list, so two people editing at once cannot overwrite each other. The page is noindexed three ways and the local fallback file is git-ignored, since it holds real contact details.

title: Stripe subscriptions, without adding a dependency
details: Checkout, the customer portal, and the webhook that keeps subscription state in step, all spoken to Stripe over its REST API with plain fetch — so the app still installs nothing. Webhook signatures are verified with Node's built-in crypto against the raw request body, which is the part that must not be wrong: a forged signature, a tampered body, a missing header and a webhook replayed ten minutes later are all rejected, each with its own reason in the log. Handlers are idempotent because Stripe retries and a sleeping free-tier host guarantees it will: every event id is claimed in a table first, and every write is an upsert keyed on the user, so a replayed event rewrites the same row instead of creating a second subscription. Events can also arrive out of order — a subscription can be created before the checkout that made it — so both paths resolve the same user and write the same row, and whichever lands first wins. A failed payment opens a 7-day grace window rather than cutting access off, and a second failure inside that window does not restart the clock. The founding-member price closes at 50 seats, counted server-side rather than protected by a coupon that could be shared; the count is of subscriptions ever created, so cancelling does not reopen a seat at a price we have stopped selling. Nothing is live: billing needs PRO_ENABLED and the Stripe keys, and both are still unset in production.

title: The upgrade prompt was rendering off the side of the screen
details: The "N more comparables available with Pro" notice was a full-width cell inside the comp table. That table scrolls horizontally and is often over 2,000 pixels wide while its visible window is only a few hundred, so the centred message landed far off the right edge and could only be found by dragging the table sideways. On a phone it was worse. The count is the whole conversion argument for the paid tier, so it now sits below the table as an ordinary block that is always in view, and the phone card list shares the same one instead of drawing a second copy. The shimmering placeholder rows stay in the table, where they read as withheld rows of data.

title: Free reports show four comps; the valuation still uses every one
details: The comp gate, still dark behind PRO_ENABLED. A free report now lists the four best comparables and says plainly how many more exist, with the rest standing in as redacted placeholder rows. The four are chosen, not truncated: sale comps fill the slots before leases (the value range is sales-based, so a list of leases would not support the number above it), and within that they are ranked by the same recency, size-fit and provenance weighting the valuation already trusts. The headline value range is deliberately NOT gated. Alongside the four visible comps the server sends an anonymized basis row for each withheld one — $/SF, size, date, transaction, provenance tier, and nothing else: no address, no sale price, no source link, no notes, no coordinates. So a free report's number is computed from the whole comp set and comes out identical to what a subscriber sees. Verified end to end: the same report gated and ungated both value the building at $6,206,732 to $6,529,080 from 14 sale comps. The locked rows are placeholders rather than blurred real data, because a CSS blur leaves the text sitting in the page source; there is nothing in them to recover. Two side doors closed at the same time: the in-report "From CompNinja's records" panel and the watchlist feed were both handing out comps with addresses and no subscription, and now return a count instead of rows. Free lookback tops out at 12 months, with longer windows shown disabled and labelled rather than hidden. The cache, the comp corpus and the market-page publisher all still see whole reports, so nothing downstream starves and one cached search still serves everybody.

title: Pro tier groundwork: one entitlement rule, behind a flag
details: Adds the single function that answers what any visitor is allowed to do — anonymous, free account, active Pro, the grace period after a failed payment, cancelled-but-still-inside-the-paid-period, and a one-off single-report unlock — plus the database schema for subscriptions, branding profiles, report purchases and monthly export tallies. Nothing is gated yet: the tier ships dark behind PRO_ENABLED, which defaults off and leaves the app behaving exactly as it does today. Deliberately fails closed, so an unrecognized subscription status or an unreadable date resolves to the free tier rather than handing out Pro. Billing tables get no local-file fallback on purpose — every other store here degrades to disk when the database is unconfigured, which is right for leads and wrong for money, since a subscription written to an ephemeral disk is a paying customer silently downgraded on the next deploy. Also the repo's first tests: 28 cases over the entitlement table, running in under a tenth of a second with no database and no server.

title: Stop paying nine times to read the same instructions
details: A billed report search costs about $0.75, and most of that is not the web searches - it is input tokens. The reason is that a search is not one call to the model but a loop: one round per web search plus a final round to write the report, and every round re-reads the entire instruction prompt from the top at full price. Measured, that prompt is about 3,300 tokens, so an 8-search report was paying for the same text nine times over, roughly 29,000 tokens before a single comp was found. Those instructions are byte-for-byte identical on every round - only the search results appended after them change - so they are now cached: the first round writes the cache and every round after it reads at about a tenth of the price. That is about 23,000 tokens off a full search, near 9 percent of its cost, and the model sees exactly the same prompt it saw before, so nothing about report quality changes. Each search now also logs its cache read and write counts, so a future prompt edit that quietly breaks caching is visible in the logs rather than showing up on a bill.

title: The property type now fills itself in from the address
details: Searching a warehouse with the type still set to Office is an easy mistake to make and an expensive one to miss - the type drives the comp search, the report's columns, the cache key and the corpus bucket, so a forgotten dropdown produces a confident report built on the wrong comps. Now, when you finish typing an address, OpenStreetMap's tag for the building at that spot sets the type for you: warehouse, apartments, house, shop, office and their relatives each map onto one of the six types. It is deliberately narrow. Generic tags (building=yes, commercial, residential) decide nothing, and a building OSM has not mapped at all never implies Land - only positive evidence moves the control, because coverage gaps cluster in exactly the rural markets where a wrong guess would do the most damage. Only the footprint at the address gets a vote, never a tagged neighbour's: on one Midtown block 40 of 41 footprints came back building=yes, so borrowing a neighbour's tag would have been the common case rather than the rare one. Four things stop it dead: a type you picked yourself is never overridden, subject details you have already typed are never wiped, an address without a street number is ignored (a bare 'Dallas, TX' geocodes to a district point and would read some random downtown tower), and every change it does make says so in one line under the dropdown with one-click Undo. Costs nothing per search - no AI call, just the free geocoder and OpenStreetMap - and every failure path leaves the form exactly as you left it.

title: Long searches no longer time out on themselves
details: A search was cut off after 100 seconds and the visitor was told "The search took too long and was stopped" - which reads as a broken site rather than a slow one. That ceiling turned out to be too tight: writing the report alone takes 40 to 70 seconds, so a busy market could legitimately run past it, and it was hit twice in one afternoon of testing. The ceiling is now 150 seconds. It is only safe to raise because a separate 30-second watchdog, added with the live progress work, already fails a genuinely stuck request fast - so the longer limit can now only be reached while the model is still actively producing output, never on a hang. The progress bar keeps moving throughout either way.

title: Comp notes got shorter, and say more
details: Streaming measurements showed the report is slow because of how long it takes to WRITE, not to search, and that the per-comp "notes" field was the single biggest thing being written: 18 to 28 percent of the whole report, up to 466 characters on one comp. Reading them showed why. Most of that length was padding of two kinds: the model narrating its own research ("Included as the nearest comparable found; full transaction details require CoStar or broker access") and restating figures that already have their own columns (size, date, price, $/SF). Notes are now capped at two short sentences and both kinds of padding are banned outright, with the caveat that changes what a price MEANS - asking versus closed, price not disclosed, portfolio or distressed sale, Modified Gross versus NNN - explicitly protected and promoted to the front. Measured on a like-for-like market: average note 139 to 104 characters, longest 188 to 115, whole report 13 percent shorter to write. Nothing was lost: every price caveat survived and now reads first, instead of being buried behind a sentence about which website the listing came from. Reports already cached keep their older, longer notes until those entries expire.

title: The progress bar now tells the truth
details: The loading card used to run on a stopwatch: seven fixed phrases on a timer, and a bar that eased to 89.5% and stopped. On a long search that meant staring at "Assembling your report, almost there" with a frozen bar for the last 30 to 40 seconds, which reads as a hang. Progress now comes from the search itself, streamed live: the real queries as they are issued ("ontario ca industrial warehouse sale 2025 comparable"), how many results came back, whether the report was built from comps CompNinja already had, and then a bar that advances on the report actually being written. Measuring it also settled where the time goes, and it was not where we assumed: the web searches finish in the first few seconds, and the model then spends 40 to 70 seconds WRITING the report. The old timer had that backwards, which is exactly why it froze. The wall-clock simulation stays as a fallback for browsers or proxies that cannot stream, cache hits still return instantly as plain JSON with none of this, and a dropped connection now shows an error instead of leaving the card spinning forever.

title: Search timing is now measured, and a parallel-search experiment sits behind a switch
details: Report generation had never been instrumented, so every explanation of why it takes a minute was guesswork. Each search now logs its wall time, search count, and token usage. First reading: a report runs 8 to 10 serial web-search rounds, and because the model re-reads every prior result each round, input tokens grow quadratically with the round count (one 8-round report: 67 seconds, 154,000 input tokens, to produce 3,000 tokens of output). Later streaming measurements corrected the conclusion drawn from that — searching is only a few seconds of the wait, and writing the report is 40 to 70 of it. A two-lane parallel search was built to halve that serial depth, one lane starting from brokerage listings and the other from news and public records, merged with address de-duplication. On a same-address A/B it ran 42% faster but returned one comp fewer, and on a dense market it barely saved time at all, because the report can only finish as fast as the slower lane. A single deep search aims its later queries at the gaps it knows it still has; two shallow lanes both rediscover the easy comps. So it ships OFF (set PARALLEL_SEARCH=on to try it) and the default report path is unchanged.

title: The building-size lookup goes first, not last
details: When no size is entered, the report looks up the building's square footage — but that instruction was an unordered afterthought in the search prompt, so comp-hunting could consume the whole search budget before the subject address was ever looked at. This hit hardest on corpus-assisted searches, which run only 3 web searches. The lookup is now an explicit first step naming where sizes actually live (assessor and parcel records, property-detail pages, listings), with a new guard against borrowing a neighboring property's size — adjacent parcels surface readily in search results, and a wrong size multiplies straight into the valuation. Verified on the tightest path: a corpus-assisted industrial search came back with the building's exact listed size, correctly sourced. A size can still come back empty when no public source exists for the exact address — by design, since honest-empty beats guessed.

title: Reports now ask for up to 12 comps instead of 8
details: More data points make the percentile-based value range steadier, so report searches now request up to 12 comps (was 8), with a modestly larger search budget and enough output headroom that a long report can't get cut off. The anti-padding rule still applies — in a thin market the model returns the honest smaller number rather than inventing rows. Market Explorer pages and the seed generator stay at 8 (their pages don't need the bigger ask, and their shared cache keys must not shift). Estimated cost per billed report search rises from about $0.60 to about $0.75; corpus-assisted searches keep their small fixed budget.

title: The report says plainly how much to trust the range
details: Three honesty fixes. When only 2 or 3 sale comps back the value range, the report now says so and calls the band a rough guide instead of silently showing the raw spread. Comps in a wholly different size class than the subject wear a small double-dagger on their size, with the trust line naming how many count less. And the report's three center statistics now agree: the market chart's line and the stat-tile spread marker both show the comp-set median (the same statistic family as the hero), and the model's market-level figure is labeled "Market Avg $/SF" so it can't be mistaken for an average of the table's comps.

title: One searchable list of recent searches on My Desk
details: "Re-run" and "Saved reports" were two lists recording the same event — every search wrote both, and both keyed on the same address and type — so the only thing that ever distinguished them was which one had dropped an entry first. They are now one list, and each property carries both actions plainly: Open reopens the saved report free, Re-run runs a fresh search. History also goes 25 deep instead of 5, with the newest 10 keeping their full report; past that a row stays re-runnable. A filter box appears once the list passes eight rows, the tail collapses behind "show more", and clearing now asks for a second click. Existing lists merge automatically on first visit.

title: Brokers now has its own page
details: "For Brokers" was a header button that scrolled to a section buried on the landing page — no URL of its own, nothing for search engines to find. It's now simply "Brokers" at /brokers: a real page carrying the contribute-and-get-credit pitch, the owner-introduction offer, and a plain-English explanation of what the Verified badge means. It's in the sitemap and linked from the header and footer of every page, including the market pages, which never had a broker link at all. The landing page drops the section. "Submit a comp" from the new page opens the same submission form as before.

title: Smarter valuation math: comp weighting and price indexing
details: The value range now weighs each sale comp by how much it deserves to move the number: recent comps count more than stale ones (2-year half-life), comps near the subject's size count more than buildings of a wholly different scale, and Verified or public-record comps count more than model estimates. Each comp's price is also indexed to the report date using the market's annual trend (a new model-supplied figure, bounded server-side), so in a moving market last year's sales stop dragging the range toward last year's prices. The comp table and chart still show raw reported figures, and the hero's trust line discloses the weighting and the trend rate used.

title: My Desk moved to its own /desk page
details: The re-run chips, saved-report chips, and the portfolio/watchlist desk moved off the home page onto a bookmarkable /desk (back/forward work; noindexed). It works signed out too — local recent searches and saved reports show with a sign-in prompt for the account areas — so the My Desk header link is now always visible. The home page condenses to hero → search → results → marketing.

title: Every comp's $/SF is now verified against its own price and size
details: The valuation range used to take the model's per-comp $/SF on faith. The server now recomputes it from the comp's stated sale price divided by building size — filling it when missing and replacing it when the figures disagree by more than 10%, with a small dagger in the table disclosing any recompute. The search prompt also now requires verifiable price + size on every sale comp and steers comp selection toward buildings of similar size (half to twice the subject), since a small building and a huge one trade at different $/SF. Older saved and shared reports get the same fill at display time, so previously unpriced comps count toward their ranges too.

title: Popup photos fit on phone screens
details: The photo made map popups wider than the phone-sized map itself, clipping the left edge with no way to scroll it into view. Popups now size their photo and text to the map's actual width — desktop is unchanged.

title: Comp confidence visible on the map
details: Map pin popups now carry the comp's color-coded source-confidence badge (green Verified down to orange Estimate), and the table legend names the scale for what it is: source confidence, strongest first. Same defensible tiers as always — no invented probability scores.

title: Submarket rows can never wear a sourced badge
details: The search prompt forbids market-level rows posing as comps, but in thin markets the model pads anyway — a Boston report returned "submarket estimate" rows claiming listing provenance. The server now enforces the rule: any comp without a street-numbered address gets its trust badge forced to Estimate, whatever the model claimed.

title: No more duplicate photos on submarket-estimate comps
details: Comps without a real street address ("Financial District, general submarket estimate") geocode to a district point, and several of them borrowed the same neighboring building's photo. Photos now also require a street-numbered address; estimate rows keep their pins with clean text popups. Downtown shots were also reframed — wider view, slight upward tilt — so tall buildings photographed from close range show a recognizable building instead of a slice of wall.

title: The property photo shows the property — or doesn't show
details: Rural reports surfaced popup photos of trees, dirt roads, and empty fields: with no mapped building footprint, every camera-aiming strategy just guesses. Photos now appear only when the building's footprint is mapped (so the picture provably frames the structure); otherwise the popup stays clean text. A second lookup server was added so a busy primary doesn't blank photos for a whole report.

title: Street View aims at the building's front door
details: House photos sometimes showed the yard or a bad angle: with no building footprint mapped, the camera aimed at a point on the street. The camera now targets the mapped building when one exists, and otherwise asks Google by address — rooftop-accurate for most houses — instead of the raw street point.

title: Hovered popups never clip the property photo
details: Hovering a pin near the top of the map showed its popup with the photo cut off by the map's edge (hover deliberately never moves the map). The popup now slides down inside the map until it fully fits — clicking still glides the map to center it properly.

title: Comp pins can no longer land in the wrong state
details: Comps sometimes came back without a state (common for residential street names) and geocoders silently guessed one — a state-less Springfield resolved to Massachusetts. Comp addresses missing a state are now anchored with the subject's own city/state, the model is required to return full addresses, and any comp geocode farther than 300 miles from the subject is rejected in favor of the model's approximate pin.

title: Clicked popups pan fully into view
details: Clicking a pin near the top of the map opened its photo popup partly cut off. A click now glides the map smoothly to center the pin and its whole popup in view — one predictable transition on every click. Hovering still never moves the map.

title: Street-level photos live on pin hover
details: Google Street View is now configured: hovering a map pin shows a real ground-level photo of the building, aimed at the structure itself. Where Street View has no coverage, the popup swaps in the free aerial close-up instead of showing no photo.

title: Popup photos center on the building itself
details: Geocoders place address points on the street in front of a property, so popup photos framed the road with the building off to the side. Each pin now looks up the actual building footprint (OpenStreetMap) and the photo centers on the building, dot on the roof. No footprint mapped = the previous framing.

title: Aerial photos frame the building, not the street
details: The popup aerial zoomed so tight that big industrial buildings showed as pavement and a roof corner — the geocoded point sits on the street frontage. The zoom now scales with the property's size, so the photo frames the whole building.

title: Aerial property photo in pin popups
details: Hovering a map pin now always shows a photo of the property: a free aerial close-up (stitched Esri imagery with a dot marking the exact spot) whenever Google Street View isn't configured. Street-level photos take over automatically once the Google key is set.

title: Map pins preview on hover
details: Hovering a map pin now opens its popup (and its Street View photo) instead of requiring a click; clicking pins the popup open until dismissed. Touch devices keep tap-to-open, and the map no longer pans under the cursor.

title: Click-to-edit changelog entries
details: Click any entry's text on /dev to edit its title and details or attach a personal note. Edits live in a durable overlay (Supabase devlog_overrides) merged over the committed devlog.json, with an edited tag and one-click restore of the original text.

title: Dev Hub changelog toolbar
details: The four filter pills became one segmented control with the active type raised as a white card and counts set as quieter secondary numbers; the search box moved inline beside it and says what it searches.

title: Dev Hub delete button
details: Deleting an idea used a native confirm() dialog, which some embedded browsers suppress — the click silently did nothing. Replaced with an inline two-step confirm: click Delete, then Confirm? (reverts after 4 seconds).

title: Street View photos in map popups
details: Clicking a map pin shows a street-level photo of the building above the popup text, served through a key-holding proxy. Dark until the Google key is configured; popups stay text-only on any failure.

title: Development Hub reliability + upgrades
details: Ideas can no longer be silently wiped by a failed load or a half-failed save (upsert-then-prune writes, editing disabled on load failure). Ideas gained Now/Next/Later priorities, notes, and a dated Shipped history; the changelog gained type filters, text search, collapsible months, a last-shipped line, and optional commit links.

title: Escape returns to the home page
details: Pressing Escape on an open report closes it back to the landing view; the report stays in Saved reports. Yields to the fullscreen map, modals, and focused inputs.

title: Development Hub
details: New /dev page: changelog timeline of every shipped fix and improvement, plus an editable Future Ideas list. Admin-key gated, like /admin.

title: In-report corpus comp offers
details: Reports now offer provenance-good comps from CompNinja's own records for the subject's market and type, with one-click add.

title: Report curation
details: Exclude or restore comps, add your own, and record a price-discovery read. Curation persists with the report, annotates exports, and never leaks user-authored comps into the corpus.

title: Fullscreen map placement
details: The fullscreen comp map now pins to the viewport instead of the report column.

title: Operating-expense benchmark
details: Non-Land reports carry a market op-ex band; enter gross income and the report benchmarks your expense ratio against it (private figures stay out of shares).

title: Per-type subject property details
details: The "Your property details" form adapts to the property type; details ride to the model and the cache key so comp selection matches the subject.

title: Per-asset-class comp columns on market pages
details: Market pages show each property type's own spec columns, derived from the same field map the reports use.

title: Corpus health alarm
details: Silent corpus write/read failures now surface as a red banner on /admin — a schema mismatch once froze the corpus for weeks without a visible symptom.

title: Research Desk restyle for /admin and market pages
details: The internal dashboard and market landing pages now match the site's Research Desk design system.

title: How-it-works page
details: The proof, method, sample exhibit, and FAQ moved to a standalone /how-it-works page with FAQ structured data.

title: Per-type comp fields for every asset class
details: Office, Retail, Multifamily, Land, and Residential each request their own extra comp fields (building class, anchor tenant, units, acreage, beds/baths…), joining Industrial's clear height and dock doors.

title: Corpus-first retrieval
details: On a cache miss the server reuses comps already harvested for that market before paying for a fresh web search — cutting the search budget when coverage is strong.

title: Search calibration quick wins
details: Recommended lookback by property type, market-radius calibration, and the search radius shown on reports.

title: Pro Analysis Toolkit
details: Debt & refi check (DSCR, LTV, refi headroom), sensitivity matrix, rent roll & rollover with WALT, shared assumptions layer, Report/Analysis tabs, and a 3-sheet XLSX export — analysis cards unlock with a free account.

title: Broker profiles and admin review
details: Pending comp submissions are approved/rejected on /admin; contributing brokers get opt-in public profile pages and visible credit on verified comps.

title: Market intelligence on market pages
details: Deal-date trend chart, live stats, and quarter block built from the comp corpus; watchlist feed medians gained direction.

title: Accounts + My Desk
details: Email+password accounts with a server-synced portfolio (value-snapshot history per re-run) and a market watchlist fed by the comp corpus. Search stays open to visitors.

title: Fullscreen map and busy-report fixes
details: Fixed the invisible fullscreen map (the "frozen website" bug) and truncated-JSON search failures on busy reports.

title: Permanent comp corpus
details: Every search's comps are harvested into a durable corpus — the raw-data layer that broker verification and retrieval build on.

title: Three-approach value reconciliation
details: The value estimate presents as a labeled reconciliation (comps, income, DCF) and the report section moved onto the Research Desk system.

title: DCF hold-or-sell card
details: A discounted-cash-flow card with four editable assumptions joins the report; billed searches now confirm the address first.

title: Market Explorer
details: Market pages generate on demand from the landing search, and ordinary report searches publish market snapshots too.

title: Landing redesign — Research Desk
details: The full redesign: cut-card logo, serif hero, stat strip, report exhibit, method section, navy footer. Funnel gaps closed with lead follow-up emails and market FAQs.

title: One unified report
details: The owner-mode/comps-mode split merged into a single report that answers and proves: value hero with automatic SF lookup, market summary, position chart, comp map, sortable table.

title: Analytics dashboard, share links, and market SEO pages
details: PII-free analytics at /admin, shareable report links, programmatic market landing pages, plus a 7-day search cache and a daily spend cap.

title: Owner valuation mode and trust badges
details: "What This Building Is Worth" hero with automatic building-size lookup and per-comp source-confidence badges (Verified / Public record / Listing / News / Estimate).

title: Report typography and design tokens
details: Comp-package numbering, muted map, consolidated design tokens, wider desktop layout, and plain-English labels.

title: Rebrand to CompNinja
details: The site moved off Adler Industrial branding to the owner's independent CompNinja brand.

title: Lead capture, broker submissions, and durable storage
details: Email-gated exports, the broker comp-submission flow with a verified comp layer, Supabase storage with file fallbacks, owner email notifications, and site SEO.

title: Comp map and search controls
details: Interactive comp map, lookback and transaction-type controls, value range, and the Residential property type.

title: Source links, saved reports, and filtering
details: Per-comp source links, locally saved reports, sale/lease filtering, recent searches, and per-IP rate limiting.

title: Market Comp Puller v1
details: Initial launch: address + property type in, a comp report out — Claude with web search behind a zero-dependency Node proxy.

title: A one-page P&L to hand to someone, separate from the working ledger
details: `node ledger/statement.js` writes CompNinja-Profit-and-Loss.xlsx: a Statement of Profit and Loss with a title block, five expense lines, accounting-convention parentheses, numbered notes, and a Supporting Detail sheet listing every transaction behind the summary. It reads the same ledger/*.csv files as ledger.js, so the two documents cannot disagree. It is deliberately a different document from CompNinja-Ledger.xlsx rather than a sheet inside it. The ledger is a working tool — fifteen categories, a transactions register, live formulas, warning text — and that is exactly what makes it the wrong thing to hand someone. The statement collapses those categories into five a reader recognises, on the rule that whoever presents it has to be able to explain every number out loud; a statement its author cannot defend is worth less than a simpler one they can. Internal distinctions that would invite a question without informing the answer (blended vs marginal search cost, tokens vs web-search fees) sum into one honest line and stay in the ledger. Same reasoning fixed a leak in add-month.js, which was writing "production (unsplit)" into the description column — bookkeeping vocabulary that reaches the Supporting Detail page. Descriptions are now plain and the split status lives in notes.

title: An expense typed into the ledger's CSV could vanish without a word
details: manual-entries.csv is meant to be hand-edited, and the natural editor for a CSV is a spreadsheet — but Excel rewrites dates in its own locale on save, turning 2026-08-01 into 8/1/26. That is not an ISO date, so the row failed `new Date()` and hit a bare `continue`: the expense simply never appeared in the ledger, with nothing anywhere saying so. Silent loss is the worst failure a set of books can have, because the total still looks plausible. Dates now parse in ISO and US spreadsheet forms (two-digit years included, rejecting impossible dates rather than letting Date roll 2026-13-45 into another month), a UTF-8 BOM is stripped so Excel's saved header does not become an unreadable first column, and every remaining skip — unparseable amount, unknown category, date outside the window — names the row and its description in the warnings block instead of dropping it quietly. Unknown categories were the other silent case: a typo'd category matched no SUMIFS and totalled nowhere while still looking entered.

title: The ledger workbook arrived blank on someone else's Excel
details: Every formula in the generated workbook shipped without a cached value — 101 of them — on the assumption that calcPr fullCalcOnLoad would make Excel compute them at open. It does not when Excel is not allowed to calculate, and an .xlsx arriving as an email attachment opens in Protected View, where calculation is off. The first time the file reached a Windows machine every figure rendered as an empty cell. This survived verification because both checking tools — openpyxl and the `formulas` engine — evaluate formulas themselves, so neither could see what a reader without calculation would get. Nothing was wrong with the arithmetic; the file just never carried its answers. The writer now emits <f> and <v> together, with every value computed in JS alongside the formula that expresses it, so the sheet reads correctly in Protected View, in Numbers, in a mail preview pane — and stays live for editing. Verified by diffing all 101 cached values against a full recalculation of the same file: zero mismatches.

title: A financial ledger that reads the Anthropic bill instead of guessing at it
details: `node ledger/ledger.js` writes CompNinja-Ledger.xlsx: revenue in, money out, net profit per month. The searching cost — the biggest line — comes from the Admin Usage & Cost API (GET /v1/organizations/cost_report), which returns the same billed amounts the Console's Cost page shows, split into tokens vs web search vs code execution.
