Revenue and processing fees come from Stripe's balance_transactions in one call, since gross, fee and net all ride the same object. Fixed costs live in two hand-edited CSVs. The Console dashboard page itself cannot be linked to a spreadsheet — it is a login-gated web page with nothing for Excel to connect to — so the API is the only honest automation, and it needs an sk-ant-admin key on an ORGANIZATION account (the Admin API is unavailable to individual accounts). Without one the ledger still runs, estimating from analytics at COST_REPORT_SEARCH the way /admin's tiles already do, and tags every such row `estimate` so a guess can never be read as an invoice. Costs are stored negative so every subtotal is a plain SUM, and a cost typed positive in the CSVs is negated by category — that mistake would otherwise turn an expense into revenue. The Summary sheet is live SUMIFS over the Transactions sheet with 200 spare rows inside the range, so hand-typed entries update the P&L without re-running anything. Zero npm dependencies held: ledger/xlsx.js writes the .xlsx from Node's own zlib, and the whole P&L was verified by recalculating the generated formulas in an independent Excel engine. Scoping came out of the first real connection attempt: the cost report covers the WHOLE organization, so in a shared org another project's spend lands in CompNinja's ledger indistinguishable from its own once summed. The fetch now always groups by workspace_id, warns when more than one workspace is billing, and takes --workspace to scope it (--list-workspaces to find the id). The same attempt showed the fallback reporting "ANTHROPIC_ADMIN_KEY is not set" when it was set but rejected — two states with completely different fixes — so the reason is now passed in, and a key that doesn't start sk-ant-admin is caught before twelve round-trips end in an unhelpful 401. Phase 2 is now a command rather than a procedure: `node ledger/add-month.js 2026-06 --tokens 3.90 --search 0.74` writes the correctly-shaped rows itself. Doing it by hand meant typing an em dash inside a category name, getting the sign right, and remembering to EDIT a month-to-date line instead of adding a second one — three silent wrong-number bugs, none of them interesting. Re-running a month REPLACES its rows, which is what makes correcting a partial month after it closes safe; only rows carrying the tool's own auto:console marker are ever touched. Then the split that makes cost-per-search mean anything: CompNinja is built by four people whose Claude tooling bills to the same organization as the production server, so the Console's all-keys total is not the cost of serving a customer. One month read more than twice its true marginal cost on that basis. The split turned out not to be makeable — the org has ~10 keys and production cannot be isolated on the Cost page — so all-keys is the working basis and the row is now labelled "AI cost per billed search (blended)", with a Summary note saying it includes R&D and is an upper bound rather than the marginal cost to price against. The machinery for a real split (an AI — development operating category, --prod-tokens/--prod-search) is in place for whenever a dedicated production key exists.

title: Every search now records how long it took and why
details: A live search ran 102 seconds against a 70-second local baseline and nothing could say where the time went: per-search timing existed only as a console line in the host's ephemeral logs, alongside the parse-rescue messages. Every billed search now records its duration, how many web searches it used, how much the model wrote, and whether a rescue layer fired, into the same PII-free analytics that already count searches (migration 012, run and verified on prod before this deploy). The /admin dashboard gained a Search speed card: typical time, slowest tenth, average search count, and rescue tallies over the last seven days. Nothing about search behavior changed; this is the measurement that decides the next speed move (host upgrade, tighter search budgets, corpus warming) instead of guessing.

title: Deploying is now a checklist, not a memory exercise
details: The deploy flow has enough sharp edges to have earned each one a scar: migrations that must run before the code that needs them, a 30-day cache that serves the old report shape to anyone verifying on a previously searched address, live CSS that stays stale for five minutes, a shared working tree where a careless git add sweeps another session's work, and a main branch that regularly holds commits dev-hub doesn't. All of it now lives in a project skill (.claude/skills/deploy) as one ordered twelve-step checklist with a common-mistakes table. Built test-first: a fresh agent was asked to deploy without the skill (it reconstructed most of the flow from CLAUDE.md but missed the CI check, the main-branch sync, and named the wrong Supabase project), then with it (followed in order, and surfaced five ambiguities around concurrent sessions that were patched and re-verified, including whose unlogged migration is whose). Ship-time counterpart to the build-time add-comp-field skill.

title: The valuation now gets graded against sales it did not see
details: Every priced corpus sale is held out and re-valued from the comps that sold before it in the same market and type, and /admin reports the median error, how often the actual price lands inside the range, and how wide that range is. Nothing had ever measured whether the weighting and reconciliation produce the right number. Getting there meant extracting the valuation core out of index.html into a shared valuation.js, so the harness runs the same arithmetic the report does rather than a copy that could drift.

title: The accuracy backtest was letting a building value itself
details: A whole-branch review of the backtest above found its address key only lowercased and collapsed whitespace, so a building the model spelled two different ways across two searches (an abbreviated street suffix, a transposed zip) read as two different properties. The real corpus held exactly that: one Caldwell, ID warehouse harvested four ways, three of them scoring as independent subjects each valued partly from itself, at a suspiciously perfect 0.0% error apiece. That inflated the published headline in the flattering direction on the one number meant to be trusted (median error read 15.6% instead of the true 19.3%; Industrial read 3.4% instead of 9.4%). Fixed two ways: the key now folds the street line's common suffixes and directionals ('Lane' and 'Ln' collapse together, so does a trailing zip typo, since only the text before the first comma is kept), and a second, independent check treats two rows as the same property whenever size and total price match exactly, because suffix folding alone was never going to catch every spelling variant. A related bug in the same function: a subject's peer set could hold the same OTHER building twice if it had been harvested more than once, pulling the weighted band toward that one sale's price twice over; peers now collapse to one row per key, keeping whichever copy sits closest to the subject's own sale date. Also fixed in the same pass: /valuation.js was cached for five minutes while index.html is never cached at all, and index.html's entire front end depends on valuation.js loading first -- a stale or missing copy would abort the whole page silently. It is now served with no caching, and the static-file route was made query-string tolerant so the standard cache-busting trick doesn't 404 it.

title: Reports can be shared with named people instead of the whole internet
details: A share now has an owner, an audience and an off switch. Invited clients sign in with the address they were invited at; the link can be revoked. A broker's private vault comps travel as anonymized basis rows, so the client's valuation matches the broker's to the dollar without an address leaving the vault, and full detail is a per-share opt-in.

title: Your firm's mark on the reports you send
details: Pro members can put a logo, firm name, preparer, phone, email, licence number and their own note on every report, on screen, in print, in the PNG and in both file exports. A report shared with a client carries the sender's mark, snapshotted when it was sent. CompNinja stays named as the author of the valuation, and the automated-estimate line survives every configuration.

title: Gut check: your numbers vs the market, on /vault
details: Per market + property type, your median $/SF and cap rates compared against public corpus quartiles and model market figures, each labeled with its source and date. Comps priced far outside the band get an outlier marker. Untrended, and framed as worth-a-look — your own records may be the better data. Private comps never leave your browser for this: the server sends only public benchmarks.

title: Gut check follow-ups from review
details: An undisclosed-price sale's cap rate now counts toward your cap-rate median (it was silently dropped; only the $/SF median needs a price). Benchmark buckets resolve concurrently instead of one at a time. The benchmarks-unavailable note no longer renders above an empty filtered table.

title: 1031 exchange guide at /1031-exchange
details: The exchange workflow in plain English — engage a qualified intermediary before closing, identify in writing within 45 days, close within 180 — plus a deadline-dates widget that runs entirely in your browser, the identification rules, and the ways exchanges commonly fail. Written for owners weighing a sale and for brokers to hand to clients. Educational only, never tax advice, and the tests enforce exactly that.

title: BOV tracker on /vault (v4 slice 2)
details: The broker's private practice log: every BOV from any source, statuses open/delivered/won/lost, tiles for this year, open, delivered and win rate. Intro requests auto-log; the rest is a small form. Vault-class privacy: DB-only, user-scoped, invisible to every owner surface.

title: Reports assemble on screen while the model writes
details: The 40-70s write phase now fills the real report: value hero as a counts-only placeholder, market summary, and comp table rows appearing as each comp streams. No dollar figures until the final render; cache hits and buffered streams behave exactly as before.

title: PNG export was a blank image
details: The report's entrance animations start every card at opacity 0 and rely on the animation to fade it in; html2canvas clones the page without running animations, so the whole capture painted transparent, at full size. The exporter now forces the cards opaque inside the clone. Print/PDF was never affected. Long-standing: the rule dates to early July.

title: Dead source links demote a comp's badge before anyone sees it
details: Each fresh report now checks its comps' source URLs (bot-walled hosts exempt, one 2.5s budget). A link that is already dead at harvest time was probably never real, so that comp's badge drops to Estimate everywhere at once: the served report, the cache, and the permanent corpus. Links that rot later change nothing.

title: Outlier comps get a quiet flag while you curate
details: A sale comp priced more than 25% outside the report's own value band now carries a small chip saying so, next to its Exclude button. It is a curation aid for you only: it never prints, never exports, and never appears on a shared link. The same 25% rule the vault gut check uses.

title: Search quality can finally be measured instead of guessed at
details: A new eval harness runs a fixed set of 12 addresses through real searches and scores what came back: how many priced sale comps, whether a valuation was possible at all, how good the sources were, how many comps sat outside the window or the market. Two runs can be compared, so a model upgrade or a prompt change is now a decision with numbers behind it. Nothing customer-facing changed.

title: A thin market can borrow its neighbors' comps
details: Searches in a small city now draw on comps already gathered in the cities immediately around it, so a Meridian report can start from what we know about Boise instead of from nothing. They are offered as candidates only: the model is told to prefer a comp in the target's own city, to use a neighbor only when the target is thin, and to report each address exactly as it stands, so the report always shows where a comp really is. The number of live searches a report runs is unchanged.

title: Comped Pro for beta testers with a shared passkey
details: A signed-in visitor can redeem a code in the pricing modal for full Pro access — everything except the private broker vault. Separate from the admin key, which also unlocks the internal dashboards. The grant is stored on the account, so it follows a tester across devices and one tester can be revoked without changing the code for everyone.

title: Vault funnel on /admin, and CSV exports can no longer carry live formulas
details: Two smaller hardening passes. The vault now logs four PII-free funnel events (page visit by outcome, template download, import by outcome) and /admin shows them as their own card, so with zero uploads to date the question of WHERE brokers fall off — never finding /vault, the Pro gate, or a refused import — finally has an answer; the events deliberately carry no market, since a broker’s markets are their private book. And every CSV the app emits (vault export, admin lead/corpus/submission downloads, the contacts book) now neutralizes cells starting with =, +, - or @, which Excel would otherwise execute as formulas; plain numbers are exempt so exported longitudes still re-import cleanly.
